nodes.name: The 13th Floor Elevators
nodes.description: Austin, Texas psychedelic rock group formed in 1965 around Roky Erickson, Tommy Hall, and Stacy Sutherland; Hall’s amplified jug and Erickson’s vocals helped define their sound. The band disbanded in 1969.

nodes.name: 3 Steps Ahead
nodes.description: Dutch gabber/hardcore alias of producer Peter-Paul Pigmans, initially developed with Rob Fabrie and Ed Bout before Pigmans continued under the name as a solo act. “Drop It” became one of the act’s best-known tracks; Pigmans died in 2003.
nodes.phaseNote: Career period is the documented 3 Steps Ahead project era, not Pigmans’s full life or later posthumous reissues. No popularity phase is inferred from sparse discography references.

nodes.name: A Tribe Called Quest
nodes.description: Queens hip-hop group whose jazz- and soul-sampled production, Afrocentric themes, and playful, thoughtful lyrics broadened the sound and subject matter of early-1990s rap. The group formed in the mid-1980s, released a final album in 2016, and gave its last performances in 2017.

nodes.name: AC/DC
nodes.description: Australian hard rock band formed in Sydney in November 1973 by brothers Malcolm and Angus Young. Its blues-rock roots and hard-rock identity overlap with heavy metal, though the band has described its music as rock and roll.

nodes.name: Acen
nodes.description: English electronic producer Acen Razvi, a key Production House artist in the UK breakbeat-hardcore/rave scene. His 1991 single “Close Your Eyes” and 1992 “Trip II the Moon” became major dance-chart records; he later released music under other names and returned to the Acen name.

nodes.name: Africa 70
nodes.description: Fela Kuti’s Nigerian Afrobeat ensemble, renamed Africa 70 from Nigeria 70 on 1 January 1971. The band became a major live draw in West Africa; the ensemble name was changed to Egypt 80 around 1980–81.

nodes.name: Afrika Bambaataa
nodes.description: South Bronx DJ, producer, and hip-hop organizer, known for early-1970s community parties, the Universal Zulu Nation, and 1982’s “Planet Rock,” which helped shape electro and hip-hop. His legacy is also affected by multiple sexual-abuse allegations. He publicly denied earlier allegations; in a separate 2021 civil suit he did not appear, and a default judgment was entered in 2025. One earlier accuser later recanted his claim in 2024, so these matters must not be conflated.

nodes.name: Ahn Sook-sun

period.estimateNote: Approximate career placement around the 1960s: Korea.net described more than 55 years of singing in 2015, and the Korea Times documents theater and hotel performances before 1979. The first professional performance year is not established.

nodes.description: South Korean pansori singer and master performer of gugak, also trained in gayageum byeongchang. She performed in theaters and hotels before joining the National Changgeuk Company in 1979, and later performed the full repertory of pansori works and received national intangible-heritage recognition.

nodes.name: Air
nodes.description: French electronic duo AIR, formed in Versailles by Nicolas Godin and Jean-Benoît Dunckel. They combine analog synthesizers, electronic production, pop melody, and filmic atmosphere; their international breakthrough came with Moon Safari (1998).

nodes.name: Alban Berg
nodes.description: Austrian composer of the Second Viennese School. After beginning study with Arnold Schoenberg in 1904, Berg developed a personal synthesis of late-Romantic expressiveness, atonality, and twelve-tone technique; Wozzeck established his wider reputation after its 1925 premiere.

nodes.name: Albert Ayler
nodes.description: Saxophonist whose forceful, spiritually charged playing became central to 1960s free jazz.

nodes.name: Ali Akbar Khan
nodes.description: Indian Hindustani classical musician and composer, widely recognized as a leading sarod virtuoso. His public career began in the 1930s; he later brought Indian classical music to new US audiences, recorded there in 1955, and founded the Ali Akbar College of Music.

nodes.name: Alice Coltrane
nodes.description: American jazz pianist, organist, harpist, composer, bandleader, and spiritual teacher. After early-1960s bebop work, she joined John Coltrane’s group in 1966 and developed an expansive solo sound using harp, organ, Indian instruments, and devotional material; she continued recording spiritual music after stepping back from secular jazz.

nodes.name: Alison Krauss
nodes.description: American singer, fiddler, and bluegrass bandleader whose work spans traditional bluegrass, country, folk, and cross-genre collaborations. She began public performances as a child, joined Union Station in 1986, and continues to record and tour.

nodes.name: Altern-8
nodes.description: Stafford electronic rave act formed by Mark Archer and Chris Peat, initially as an outlet alongside Nexus 21. Their original early-1990s run mixed breakbeats, heavy bass, samples, and visual pranks; Archer later revived the name for live shows and new releases.

nodes.name: Alton Ellis
nodes.description: Jamaican singer, songwriter, and pianist whose work bridged ska, rocksteady, and reggae. He began recording with Eddy Perkins as Alton & Eddie in 1959; his 1960s rocksteady recordings helped define the style, and he continued recording after relocating to the UK.

nodes.name: Amon Düül II
nodes.description: Munich group that grew out of the Amon Düül art commune in 1968 and became one of krautrock’s leading improvising rock bands with albums such as Yeti. It disbanded in 1981; later reunions include 1995 and activity from 2010.

nodes.name: Andy C
nodes.description: English drum-and-bass DJ, producer, and co-founder of RAM Records with Ant Miles. He became a central figure through early releases and high-profile DJ sets, while RAM grew into a major drum-and-bass label.

nodes.name: Anton Webern
nodes.description: Austrian composer, conductor, and musicologist whose concise, intensely organized works became influential in modernist and serial music. The earliest surviving compositions date from 1899; later study with Arnold Schoenberg beginning in 1904 shaped his development. His music was marginalized under Nazi rule and gained wider recognition after his death.

nodes.name: Aphex Twin
nodes.description: Richard D. James’s electronic music project, whose first record appeared in 1991; known for work spanning ambient, techno, and experimental electronic music.

nodes.name: Aretha Franklin
nodes.description: American gospel-rooted singer and pianist whose 1967 Atlantic recordings, including “Respect,” became defining soul music and a major civil-rights era soundtrack.

phases.note: Atlantic breakthrough is well documented; this label and intensity are editorial, not a measured popularity series.
Move to Arista marks a label and repertoire transition; it is not a quantitative popularity threshold.
Mid-1980s crossover resurgence is an editorial career phase; no numeric popularity measure implied.

nodes.phaseNote: Career phases mark documented career transitions, especially the Columbia-to-Atlantic breakthrough and later Arista era. Prominence shades are editorial approximations, not measured popularity. Posthumous listening is not modeled.

nodes.name: Armand van Helden
nodes.description: American house DJ and producer who emerged from Boston’s club scene and became internationally known through 1990s house productions and remixes.

nodes.name: Armando
nodes.description: Chicago DJ and producer Armando Gallop, a formative acid-house figure known for hardware-driven tracks including “Land of Confusion” and “151.”

nodes.name: Armin van Buuren
nodes.description: Dutch DJ, producer, and radio host whose long-running A State of Trance program and productions made him a prominent figure in trance.

nodes.name: Art Blakey
nodes.description: Drummer whose Jazz Messengers became a defining hard-bop ensemble and a training ground for younger musicians.

nodes.name: Artful Dodger
nodes.description: Southampton UK garage and 2-step production duo of Mark Hill and Pete Devereux, whose late-1990s productions and Craig David collaborations brought the style into the UK charts.

nodes.name: Astor Piazzolla
nodes.description: Argentine composer and bandoneón player who reshaped tango through works combining tango traditions with jazz and classical elements.

nodes.name: Astral Projection
nodes.description: Israeli electronic duo Avi Nissim and Lior Perlmutter, whose earlier SFX production partnership fed into Astral Projection and the Goa/psychedelic trance scene.

nodes.name: Astrud Gilberto
nodes.description: Brazilian-American singer whose English-language performance on “The Girl from Ipanema” helped carry bossa nova to international audiences; she later built a solo recording career.

nodes.name: At the Drive-In
nodes.description: El Paso post-hardcore band whose intense touring and 2000 album Relationship of Command made it one of the era’s defining alternative rock acts; the band later reunited.

nodes.name: Autechre
nodes.description: English electronic music duo Rob Brown and Sean Booth, part of Warp’s catalog; their sound grew from Manchester-area underground electro into intricate, experimental electronic music.

nodes.name: Avicii
nodes.description: Swedish DJ and producer Tim Bergling, known as Avicii, whose melodic electronic dance productions reached global pop audiences before his death in 2018.

nodes.name: Babes Wodumo
nodes.description: South African singer and dancer Bongekile Simelane, a prominent gqom performer whose 2016 hit “Wololo” brought her national recognition.

nodes.name: Johann Sebastian Bach
nodes.description: German Baroque composer whose sacred, orchestral, and keyboard works unite intricate counterpoint with expressive harmony.

nodes.name: Bad Bunny
nodes.description: Puerto Rican singer and rapper Benito Antonio Martínez Ocasio, known as Bad Bunny, who emerged through online releases and became a major figure in Latin trap and reggaeton.

nodes.name: Baltimora
nodes.description: Milan-based Italo disco and synth-pop studio project created by producer Maurizio Bassi and fronted on stage by Northern Irish singer and dancer Jimmy McShane; best known for “Tarzan Boy.”

nodes.name: Basic Channel
nodes.description: Berlin duo and label of Moritz von Oswald and Mark Ernestus, linked to the Hard Wax record shop. Its cryptic 1993–94 twelve-inch singles helped establish dub techno and minimal techno.

nodes.name: Bauhaus
nodes.description: English post-punk band whose 1979 single “Bela Lugosi’s Dead” became a touchstone of gothic rock; the original group disbanded in 1983 and reunited intermittently.

nodes.name: B.B. King
nodes.description: Mississippi-born blues singer and guitarist who began recording in Memphis in 1949 and became the model for jazz-inflected urban blues guitar, playing hundreds of shows a year well into old age. He had performed locally since the early 1940s.

nodes.name: Bee Gees
nodes.description: Australian-British sibling vocal group whose close harmonies and songwriting spanned pop, soul, and disco; the Saturday Night Fever soundtrack made them central to late-1970s disco.
nodes.phaseNote: The group began its Australian activity in 1958, achieved international success in 1967 and reached a major peak with Saturday Night Fever in 1977. The original trio ended in 2003; surviving-member appearances were intermittent. No complete prominence curve is assigned.

nodes.name: Beenie Man
nodes.description: Jamaican dancehall deejay and singer Moses Davis, known as Beenie Man, who began recording as a child and later became an internationally prominent dancehall artist.

nodes.name: Ludwig van Beethoven
nodes.description: Composer whose symphonies, sonatas, and quartets bridge Classical forms and Romantic expression.

nodes.name: Belleville Three
nodes.description: Juan Atkins, Derrick May and Kevin Saunderson, high-school friends from Belleville, Michigan, who shaped Detroit techno in the 1980s through mixtapes and their labels Metroplex, Transmat and KMS. Mostly a shared label for parallel careers, the trio reunited on stage as the Belleville Three in 2017.

nodes.name: Benga
nodes.description: South London producer and DJ Adegbenga “Benga” Adejumo, an early dubstep contributor whose 2002 “Skank” was an early release on Croydon’s Big Apple label.

nodes.name: Benny Goodman
nodes.description: American jazz clarinetist and bandleader whose early professional work led to a nationally prominent swing orchestra and the 1935 Palomar Ballroom breakthrough.

nodes.name: Beyoncé
nodes.description: Houston singer who rose to fame with Destiny’s Child in the late 1990s and went solo with Dangerously in Love (2003), which won the Grammy for Best Contemporary R&B Album. She began performing in the early-1990s group that became Destiny’s Child.

nodes.name: Bhimsen Joshi
nodes.description: Indian Hindustani classical vocalist of the Kirana gharana, noted for khayal and devotional repertoire; his documented public performance career began in 1941.

nodes.name: Bill Monroe
nodes.description: American singer, mandolinist, and bandleader widely known as the “Father of Bluegrass.” After early-1930s radio work with his brothers, he formed the Blue Grass Boys in 1938; the classic ensemble sound crystallized in the mid-1940s.

nodes.name: Billie Holiday
nodes.description: Jazz singer whose rhythmic phrasing and expressive interpretation reshaped popular-song performance. Began singing in Harlem clubs around 1930–31 and recorded from 1933 through 1959.

nodes.name: Black Sabbath
nodes.description: Birmingham heavy metal band, first known as Earth, whose dark, heavily amplified sound helped define early heavy metal; its final performance with Ozzy Osbourne was in 2025.

nodes.name: Blackpink
nodes.description: South Korean girl group formed by YG Entertainment; their official public debut came with the SQUARE ONE single album on August 8, 2016.

nodes.name: Blake Baxter
nodes.description: Detroit techno producer and DJ of the first wave, nicknamed “The Prince of Techno”, who recorded for KMS and Underground Resistance.

nodes.name: blink-182
nodes.description: American pop-punk band formed in Southern California in 1992; their independent 1995 debut album Cheshire Cat helped build an early following before major-label success.

nodes.name: Blur
nodes.description: English rock band formed in London in 1988, initially as Seymour; their 1990 debut single preceded the 1990s Britpop breakthrough.

nodes.name: Bob Dylan
nodes.description: American singer-songwriter whose early-1960s Greenwich Village folk work developed into a wide-ranging recording career; recipient of the 2016 Nobel Prize in Literature.

nodes.name: Bob Marley
nodes.description: Jamaican singer and songwriter whose recording career began in 1961 and whose group the Wailing Wailers formed in 1963; his work helped bring reggae to a global audience.

nodes.name: Bobby Orlando
nodes.description: American songwriter, producer and independent label founder Bobby Orlando, a key figure in 1980s Hi-NRG and electronic dance pop.

nodes.name: Boom Shaka
nodes.description: South African kwaito group formed by Junior Sokhela, Lebo Mathosa, Theo Nhlengethwa and Thembi Seete; its early-1990s singles and performance style helped popularize the genre. The group later reunited.

nodes.name: The Brand New Heavies
nodes.description: Ealing, London band among the first acts on the Acid Jazz label, whose funk-and-soul grooves helped carry acid jazz into the early-1990s charts.

nodes.name: Brian Eno
nodes.description: English musician, producer and visual artist who first came to prominence as a founding member of Roxy Music, then developed an influential solo and production career spanning ambient and experimental music.

nodes.name: Bring Me the Horizon
nodes.description: Sheffield rock band formed in 2004, whose sound has shifted from early deathcore through metalcore toward broader alternative and electronic styles.

nodes.name: BTS
nodes.description: South Korean group that debuted under Big Hit Entertainment in June 2013, initially with a hip-hop focus and later across a wider range of pop and R&B styles.

nodes.name: Burial
nodes.description: English electronic producer associated with dubstep, whose anonymous early releases on Hyperdub helped shape the sound’s introspective, sample-based branch.

nodes.name: Burna Boy
nodes.description: Nigerian singer and songwriter Damini Ogulu, known as Burna Boy, whose 2012 single “Like to Party” introduced him widely and preceded the 2013 debut album L.I.F.E.

nodes.name: Burzum
nodes.description: Norwegian black metal solo recording project created by Varg Vikernes; the name was adopted in 1991, with the first album released in 1992. The catalogue includes a later return to music.

nodes.name: Calypso Rose
nodes.description: Tobagonian calypsonian Linda McCartha Sandy-Lewis, known as Calypso Rose, who began performing in calypso tents as a teenager and became a leading songwriter and performer. She won Trinidad’s Road March in 1977 and Calypso Monarch in 1978.

nodes.name: Ras Shorty I

period.estimateNote: RBMA says charges following his 1973 Calypso Monarch finals performance capped his first decade of career activity. The 1960s start is inferred, not a documented debut; the latest activity documented in the reviewed sources is the 1999 Jamoo Victory album, making 1999 an approximate period end rather than a confirmed career-cessation date.

nodes.description: Trinidadian calypsonian Garfield Blackman, first known as Lord Shorty, was a pioneer in soca’s emergence. He later adopted the name Ras Shorty I and developed faith-based Jamoo music; soca’s origins involved multiple contributors.

nodes.name: Machel Montano

period.estimateNote: A 2023 Caribbean Beat feature describes a 40-year career, implying an approximate early-1980s anchor; a 2009 profile says he rose as a child star but gives no start year.

nodes.description: Trinidadian soca performer who rose as a child star and built a long-running career incorporating varied musical influences and cross-genre collaborations.

nodes.name: Can
nodes.description: Cologne group formed in 1968 by Holger Czukay, Irmin Schmidt, Michael Karoli and Jaki Liebezeit, combining tape editing, jazz-trained metronomic drumming, and long group improvisations. Its main run ended in 1979, followed by sporadic reunions through 1999.

nodes.name: Candlemass
nodes.description: Swedish epic doom metal band formed by bassist and songwriter Leif Edling in 1984; their 1986 album Epicus Doomicus Metallicus became a landmark of the style.

nodes.name: Cannibal Corpse
nodes.description: American death metal band formed in Buffalo, New York, in 1988; their 1990 debut Eaten Back to Life established their recording career before they relocated to Florida.

nodes.name: Carl Craig
nodes.description: Second-wave Detroit polymath, May's protégé — stretched techno toward jazz and orchestras on Planet E.

nodes.name: Carlos Vives
nodes.description: Colombian singer, songwriter and actor whose recording career began with 1986 pop album Por Fuera y Por Dentro; his 1993 Clásicos de la Provincia fused vallenato with contemporary pop and brought international recognition.

nodes.name: Carpenter Brut
nodes.description: French electronic music project by an anonymous producer, combining synthwave, horror-film soundtracks, metal and electronic dance music; its first EP appeared in 2012.

nodes.name: Cassius
nodes.description: Cassius is the French electronic duo of Philippe Zdar and Hubert “Boom Bass” Blanc-Francard, associated with French touch. The project began in 1996 under an earlier name; Blanc-Francard continued Cassius after Zdar’s death in 2019.

nodes.name: Cecil Taylor
nodes.description: Pianist and composer known for percussive intensity and freely structured improvisation.

nodes.name: Celia Cruz
nodes.description: Celia Cruz was a Cuban singer whose career included Cuban dance music, guaracha, and internationally prominent salsa. She joined La Sonora Matancera in 1949/1950 and became a defining salsa performer.

nodes.name: Cesária Évora

period.estimateNote: Broad career start based on biographies placing her first singing in local bars at sixteen; the exact year is not established. End reflects her death.

nodes.description: Cabo Verdean singer whose performances helped bring morna to international audiences; widely known as the “Queen of Morna.”

nodes.name: Bana

period.estimateNote: Broad start marker: biographies place the beginning of his musical career during the 1950s; no exact first performance is established. End reflects his death.

nodes.description: Cabo Verdean singer known as the “King of Morna” and a prominent performer of the tradition.

nodes.name: Ildo Lobo

period.estimateNote: Broad career start for his work as vocalist with Os Tubarões; his solo album Nôs Morna (1996) is a later documented milestone, not his debut. End reflects his death.

nodes.description: Cabo Verdean vocalist known for his morna performances, including the album “Nôs Morna” (1996), and for his work with Os Tubarões.

nodes.name: Charlie Parker
nodes.description: Alto saxophonist whose melodic and harmonic innovations were central to bebop.

nodes.name: The Chemical Brothers
nodes.description: The Chemical Brothers are British electronic duo Tom Rowlands and Ed Simons, formed in Manchester in 1989. They initially worked as the Dust Brothers; their first track, “Song to the Siren,” helped launch their recording career before they adopted the Chemical Brothers name.

nodes.name: Cheng Yanqiu
nodes.description: Cheng Yanqiu was a leading Peking opera actor and founder of the Cheng school of performance, especially known for qingyi roles and a distinctive vocal style.

nodes.name: Chet Baker
nodes.description: Trumpeter and singer known for the lyrical, restrained sound of West Coast cool jazz.

nodes.name: Chic
nodes.description: Chic is an American disco and funk band formed by Nile Rodgers and Bernard Edwards in 1976, with drummer Tony Thompson, keyboardist Raymond Jones, and singer Norma Jean Wright. The group has had hiatuses and later incarnations.

nodes.name: Chief Keef
nodes.description: Chief Keef is a Chicago rapper whose viral 2011 “Bang” video and early mixtapes brought him to prominence and helped carry Chicago drill into wider attention.

nodes.name: Chitti Babu
nodes.description: Carnatic veena virtuoso from Andhra Pradesh who worked in Madras film music before building a large concert following.

nodes.name: Frédéric Chopin
nodes.description: Frédéric Chopin was a Polish composer and pianist whose early published piano music drew on Polish dance forms and whose later work shaped the Romantic piano repertoire.

nodes.name: Chuck Berry
nodes.description: Chuck Berry was an American guitarist, singer, and songwriter whose country, blues, and R&B fusion, guitar riffs, and storytelling helped define early rock and roll. His St. Louis club career began in 1953; “Maybellene” brought national recognition in 1955.

nodes.name: Clifford Brown
nodes.description: Trumpeter whose work with Max Roach is a landmark of early hard bop.

nodes.name: College
nodes.description: College is the solo electronic music project of French composer David Grellier. Its first EP, Teenage Color, and debut album, Secret Diary, were released in 2008; “A Real Hero” later brought wider recognition through the 2011 film Drive.

nodes.name: Com Truise
nodes.description: Com Truise is the electronic music project of American producer Seth Haley. His first official release, the Cyanide Sisters EP, appeared in 2010; its later Ghostly International reissue and 2011 debut album expanded the project’s reach.

nodes.name: Common
nodes.description: Common is a Chicago rapper and actor who debuted as Common Sense with the 1992 album Can I Borrow a Dollar? His early work established an underground following before later mainstream success.

nodes.name: Compay Segundo
nodes.description: Compay Segundo (Francisco Repilado) was a Cuban son singer, guitarist, clarinettist, and armónico inventor. He performed with bands from the 1920s–30s, became widely known with Los Compadres in the 1940s, and gained renewed international attention through Buena Vista Social Club in 1997.

nodes.name: Congo Natty
nodes.description: Congo Natty is the artist and label identity of British producer Michael West, also known as Rebel MC and other aliases. His career began in the late 1980s with Double Trouble’s “Street Tuff”; as Rebel MC/Congo Natty he helped shape the early UK jungle sound.

nodes.name: Converge
nodes.description: Converge is a Salem, Massachusetts band founded by vocalist Jacob Bannon and guitarist Kurt Ballou in 1990. Its first demos appeared in 1991; its first full-length, Halo in a Haystack, followed in 1994.

nodes.name: Count Basie
nodes.description: Jazz pianist and bandleader central to Kansas City swing; known for blues-inflected phrasing, a light, propulsive piano style, and distinctive big-band rhythm sections.

nodes.name: Craig David
nodes.description: English singer and songwriter who emerged from the UK garage scene.

nodes.name: Cream
nodes.description: British power trio central to blues rock. Original activity ran 1966-1968, with reunion performances in 1993 and 2005; the career envelope includes those breaks.

nodes.name: Crime Mob
nodes.description: Atlanta rap group whose crunk sound broke nationally with “Knuck If You Buck” (2004); members later reunited for performances and recordings.

nodes.name: Cybotron
nodes.description: The Detroit electronic group formed around Juan Atkins and Richard “3070” Davis, with Jon-5 joining later. Its early singles, including “Clear” and “Techno City,” connect electro, funk, and the emerging Detroit techno vocabulary; the project later resumed recording.

nodes.name: Daft Punk
nodes.description: French electronic music duo Thomas Bangalter and Guy-Manuel de Homem-Christo, whose house and dance productions helped popularize French house internationally.

nodes.name: D’Angelo
nodes.description: Virginia-born singer, multi-instrumentalist and producer whose Brown Sugar (1995), Voodoo (2000) and Black Messiah (2014) helped define neo-soul within modern R&B. He died in 2025.

nodes.name: Daniel Bell
nodes.description: Detroit-associated techno DJ and producer who recorded as DBX and helped develop minimal techno and house through stripped-back, groove-led tracks.

nodes.name: Darkthrone
nodes.description: Norwegian metal band that evolved from its early thrash and death metal roots into influential black metal, later ranging across black, thrash, doom and heavy metal.

nodes.name: Dave Brubeck
nodes.description: Pianist and composer associated with cool jazz and experiments in unusual meters.

nodes.name: David Bowie
nodes.description: English singer-songwriter, musician and actor whose work moved across pop, rock, soul, electronic and experimental styles; “Space Oddity” brought his first major chart breakthrough in 1969.

nodes.name: David Morales
nodes.description: New York house DJ, producer and remixer whose Paradise Garage work and Def Mix productions helped carry club music into wider pop and dance audiences.

nodes.name: Davido
nodes.description: Nigerian-American singer, songwriter and producer whose 2011 singles “Back When” and “Dami Duro” established his early Nigerian career; his work draws on Afrobeats, Afropop and other styles.

nodes.name: De La Soul
nodes.description: Long Island hip-hop trio whose sample-rich, playful and eclectic production became central to the alternative hip-hop identity of the Native Tongues collective.

nodes.name: deadmau5
nodes.description: Canadian electronic music producer and DJ Joel Zimmerman, known as deadmau5, associated with progressive house and techno; his early-2000s online releases preceded broader dance-scene prominence.

nodes.name: Death
nodes.description: Florida metal band led by Chuck Schuldiner, foundational to death metal; later albums developed a more technical and progressive sound. The band ceased after Schuldiner’s death in 2001.

nodes.name: Claude Debussy
nodes.description: French composer whose changing orchestral, piano and stage works used distinctive timbre and harmony to expand the musical language of the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries.

nodes.name: Deep Purple
nodes.description: British hard-rock band with a rotating lineup, formed in 1968. Their sound developed from early classical-rock experiments to the hard-rocking Mark II era; after a 1976–1984 breakup, the band reunited and continued recording and touring.

nodes.name: Deepchord
nodes.description: Detroit dub-techno project of Rod Modell (originally with Mike Schommer), later linked to the Echospace collaborations with Stephen Hitchell.

nodes.name: Depeche Mode
nodes.description: English electronic band formed in Basildon in 1980, moving from early synth-pop toward darker, more expansive electronic rock; the group remains active.

phases.note: Formation and early live activity; chart breakthrough came later.
Black Celebration marks a darker stylistic turn; Music for the Masses and the 1988 Rose Bowl show document international expansion, while the 1990–93 chart peak is independently documented.
Ultra reached No. 1 in the UK; subsequent releases show continued activity rather than a career endpoint.

nodes.phaseNote: Editorial prominence phases: early formation and synth-pop emergence; an approximate 1986–1996 peak spanning the group’s stylistic expansion and major chart successes; then an established, continuing career. Boundaries express a documented interpretation, not measured popularity or periods of inactivity.

nodes.name: Derrick May
nodes.description: Detroit DJ and producer, one of the Belleville Three. Recording as Rhythim Is Rhythim, he released “Strings of Life” on his Transmat label; his work and touring helped carry Detroit techno to international audiences.

nodes.name: Desmond Dekker
nodes.description: Jamaican singer and songwriter whose ska and rocksteady recordings with the Aces, including “007 (Shanty Town),” helped carry Jamaican music abroad; “Israelites” became an international hit.

phases.note: Jamaican recording career documented by the National Library of Jamaica.
“Israelites” reached No. 1 in the UK and the US top ten; distinguish the 1969 UK chart run from earlier Jamaican release/recording references.
Later touring and recordings continued after the 1960s peak, though chart success declined.

nodes.phaseNote: Career phases are editorial: Jamaican recording emergence from 1963, international peak around “Israelites” (UK chart peak in 1969), and continued recording and touring after the 1960s chart peak until Dekker’s death in 2006. The dates mark sourced milestones, not an exact popularity curve.

nodes.name: Dick Dale
nodes.description: American guitarist and singer, a seminal surf-rock guitarist whose loud, reverb-rich instrumental style drew on rockabilly and Middle Eastern musical influences. “Let’s Go Trippin’” (1961) and “Misirlou” (1962) became signature recordings; Pulp Fiction brought “Misirlou” to a new audience in 1994.

phases.note: Early country-bar and local-TV performance followed the family’s move to California in 1954; the decade marker is approximate.
“Let’s Go Trippin’,” the Rendezvous Ballroom shows, and the 1962 “Misirlou” recording anchor Dale’s foundational surf-guitar period.
Surf music lost mainstream favor; Dale continued recording and performing, with a major renewed audience after “Misirlou” appeared in Pulp Fiction (1994).

nodes.phaseNote: Editorial prominence phases: early local performance in the 1950s; a documented surf-guitar peak beginning with Dale’s 1961 breakthrough and 1962 recording; then a long-running career with reduced mainstream prominence and renewed attention after Pulp Fiction in 1994. Dale was a major pioneer, though “inventor of surf rock” is too exclusive a claim for a broader scene.

nodes.name: Digital Mystikz
nodes.description: South London dubstep production duo of Mala and Coki. Their first Digital Mystikz release appeared in 2003; the duo’s deep, sound-system-oriented productions and their related DMZ label and club night helped shape early dubstep.

nodes.name: Distruction Boyz
nodes.description: Durban gqom production duo of Que (Thobani Mgobhozi) and Goldmax (Zipho Mthembu). They say they began producing in 2012, reached a national audience through work on Babes Wodumo’s “Wololo” (2016), and released the gold-certified Gqom Is the Future in 2017.

nodes.name: Divine
nodes.description: American drag performer, actor, and Hi-NRG singer. His first catalogued single, “Born to Be Cheap,” was released in 1981; his 1980s dance recordings included Bobby Orlando productions and the 1984 UK Top 20 hit “You Think You’re a Man.”

nodes.name: Dizzee Rascal
nodes.description: English rapper, MC, and producer from Bow, East London, and a leading early grime artist. His 2003 debut Boy in da Corner won the Mercury Prize; later pop crossover hits included five UK No. 1 singles, followed by a return toward grime and hip-hop on Raskit (2017) and Don’t Take It Personal (2024).

phases.note: Approximate early-career period: pirate-radio MCing and joining Roll Deep in 2002 precede his first solo single.
Boy in da Corner brought grime international attention and won the 2003 Mercury Prize; mainstream chart success followed, including five UK No. 1 singles across 2008–10.
Raskit marked a return toward grime and hip-hop; subsequent releases include the 2024 album Don’t Take It Personal.

nodes.phaseNote: Editorial arc: approximate early radio/crew activity; the critical breakthrough of Boy in da Corner and a wider 2000s career that also included a major pop-chart run in 2008–10; then a return toward grime and hip-hop with continued releases. Boundaries are milestones, not a measured popularity curve.

nodes.name: Dizzy Gillespie
nodes.description: Trumpeter and composer central to bebop and the development of Afro-Cuban jazz.

nodes.name: DJ Hype
nodes.description: British DJ, producer, and label builder who emerged from Hackney reggae sound-system and pirate-radio culture. His early hardcore productions with Phivos Sebastiane as The Scientist preceded his central role in jungle and drum and bass; he later helped build Ganja and Playaz labels.

phases.note: Fantasy FM pirate-radio shows mark a public broadcast milestone; the DJ’s earlier reggae sound-system work predates this.
Hype dates jungle’s emergence to 1992–93; his 1993 “Shot in the Dark” reached pop charts, followed by Ganja Records (1994–96).
He moved into a sustained label, radio, and international DJ career through True/Real Playaz and Playaz Recordings.

nodes.phaseNote: Approximate prominence arc: pirate radio and early rave in the late 1980s; jungle’s formation and the Ganja era around 1992–96; then a long-established drum-and-bass DJ, radio, and label career. The phases mark sourced scene and career milestones, not measured popularity.

nodes.name: DJ Minx
nodes.description: Detroit DJ and producer active since the early 1990s. She founded the Women on Wax collective in 1996 and launched Women on Wax Recordings in 2001, creating platforms for women DJs and producers in the regional scene.

nodes.name: DJ Paul Elstak
nodes.description: Rotterdam DJ and producer, called the “Godfather of Hardcore”, who founded Rotterdam Records in 1992 and later scored happy-hardcore hits such as “Rainbow in the Sky”.

nodes.name: DJ Pierre
nodes.description: Chicago DJ, producer and Phuture co-founder Nathaniel Pierre Jones, known as DJ Pierre. His TB-303 experimentation with group members Herb J and Spanky helped shape acid house; the sound grew from collaborative Chicago club practice and predates Phuture’s 1987 commercial release.

nodes.name: DJ Rashad
nodes.description: Chicago footwork producer, DJ and dancer Rashad Harden, known as DJ Rashad. He came up in local dance-battle and juke scenes, co-founded the Teklife crew with DJ Spinn, and helped bring footwork to international audiences through touring and the 2013 album Double Cup.
nodes.phaseNote: No individual popularity phases added: available sources document local career beginnings and a widely recognized 2013 album, but do not measure a full career peak curve.

nodes.name: DJ Screw
nodes.description: Houston DJ and mixtape producer who developed the slowed, chopped-and-screwed style and led the Screwed Up Click.

nodes.name: DJ Shadow
nodes.description: California DJ and producer Josh Davis, known for sample-based instrumental hip-hop; released music as DJ Shadow beginning in 1991.

nodes.name: Dolly Parton
nodes.description: American singer-songwriter whose country and Appalachian roots repertoire later crossed into pop, film and bluegrass; performed publicly as a child and entered Nashville in 1964.

nodes.name: Donna Summer
nodes.description: American singer and songwriter whose European musical-theatre work preceded her mid-1970s international disco breakthrough and later pop, rock and electronic recordings.
nodes.phaseNote: The 1975 international breakthrough is documented, while her earlier career predates it. No complete prominence curve is assigned.

nodes.name: Dorival Caymmi
nodes.description: Bahian Brazilian singer-songwriter whose songs draw on Afro-Brazilian traditions and coastal life; entered professional music in the mid-1930s and recorded from 1939.

nodes.name: Dorothy Ashby
nodes.description: Detroit-born jazz harpist and composer who established the harp as a solo jazz instrument and later incorporated the Japanese koto into her work.

nodes.name: Dr. Dre
nodes.description: Compton DJ, rapper and producer whose early electro group work preceded N.W.A., Death Row and Aftermath; central to West Coast hip-hop and G-funk.

nodes.name: Drive Like Jehu
nodes.description: San Diego post-hardcore band formed by former Pitchfork members Rick Froberg and John Reis; released its debut album in 1991.

nodes.name: Duke Ellington
nodes.description: Pianist, bandleader, and composer whose orchestra expanded jazz's expressive and structural possibilities.

nodes.name: E-40
nodes.description: Vallejo rapper and entrepreneur who debuted with Most Valuable Players/The Click before a solo career that helped bring Bay Area rap to wider audiences.

nodes.name: Earl Scruggs
nodes.description: American banjo player whose three-finger style became a defining sound of bluegrass; joined Bill Monroe’s Blue Grass Boys in 1945.

nodes.name: Chief Commander Ebenezer Obey
nodes.description: Nigerian jùjú singer, guitarist and bandleader who began in Lagos bands in the 1950s and founded the International Brothers in 1964.

nodes.name: Eddie Fowlkes
nodes.description: Detroit DJ and producer associated with the first wave of Detroit techno.

nodes.name: Egyptian Lover
nodes.description: Los Angeles electro-rap DJ, producer and MC associated with Uncle Jamm’s Army and early West Coast electro; began a solo recording career in 1984.

nodes.name: Ella Fitzgerald
nodes.description: Jazz vocalist celebrated for scat improvisation and interpretations of the American songbook. Her career began with the 1934 Apollo amateur contest; the Library of Congress dates her final performance to December 1992.

nodes.name: Elvis Presley
nodes.description: American singer whose 1954 Sun recordings fused country and rhythm-and-blues sources and helped propel rock and roll to mass audiences.

nodes.name: Erik Satie
nodes.description: French composer and pianist whose early piano works emerged in the 1880s; he also worked extensively in Parisian cabaret before later avant-garde collaborations.

nodes.name: Erykah Badu
nodes.description: Dallas singer-songwriter and actor whose 1994 performance opening for D’Angelo led to her 1997 debut album, Baduizm, and prominent association with neo-soul.

nodes.name: E.T. Mensah
nodes.description: Ghanaian trumpeter, saxophonist and bandleader who joined the Accra Orchestra in 1932, led The Tempos from 1950, and became a defining dance-band highlife figure.

nodes.name: Ewan Pearson
nodes.description: English electronic music producer, remixer and DJ who released early 12-inch records under aliases Villa America and Dirtbox in 1994, later recording as Maas and Ewan Pearson.

nodes.name: Fairuz
nodes.description: Lebanese singer whose recordings and performances with the Rahbani brothers helped shape modern Lebanese and Arab popular song.

nodes.name: Fania All-Stars
nodes.description: A rotating salsa collective assembled by Fania Records in New York, bringing leading label musicians together for landmark concerts, recordings and international tours. After its core era ended in the mid-1980s, the group reunited for concerts in the late 1990s.

nodes.name: Farley "Jackmaster" Funk
nodes.description: Chicago DJ and producer whose Hot Mix 5 broadcasts from 1981 helped bring house music to a wider local audience; his mid-1980s records became early house landmarks.

nodes.name: Farrukh Fateh Ali Khan
nodes.description: Pakistani qawwali harmonium player and vocalist in Nusrat Fateh Ali Khan’s party; he remained with the ensemble through its first leadership era and continued after Nusrat’s death.

nodes.name: Fatboy Slim
nodes.description: English DJ and producer Norman Cook, also known as Fatboy Slim. After early success with the Housemartins and Beats International, his Fatboy Slim recordings helped make big beat a global dance-pop force in the late 1990s.

nodes.name: Faust
nodes.description: Hamburg group assembled in 1970 around producer Uwe Nettelbeck for Polydor, recording collage-like experimental rock at a converted school in Wümme; its 1971 debut is a krautrock landmark. The original run ended in 1975, and members revived the name from 1990.

nodes.name: Fela Kuti
nodes.description: Nigerian composer, bandleader, saxophonist and political activist whose experiments with Koola Lobitos and later bands helped shape Afrobeat. He worked with drummer Tony Allen for fifteen years; scholarship places the style’s formation in a wider Lagos scene and recognizes other contributors rather than a sole-inventor account.

phases.note: Fela moved to London to study music in 1958; his early highlife-jazz band and later recordings precede the Afrobeat name.
Africa 70 and the early-1970s Afrobeat sound mark a major career transition, not an uncontested single-artist invention.

nodes.phaseNote: Career phases distinguish early musical formation from the later Afrobeat period. Dates reflect Fela’s career, not an exclusive genre-origin claim; his collaboration with Tony Allen and the wider Lagos scene are essential context.

nodes.name: Fischerspooner
nodes.description: New York art, music and performance project founded by Warren Fischer and Casey Spooner in 1998. Its theatrical multimedia shows helped define the early electroclash moment; “Emerge” reached the UK top 40 in 2002. The project combined electronic pop, choreography, costumes and performance art.

nodes.name: Frankie Knuckles
nodes.description: New York-born DJ, producer and remixer who became a central figure in Chicago house. His Warehouse residency from 1977 helped shape the sound and gave house its name; he continued as a recording artist and remixer until his death.

nodes.name: Fugazi
nodes.description: Washington, D.C. post-hardcore band known for a self-managed, DIY approach and affordable all-ages shows. They played from 1987 through their final public performance in 2002, then entered an indefinite hiatus.

nodes.name: Future
nodes.description: Atlanta rapper and songwriter whose Auto-Tuned melodic approach helped shape 2010s trap and mainstream hip-hop. He released his first mixtapes in 2010 and broke through nationally soon after.

nodes.name: Gamelan Madu Sari
nodes.description: Vancouver community gamelan ensemble formed during Expo 86, performing Javanese repertory and new works for gamelan. Its first album of new music, New Nectar, appeared in 2004.

nodes.name: Gamelan Sekar Tunjung
nodes.description: Gamelan ensemble documented performing in Yogyakarta on the 1992 recording The Music of K.R.T. Wasitodiningrat, directed by Djoko Waluyo.

nodes.name: Gamelan Son of Lion
nodes.description: New York composers’ collective and repertory ensemble founded around Barbara Benary’s Javanese-style gamelan instruments. Gamelan Son of Lion creates contemporary music for the ensemble alongside traditional forms.

nodes.name: Gang Starr
nodes.description: New York hip-hop duo of Guru and DJ Premier, influential for jazz-inflected production, DJ cuts and socially conscious rap. Guru formed Gang Starr around 1987; his partnership with Premier began in 1989. After intermittent albums and Guru’s 2010 death, Premier issued new Gang Starr tracks using unreleased Guru verses, including 2019’s “Family and Loyalty”.

nodes.name: Gary Numan
nodes.description: English singer, songwriter and producer who first emerged with Tubeway Army before releasing solo work. His 1979 chart success with “Cars” and The Pleasure Principle helped bring synthesizer-led pop to a wide audience.

phases.note: The 1979 release and chart success of “Cars” and The Pleasure Principle anchor this phase; the prominence label is interpretive.

nodes.phaseNote: Editorial career prominence: Tubeway Army and the 1979 solo breakthrough, a quieter period, the darker sound from Sacrifice onward, and the later Savage and Intruder releases. Milestone dates are documented; these relative shades are not measured popularity.

nodes.name: Gazebo
nodes.description: Italian singer-songwriter and producer Paul Mazzolini, known as Gazebo, associated with Italo disco. His first single under the name, “Masterpiece,” appeared in 1982; “I Like Chopin” became his international breakthrough in 1983.

nodes.name: Genesis
nodes.description: British band that developed from theatrical progressive rock into a broader pop-rock sound, with multiple hiatuses and reunions.

nodes.name: George Clinton
nodes.description: Singer, songwriter and producer who formed the doo-wop group the Parliaments in 1955 and later led Parliament and Funkadelic, building the P-Funk universe of the 1970s.

nodes.name: Geto Boys
nodes.description: Houston rap group formed by Rap-A-Lot Records founder James Smith. The group became a landmark Southern hip-hop act through confrontational storytelling and later lineup changes; its final reunion plans followed Bushwick Bill’s terminal illness in 2019.

nodes.name: Giorgio Moroder
nodes.description: Italian producer, songwriter, performer and DJ whose early work in pop groups led to a successful solo career and a defining role in electronic disco. His 1969 single “Looky Looky” was an early commercial milestone; later productions helped shape synth-based dance music.

nodes.name: Goa Gil
nodes.description: American-born DJ, musician and party organizer who helped shape Goa’s psychedelic dance culture. He organized long-form beach gatherings from the 1970s and became a prominent figure in the later Goa trance and psytrance scenes.

nodes.name: Godspeed You! Black Emperor
nodes.description: Montreal post-rock collective known for long, layered instrumental compositions, orchestral ensembles and projected film. The group formed in 1994; its debut vinyl edition appeared in 1997, followed by an extended hiatus and a return to recording and touring in 2010.

nodes.name: Goldie
nodes.description: British DJ, producer and visual artist whose early releases helped shape jungle and drum and bass. He founded the Metalheadz label in 1994 and released Timeless in 1995, a landmark album that brought drum and bass to wider audiences.

phases.note: Timeless was released in September 1995 and is described as a landmark in UK dance music; the prominence label is scene-relative editorial interpretation.

nodes.phaseNote: Editorial career prominence centered on the early jungle singles and the 1995 Timeless breakthrough, followed by ongoing production and later releases. This is scene-relative editorial shading, not a ranking against mainstream artists or measured listening.

nodes.name: GosT
nodes.description: Texas electronic musician and producer James Lollar, who released music as GosT. Beginning with the 2013 Skull project, his dark synthwave work blended electronic production with horror and metal influences.

nodes.name: Grandmaster Flash and the Furious Five
nodes.description: South Bronx hip-hop group led by DJ Grandmaster Flash and the Furious Five MCs. The original lineup rose to prominence in the early 1980s, split in 1983, reunited for a 1988 album and a 1994 old-school tour.

nodes.name: Grateful Dead
nodes.description: San Francisco band that emerged from the mid-1960s psychedelic scene and became known for long-form concert improvisation, constant touring, and a fan taping culture. It ended in 1995 after Jerry Garcia’s death.

nodes.name: Gravediggaz
nodes.description: New York hip-hop supergroup formed by Prince Paul with RZA, Frukwan and Poetic. Its dark humor and horror-themed production helped popularize horrorcore; after the 1994 and 1997 albums, the group returned from several years of inactivity for Nightmare in A-Minor (2002).

nodes.name: Green Day
nodes.description: Green Day is an American punk rock band formed in the East Bay, California, in 1987 as Sweet Children. The band helped bring punk and pop-punk to a broad 1990s audience and remains active.

nodes.name: George Frideric Handel
nodes.description: Baroque composer of operas, oratorios, and instrumental music, with a career centered in London.

nodes.name: Joseph Haydn
nodes.description: Classical composer central to the development of the symphony and string quartet.

nodes.name: Hazell Dean
nodes.description: English singer associated with Hi-NRG dance music.

nodes.name: Headhunterz
nodes.description: Dutch hardstyle DJ and producer Willem Rebergen, whose melodic anthems and Project One duo with Wildstylez helped carry hardstyle to international EDM stages in the late 2000s and 2010s.

nodes.name: Hildegard of Bingen
nodes.description: Medieval composer of sacred monophonic songs and the music drama Ordo Virtutum. Dates approximate her documented composing period, not her lifespan.

nodes.name: Horace Silver
nodes.description: Pianist and composer who brought blues and gospel inflections to hard bop.

nodes.name: Illapu
nodes.description: Illapu is a Chilean Andean folk group founded in Antofagasta in 1971. Its music combines Andean and Latin American traditions with political song and later rock, jazz and classical influences; exile and return shaped its history.

nodes.name: Imperial Court Ensemble
nodes.description: Gagaku musicians of the Music Department of the Imperial Household (Kunaichō Gakubu), set up in the early Meiji era from the former court and shrine musician guilds; credited on Western releases as the Imperial Court Ensemble.

nodes.name: Incognito
nodes.description: London jazz-funk collective led by Jean-Paul 'Bluey' Maunick, later signed to Gilles Peterson's Talkin' Loud label during the acid-jazz boom.

nodes.name: Iron Maiden
nodes.description: British heavy-metal band associated with galloping rhythms, harmonized guitars, and long-form storytelling.

nodes.name: Ivy Queen
nodes.description: Puerto Rican singer-songwriter and a pioneering woman in reggaeton, first performing with The Noise before her solo career.

nodes.name: James Brown
nodes.description: American singer, bandleader and songwriter central to soul and funk.

phases.note: “Living in America” was a major 1985 career milestone. It supports the date anchor, not a measured prominence score.

nodes.phaseNote: Editorial career prominence anchored to the soul breakthrough, the mid-1960s and early-1970s funk records, and the 1985 Living in America crossover. These are approximate career eras, not chart or streaming scores. His active career ends in 2006.

nodes.name: Jamiroquai
nodes.description: London funk and acid-jazz band fronted by Jay Kay, first signed to Acid Jazz and among the genre’s most commercially successful acts.

nodes.name: Jeff Mills
nodes.description: The Wizard. Co-founded Underground Resistance, then defined hard minimal techno on Axis and early Tresor.

nodes.name: Jefferson Airplane
nodes.description: San Francisco psychedelic-rock band. Original activity ran 1965-1972, with a 1989 reunion and a final 1996 appearance; dates include those breaks.

nodes.name: Jelly Roll Morton
nodes.description: New Orleans pianist, bandleader, and composer associated with early jazz arrangements.

nodes.name: Jesse Saunders
nodes.description: Chicago DJ, producer, and songwriter whose 1983 production and 1984 release of “On & On” helped establish house music on record.

nodes.name: Jimi Hendrix
nodes.description: Guitarist and songwriter who expanded amplified blues and psychedelic rock through feedback, effects, and improvisation.

nodes.name: João Bosco
nodes.description: Brazilian singer-songwriter and guitarist whose recording career began with “Agnus Sei” in 1972; his first solo LP followed in 1973.

nodes.name: John Coltrane
nodes.description: Saxophonist whose work moved from bebop and hard bop into modal and freer improvisation.

nodes.name: Johnny Ventura
nodes.description: Dominican merengue singer and bandleader who helped modernize the genre through his orchestra and recordings.

nodes.name: Jorge Ben Jor
nodes.description: Brazilian singer-songwriter and guitarist whose samba, soul and rock inflections shaped a distinctive popular sound; his debut album Samba Esquema Novo appeared in 1963.

nodes.name: Josquin des Prez
nodes.description: Renaissance composer of masses, motets, and secular vocal works.

nodes.name: Joy Division
nodes.description: Manchester post-punk band known for stark arrangements and a brooding atmosphere.

nodes.name: Juan Atkins
nodes.description: Detroit producer and DJ (1962–2026) whose work with Cybotron and as Model 500 helped shape early techno. Atkins used the word “techno” for Cybotron’s music before it became a name for the Detroit style; he was one of the Belleville Three and founded Metroplex.

nodes.name: Juan Flores
nodes.description: Chilean musician and multi-instrumentalist who joined Inti-Illimani’s later lineup in 2002.

nodes.name: Judas Priest
nodes.description: English heavy-metal band formed in Birmingham in 1969; the early lineup preceded the later recording lineup that established its signature sound.

nodes.name: Kabza De Small
nodes.description: South African DJ and producer who helped popularize amapiano; began DJing in 2009 and released his debut album in 2016.

nodes.name: Kanda Bongo Man
nodes.description: Congolese soukous singer who began with Kinshasa dance bands in the 1970s and later became an international bandleader.

nodes.name: Kavinsky
nodes.description: Kavinsky is documented in the cited genre histories and artist reference.

nodes.name: Keak da Sneak
nodes.description: Oakland rapper and hyphy pioneer who began recording in the 1990s with 3X Krazy before a solo career.

nodes.name: Kelli Hand (K-HAND)
nodes.description: Detroit DJ and producer whose releases as K-HAND made her an important figure in the city’s house and techno communities. She was recognized for opening space for Black women in a male-dominated scene and continued recording and performing into her final years.

nodes.name: Kerri Chandler
nodes.description: New Jersey house DJ and producer, active behind the decks as a teenager and releasing his first records in the early 1990s.

nodes.name: Kevin Saunderson
nodes.description: Detroit DJ and producer, one of the Belleville Three. He founded KMS Records and produced house and techno releases as well as the charting project Inner City.

nodes.name: Killswitch Engage
nodes.description: American metalcore band formed in 1999; its debut album appeared in 2000.

nodes.name: Kim So-hee
nodes.description: Korean pansori singer and holder of national intangible cultural heritage status, known for her interpretations of Chunhyangga.

nodes.name: King Crimson
nodes.description: London progressive-rock band whose 1969 debut, In the Court of the Crimson King, became a genre benchmark; later lineups led by Robert Fripp combined complex meters, improvisation, and experimental textures. Activity ran in separate eras with long breaks until 2021.

nodes.name: King Sunny Adé
nodes.description: Nigerian jùjú singer and bandleader who led the Green Spots and African Beats and brought jùjú to international audiences.

nodes.name: King Tubby
nodes.description: Jamaican sound-system operator, electronics technician and recording engineer whose studio experiments helped establish dub mixing.

nodes.name: Kode9
nodes.description: Scottish DJ and producer associated with dubstep and the Hyperdub label.

nodes.name: Korn
nodes.description: American metal band formed in 1993 whose 1994 self-titled debut helped popularize nu metal.

nodes.name: Kraftwerk
nodes.description: Düsseldorf's man-machines. 'Trans-Europe Express' and 'Computer World' are cited by Juan Atkins and Afrika Bambaataa alike as the source code.

phases.note: Tour de France Soundtracks (2003) marked a documented return to new studio material after a long gap; this phase describes recording activity and visibility.

nodes.phaseNote: Editorial career prominence anchored to Autobahn, Trans-Europe Express, Computer World, and the 2003 Tour de France Soundtracks return. This describes recording-era visibility, not the continuing magnitude of Kraftwerk's influence or measured listening.

nodes.name: Kyuss
nodes.description: American desert-rock band formed in 1987 as Sons of Kyuss; the group became a leading influence on stoner rock before disbanding in 1995.

nodes.name: Lalon Fakir
nodes.description: Bengali Baul-Fakir poet, composer and spiritual teacher whose songs circulated orally; his life dates and song attributions remain disputed.

nodes.name: Larry Heard
nodes.description: Chicago house producer and multi-instrumentalist who recorded as Mr. Fingers and helped shape deep house.

nodes.name: Larry Levan
nodes.description: Paradise Garage resident; his eclectic, emotional marathon sets defined garage house and modern DJ culture.

nodes.name: Lauryn Hill
nodes.description: New Jersey singer and rapper who rose with the Fugees’ The Score (1996); her solo album The Miseducation of Lauryn Hill (1998) won five Grammys, including Album of the Year.

nodes.name: Led Zeppelin
nodes.description: English rock band formed in 1968 and disbanded in 1980 after John Bonham’s death; members reunited for select later performances, including 2007.

nodes.name: Léonin
nodes.description: Notre-Dame school composer associated with early polyphonic organum. Activity dates are approximate because biographical evidence is limited.

nodes.name: Lil Durk
nodes.description: Chicago rapper and singer whose OTF mixtapes began in 2011 before a major-label debut album in 2015.

nodes.name: Lil Jon & the East Side Boyz
nodes.description: Atlanta crunk group that debuted in 1997; its best-known studio era ended after Crunk Juice (2004), with 2005 used as a rounded final activity marker.

nodes.name: Lil Keke
nodes.description: Houston rapper and Screwed Up Click member whose debut album Don’t Mess Wit Texas appeared in 1997.

nodes.name: Lil Wayne
nodes.description: New Orleans rapper who began recording for Cash Money as a child, joined the Hot Boys in the 1990s and launched a solo album career in 1999.

nodes.name: Linkin Park
nodes.description: American rock band formed as Xero in 1996, later renamed Hybrid Theory and Linkin Park; its debut album was released in 2000.

nodes.name: Little Richard
nodes.description: American singer and pianist whose powerful gospel-inflected vocals and rock-and-roll recordings influenced generations of performers.

nodes.name: Lord Kitchener
nodes.description: Trinidadian calypsonian whose career began in Arima in the late 1930s and later brought calypso to British audiences.

nodes.name: Los Ángeles Azules
nodes.description: Mexican cumbia group formed in 1976 in Iztapalapa; its official activity and national breakthrough followed in the early 1980s.

nodes.name: Louis Armstrong
nodes.description: New Orleans trumpeter and singer whose improvisation helped make the jazz soloist central to the music.

nodes.name: LTJ Bukem
nodes.description: English DJ and producer associated with atmospheric jungle and drum and bass.

nodes.name: Luzmila Carpio
nodes.description: Bolivian Quechua singer and cultural advocate whose professional career began in childhood and whose first recordings appeared in 1969.

nodes.name: Mac Dre
nodes.description: Vallejo rapper and Bay Area rap pioneer whose early cassette single “Too Hard for the F---ing Radio” gained local notice in 1989.

nodes.name: Machito
nodes.description: Cuban-born singer and bandleader whose Afro-Cubans, formed in New York in 1940 with Mario Bauzá as musical director, are widely credited with launching Latin jazz.

nodes.name: Macintosh Plus
nodes.description: Vaporwave recording alias of producer Ramona Xavier (also known as Vektroid), best known for the 2011 album Floral Shoppe.

nodes.name: Mahavishnu Orchestra
nodes.description: John McLaughlin's fusion ensemble combined jazz improvisation, rock intensity, and complex rhythmic structures; activity included multiple lineups and breaks.

phases.note: The Inner Mounting Flame (1971) and Birds of Fire (1973); arena-level jazz-rock.
Disbanded in 1976; McLaughlin turns to Shakti.
Re-formed lineup active 1984–87.

nodes.phaseNote: Editorial shading of active career, not a measured ranking: first-lineup peak 1971–75, hiatus 1976–84, and a lower-profile reunion 1984–87.

nodes.name: Major League DJz
nodes.description: South African twin DJ and producer duo Banele and Bandile Mbere, who moved from party promotion into music production and helped popularize amapiano internationally.

nodes.name: Man Parrish
nodes.description: New York electro and synth-pop producer best known for the 1982 track “Hip Hop, Be Bop (Don’t Stop).”

nodes.name: Mandoza
nodes.description: South African kwaito artist who began in underground group Chiskop in the early 1990s, then launched a successful solo career in 1999.

nodes.name: Maqbool Sabri
nodes.description: Pakistani qawwali singer who formed a troupe with his brother Ghulam Farid Sabri in 1956 and continued leading the Sabri Brothers after 1994.

nodes.name: Marshall Jefferson
nodes.description: Chicago house producer whose 1986 releases, especially “Move Your Body,” helped define piano-led house.

nodes.name: Marvin Gaye
nodes.description: American soul singer and songwriter known for socially engaged and intimate recordings.

phases.note: What’s Going On was released in 1971 and marks a major career and artistic turning point; prominence remains an editorial judgment.
“Sexual Healing” (1982) marked a late-career commercial comeback; the phase label is qualitative.

nodes.phaseNote: Editorial career prominence: early Motown success, the 1971 What's Going On period, later-1970s recordings, and the 1982 Sexual Healing comeback. Dates anchor a qualitative interpretation of his biography, not measured popularity; the active career ends in 1984.

nodes.name: Massive Attack
nodes.description: Bristol music collective formed in 1988 from members of the earlier Wild Bunch scene; its debut album Blue Lines appeared in 1991.

nodes.name: Masters at Work
nodes.description: New York house production and remix duo Kenny “Dope” Gonzalez and Louie Vega, whose collaboration developed around 1990 after earlier use of the Masters at Work name by Todd Terry.

nodes.name: McCoy Tyner
nodes.description: Pianist associated with John Coltrane's quartet and a powerful modal harmonic language.

nodes.name: Megadeth
nodes.description: American thrash metal band formed in Hollywood in June 1983 by Dave Mustaine and David Ellefson; its first concert followed in February 1984.

nodes.name: Mei Lanfang
nodes.description: Peking opera performer and innovator whose stage career began in childhood; international tours introduced the art form to audiences abroad.

nodes.name: Metallica
nodes.description: American heavy metal band formed in Los Angeles in 1981 by James Hetfield and Lars Ulrich; their early thrash metal records helped establish the genre.

nodes.name: Michael Jackson
nodes.description: American singer and dancer whose music career began as a child member and lead vocalist of the Jackson 5 before an exceptionally successful solo career.

nodes.name: Mighty Sparrow
nodes.description: Grenadian-born Trinidadian calypsonian and songwriter, widely known as the “Calypso King of the World”; his 1956 hit “Jean and Dinah” brought his breakthrough.

nodes.name: Mike “Mad Mike” Banks
nodes.description: Detroit producer and label operator who co-founded Underground Resistance with Jeff Mills. Banks helped shape the collective’s independent release network and its politically engaged second-generation techno work.

nodes.name: Miles Davis
nodes.description: American jazz trumpeter, composer and bandleader whose changing ensembles helped shape bebop, cool jazz, modal jazz and electric fusion. Davis moved to New York in 1944 to study at Juilliard but quickly entered the professional jazz scene; his first recordings as a sideman followed in 1945. His career spanned major stylistic changes through his death in 1991.

nodes.name: Milly Quezada
nodes.description: Dominican merengue singer whose career began in New York in 1975 with the band Milly y los Vecinos, later Milly, Jocelyn y los Vecinos.

nodes.name: Ministry
nodes.description: American band founded by Al Jourgensen in Chicago in 1981; it moved from early synth-pop toward influential industrial metal. Jourgensen announced the band’s ending with its 2026 final album.

nodes.name: Minoru Muraoka
nodes.description: Japanese shakuhachi player who moved between traditional and contemporary Japanese music and jazz, including the 1970 album New Dimensions and work with Herbie Mann.

nodes.name: Miss Kittin
nodes.description: French electronic musician and DJ Caroline Hervé, initially billed as Miss Kittin and now as Kittin; her collaboration with The Hacker began with the Champagne EP.

nodes.name: MJ Cole
nodes.description: English UK garage producer and DJ whose breakthrough track “Sincere” emerged in 1998 and became a defining 2-step recording.

nodes.name: Mogwai
nodes.description: Scottish post-rock band formed in Glasgow in 1995; their debut album, Mogwai Young Team, followed in 1997.

nodes.name: Mongo Santamaría
nodes.description: Cuban percussionist and bandleader who began performing professionally in Havana in 1937, later bringing Afro-Cuban rhythms into US jazz and popular music.

nodes.name: Moodymann
nodes.description: Detroit house producer and DJ Kenny Dixon Jr., whose KDJ label and records helped shape Detroit deep house; his debut album Silentintroduction appeared in 1997.

nodes.name: Morbid Angel
nodes.description: Florida death metal band founded by Trey Azagthoth in 1984; its 1989 album Altars of Madness became a landmark of extreme metal.

nodes.name: Motorbass
nodes.description: French house duo of Philippe Zdar and Étienne de Crécy, associated with the early French touch scene; their sole album Pansoul appeared in 1996.

nodes.name: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart
nodes.description: Classical composer of operas, concertos, symphonies, and chamber music, active from childhood.

nodes.name: Muddy Waters
nodes.description: Mississippi Delta singer and guitarist first recorded for the Library of Congress in 1941; after moving to Chicago in 1943 his amplified band defined Chicago blues.

nodes.name: Munir Bashir
nodes.description: Iraqi oud virtuoso, scholar and cultural ambassador who developed the solo oud recital and became a leading representative of maqam and taqsim traditions.

nodes.name: My Bloody Valentine
nodes.description: Irish-English alternative rock band formed in Dublin in 1983; their layered guitar sound became central to shoegaze, especially on 1991’s Loveless.

nodes.name: Nas
nodes.description: American rapper Nasir Jones, known as Nas, whose recorded career began with a guest verse on Main Source’s “Live at the Barbeque” in 1991; Illmatic followed in 1994.

nodes.name: Neon Indian
nodes.description: Electronic music project of Alan Palomo, associated with chillwave; its No Way Down EP appeared in 2008, with wider attention and debut album Psychic Chasms in 2009.

nodes.name: Neophyte
nodes.description: Rotterdam gabber group founded in 1992 by Jeroen Streunding with Danny Greten and Robin van Roon, first released on Rotterdam Records.

nodes.name: Neu!
nodes.description: German band whose motorik sound became influential in krautrock and later rock.

phases.note: NEU! began its original recording period in 1971. This anchors the band’s active era, not its later influence.
The original NEU! recording period ended in 1975; the “niche” label is an editorial characterization of the subsequent inactive period.
The members reconvened for studio sessions in 1985–86; this was not a documented return to regular public performance.

nodes.phaseNote: Editorial career phases: the original 1971–1975 recording period and the documented 1985–1986 reunion. The hidden gap represents inactivity of the band, not loss of influence. Relative shades within the active periods are qualitative.

nodes.name: New Edition
nodes.description: Boston R&B vocal group formed in Roxbury in 1978; their 1983 debut single “Candy Girl” launched national and international success.

nodes.name: Newcleus
nodes.description: Brooklyn electro and hip-hop group emerging from the Jam-On Productions DJ collective; its first Newcleus credited single “Jam-On Revenge” was released in 1983.

nodes.name: Nine Inch Nails
nodes.description: American industrial rock project founded by Trent Reznor in Cleveland in 1988; its 1989 debut Pretty Hate Machine brought early commercial success.

nodes.name: Nirvana
nodes.description: American rock band formed in Aberdeen, Washington, in 1987; Nevermind’s 1991 release brought grunge and alternative rock to mass audiences. The band ended after Kurt Cobain’s death in 1994.

nodes.name: Noisia
nodes.description: Groningen drum and bass trio known for neurofunk and sound design. After announcing a farewell in 2019 and playing a last show in 2022, the trio announced a reunion and new music in September 2026.

nodes.name: Nusrat Fateh Ali Khan
nodes.description: Pakistani qawwali vocalist who debuted as lead singer of his family ensemble in 1965 and later expanded the tradition to international audiences and cross-genre collaborations.

nodes.name: N.W.A
nodes.description: Compton hip-hop group central to the rise of gangsta rap. Formed in 1986, N.W.A released its first group records in 1987 and had effectively ended by 1991 after key members departed.

nodes.name: Oasis
nodes.description: Manchester rock band formed in 1991 from the earlier group Rain, with Liam and Noel Gallagher becoming its defining frontmen and songwriters. After splitting in 2009, Oasis reunited for live performances in 2025.

nodes.name: Octave One
nodes.description: Detroit electronic group led by brothers Lenny and Lawrence Burden, who debuted on Transmat in 1989 with “I Believe” and run the 430 West label; known for the live-played anthem “Blackwater”.

nodes.name: Oneohtrix Point Never
nodes.description: American electronic musician and composer Daniel Lopatin’s project, active under the Oneohtrix Point Never name since 2007, known for experimental synthesis, sampling and soundtrack work.

nodes.name: Ornette Coleman
nodes.description: American alto saxophonist and composer whose 1958 debut and 1959 New York quartet performances helped establish free jazz and reshape improvisation.

nodes.name: Osibisa
nodes.description: Ghanaian-Caribbean Afro-rock group formed in London in 1969 by Teddy Osei and fellow West African and Caribbean musicians; its 1971 debut album brought it broad notice.

nodes.name: Otis Redding
nodes.description: American soul singer and songwriter who joined Johnny Jenkins and the Pinetoppers in 1958, then built a major solo career before dying in a 1967 plane crash.
nodes.phaseNote: Editorial career prominence: early recordings followed by his mid-1960s Stax breakthrough. The career ends with his death in 1967; the posthumous success of (Sittin' On) The Dock of the Bay is not treated as another active-career phase.

nodes.name: OutKast
nodes.description: Atlanta hip-hop duo of André 3000 and Big Boi, formed in the early 1990s and signed as LaFace’s first hip-hop act; the debut album arrived in 1994.

nodes.name: Giovanni Pierluigi da Palestrina
nodes.description: Italian Renaissance composer of sacred polyphony, appointed organist and choirmaster at San Agapito in his hometown in 1544; later led music at St Peter’s in Rome.

nodes.name: Papa Wemba
nodes.description: Congolese singer and bandleader who joined Zaiko Langa Langa around 1969–70, helped shape Kinshasa’s soukous scene, and founded Viva La Musica in 1977. His later European work helped carry Congolese popular music to international audiences. Died in 2016.

nodes.name: Park Dong-jin
nodes.description: Korean pansori singer and teacher who studied with leading masters in the 1930s, built early performance work among gisaeng communities, and later became renowned for reviving and completing full pansori cycles.

nodes.name: Parliament-Funkadelic
nodes.description: Funk collective led by George Clinton, combining Funkadelic (founded 1968) and Parliament (from 1970) and later touring as the P-Funk All Stars. It grew out of Clinton’s 1950s doo-wop group the Parliaments.

nodes.name: Parvathy Baul
nodes.description: Bengali Baul practitioner, singer and performer who trained with Baul masters; her transformation into a Baul practitioner is dated to 1997, with a reported first public performance in 2001.

nodes.name: Patrick Cowley
nodes.description: American disco and Hi-NRG producer who helped shape San Francisco’s gay dance scene through electronic production, collaborations with Sylvester, and Megatone Records; active professionally from 1977 until his death in 1982.

nodes.name: Paul van Dyk
nodes.description: German DJ and producer whose Berlin club career began in 1991; early releases and remixes in the 1990s helped define popular trance, including “For an Angel.”

nodes.name: Peaches
nodes.description: Canadian musician Merrill Nisker, known as Peaches, whose 2000 album The Teaches of Peaches established her as a solo performer; earlier music was released under her own name.

nodes.name: Pearl Jam
nodes.description: Seattle rock band emerging from the members of Mother Love Bone in 1990; the Pearl Jam name was adopted in 1991 before the debut album Ten.

nodes.name: Perfume
nodes.description: Japanese electropop trio formed in Hiroshima in 1999; its regional independent debut preceded major-label debut in 2005 and national breakthrough in 2007.

nodes.name: Pérotin
nodes.description: French composer associated with Notre-Dame in Paris and the development of large-scale polyphonic organum around 1200.

nodes.name: Perturbator
nodes.description: French electronic musician James Kent’s dark synthwave project, active from 2012; early releases and Hotline Miami placements helped bring the project to broader attention.

nodes.name: Pet Shop Boys
nodes.description: English synth-pop duo Neil Tennant and Chris Lowe, who began writing together in 1981 and adopted the Pet Shop Boys name before their first single in 1984.

nodes.name: Philip Glass
nodes.description: American composer and pianist who emerged from New York’s avant-garde scene; his Philip Glass Ensemble began in 1967 and Einstein on the Beach brought wider recognition in 1976.

nodes.name: Phuture
nodes.description: Chicago house group of DJ Pierre, Spanky and Herb J, formed in 1985; its track “Acid Tracks,” first tested in clubs and then released in 1987, helped define acid house.

nodes.name: Pixies
nodes.description: Boston alternative rock band formed in 1986; after splitting in 1993 and reuniting in 2004, the band returned to recording and touring.

nodes.name: Pizzicato Five
nodes.description: Japanese pop group formed in 1984 by Yasuharu Konishi, Keitarō Takanami, Ryō Kamomiya and Mamiko Sasaki; it disbanded in 2001.

nodes.name: Pole
nodes.description: Berlin-based project of Stefan Betke, whose crackling, filter-driven dub basslines on the albums 1–3 (1998–2000) became a touchstone of glitchy dub techno.

nodes.name: Poncho Sanchez
nodes.description: Conga player and bandleader who joined Cal Tjader’s group in 1975 and became a long-running Concord Picante Latin jazz star, winning the 2000 Grammy for Best Latin Jazz Performance with Latin Soul.

nodes.name: Pop Smoke
nodes.description: Brooklyn rapper Bashar Jackson, known as Pop Smoke, began recording in 2018 and broke through in 2019 with “Welcome to the Party”; he was killed in 2020, before his debut studio album was released posthumously.

nodes.name: Portishead
nodes.description: Bristol band formed in 1991 by Geoff Barrow and Beth Gibbons, later joined by Adrian Utley; after a long hiatus beginning around 1999, they returned with Third in 2008 and occasional performances in 2022 and 2025.

nodes.name: Prince
nodes.description: American singer, songwriter and multi-instrumentalist associated with Minneapolis funk.

phases.note: Musicology (2004) and its tour marked a documented mainstream comeback; the “golden-age” shade is relative to this artist’s career and remains interpretive.

nodes.phaseNote: Editorial career prominence: early solo releases, the 1980s breakthrough centered on Purple Rain, early-1990s success, and the 2004 Musicology comeback. Shades are qualitative and approximate, not measured popularity. The active career ends in 2016.

nodes.name: Prince Buster
nodes.description: Jamaican singer, producer and sound-system operator whose early-1960s productions helped shape ska and rocksteady. After reduced musical activity, he returned to recording in the early 1990s and toured; later revivals renewed attention to his 1960s catalog.

nodes.name: Prince Royce
nodes.description: Bronx-born bachata singer Geoffrey Royce Rojas, known as Prince Royce; his first single circulated online in 2009, before his self-titled debut album and breakout in 2010.

nodes.name: Psy
nodes.description: South Korean rapper and singer Park Jae-sang, known as PSY; his recording career began with the 2001 album PSY from the PSYcho World!, long before the international success of “Gangnam Style” in 2012.

nodes.name: Public Enemy
nodes.description: Long Island hip-hop group led by Chuck D and Flavor Flav, formed as a group in 1985 and first recorded for Def Jam in 1987; politically charged lyrics and dense Bomb Squad production became defining features.

nodes.name: Purna Das Baul
nodes.description: Bengali Baul singer Purna Das began professional public performances as a child, including All India Radio work in 1942; he helped bring Baul music to international audiences, notably on the 1962 World Youth Festival tour.

nodes.name: Queen
nodes.description: British rock band formed in 1970 by Freddie Mercury, Brian May and Roger Taylor; John Deacon’s arrival in 1971 completed the classic lineup. The surviving members continue to perform as Queen with Adam Lambert.

nodes.name: Queens of the Stone Age
