nodes.name: EDM
nodes.description: In North American music-industry usage, “EDM” became a catch-all label in the late 2000s for dance and club electronic music, especially commercially oriented festival sounds. It is a broad marketing category overlapping house, trance and other styles, not one stable musical form or the origin of electronic dance music.
nodes.phaseNote: Removed the unsupported 2008 golden-age and 2018 established phases. Available sources support the term’s late-2000s uptake and festival-market association, not a single popularity curve for the umbrella category.

nodes.name: Electro
nodes.description: A Black American electronic dance and hip-hop style associated with drum-machine rhythms, synthesized bass and vocoders. Afrika Bambaataa and the Soulsonic Force’s 1982 “Planet Rock” is widely treated as a foundational electro recording; electro continued beyond its early-1980s breakthrough and developed regional offshoots.
nodes.phaseNote: Removed the unsupported 1990 end date and narrow golden-age phase. 1982 is a landmark recording date, not the invention of electronic dance music or the end of electro.

nodes.name: Electro house
nodes.description: A 2000s house branch combining house rhythms with prominent electro-influenced synth timbres and forceful production.
nodes.phaseNote: No prominence phases retained. Available sources document electro-house as a 2000s production/scene category but do not establish a measured genre-wide peak or decline.

nodes.name: Electroclash
nodes.description: A turn-of-the-millennium club scene combining electro, synth-pop/new wave references, punk attitude and theatrical performance; also a press and nightlife label.
nodes.phaseNote: Approximate late-1990s emergence and early-2000s visibility; this reflects an identifiable club/press scene, not a measured peak or the disappearance of related electro-pop styles.

nodes.name: Emo
nodes.description: A shifting family of rock styles usually traced to 1980s Washington, DC hardcore and later independent scenes. The label has been disputed by musicians and applied to distinct later waves; some emo-associated bands reached broad mainstream visibility in the early 2000s.
nodes.phaseNote: These broad anchors distinguish the contested 1980s DC lineage from early-2000s mainstream visibility; they do not describe one continuous sound or an end date. Removed the unsupported 1993 “golden age” and 2003 niche phase.

nodes.name: Folk revival
nodes.description: The twentieth-century folk-revival tradition represented here centers on vernacular song, singer-songwriters and revival performance in the United States and Britain; it does not stand for every traditional music worldwide.

phases.note: Lomax's Library of Congress recordings of Guthrie and the Almanac Singers (1941) seed the revival.
The Weavers' 1950 hit 'Goodnight, Irene' makes revival folk a commercial pop phenomenon.
Kingston Trio's 'Tom Dooley' (1958), Newport 1959 and Baez/Dylan drive the boom to its mid-1960s peak.
The commercial boom recedes into folk-rock and singer-songwriter currents; revival performance continues.

nodes.phaseNote: Editorial shading, not a measured ranking: 1930s roots (Library of Congress field recordings, Guthrie, Almanac Singers), a 1950 commercial breakthrough with the Weavers, a 1958–mid-1960s boom, then continuing but less central activity. Replaces an unsupported 1945–2010 golden age.

nodes.name: Juke / footwork
nodes.description: A Black Chicago electronic music and dance tradition rooted in house and battle-dance culture. Footwork tracks use rapid, syncopated patterns and tightly cut samples; juke and footwork overlap, but local dancers and producers do not always use the terms interchangeably.
nodes.phaseNote: 1990s marks battle-dance emergence; 2007 is a documented international visibility moment, not the start or local peak. Removed unsupported 2001 “golden age” and 2018 establishment date.

nodes.name: Free jazz
nodes.description: Jazz that experiments with or abandons fixed chord progressions, regular meter, and conventional ensemble roles in favor of freer improvisation.

phases.note: Ornette Coleman’s 1958–59 groups; the 1960 album Free Jazz names the idiom.
Mid-1960s energy music of Coltrane, Sanders, Ayler and Taylor.

nodes.phaseNote: Editorial shading, not a measured ranking. Britannica dates emergence to the late 1950s, the height to the 1960s, and says free jazz “remained a major development” thereafter (AACM, European free improvisation), so the former 1975 end was removed and the post-1973 phase is a lower-intensity established tradition.

nodes.name: French house
nodes.description: French-produced house associated with looped disco and funk samples, filtering and club production; it overlaps with but does not encompass the broader French Touch label.

phases.note: Homework (1997) and late-1990s international club hits anchor the first broad export wave; 1997 is an approximate marker, not a point of origin.

nodes.phaseNote: Approximate international club and press visibility: the style grew from early-1990s French production and reached a broad international profile around Homework, Cassius and Stardust in 1997–99. The phases describe one historical wave, not the ongoing reach of French house or all French Touch music.

nodes.name: French Touch
nodes.description: A Paris-centred electronic-music movement and export label of the late 1990s and early 2000s, spanning filter house, disco-inflected house, electro-pop and more. Scholarship treats it variously as a scene, a sound or a brand; it is broader than French house.

phases.note: French Touch scene infrastructure and Daft Punk’s first single date to 1994; term/scene histories also point to earlier roots.
1997–2000 is a narrow international breakthrough wave, not the start or entire history of French electronic music.
Artists and styles continued; by the early 2000s the first-wave formula was losing novelty, while later waves and descendants emerged.

nodes.phaseNote: Phases distinguish scene formation from the best-documented international wave and later continuation. The “golden-age” label refers to the 1997–2000 movement window used by a museum exhibit, not a measurable genre-wide popularity index.

nodes.name: Funk

phases.note: Carnegie Hall places funk’s emergence in the late 1960s, with James Brown and Sly and the Family Stone as pioneers.
Funk became widely popular during the 1970s, following its late-1960s formation; this is a broad U.S. popular-record era, not a measured peak.
Most traditional funk bands had faded from the popular soundscape by the early 1980s; the style continued through electro-funk and hip-hop and R&B sampling.

nodes.phaseNote: Approximate U.S. popular-record visibility: late-1960s formation, 1970s peak as a dance-music form, then from the early 1980s continued influence through electro-funk, R&B and hip-hop sampling rather than chart-leading bands. Editorial shading, not a measured global ranking.
nodes.description: A rhythm-centered Black American music family developed by artists and bands in the 1960s and popularized widely in the 1970s. It includes distinct regional and band styles, and its bass, drum, and horn patterns continued to circulate through later R&B and hip-hop sampling.

nodes.name: G-funk
nodes.description: A West Coast hip-hop style built around funk-derived bass and synthesizer lines, deep grooves and rap production. Dr. Dre’s The Chronic (1992) was a major mainstream breakthrough, while claims about who originated G-funk are contested among Los Angeles artists and producers.
nodes.phaseNote: The Chronic’s 1992 breakthrough marks a commercial wave; one scholarly history places a G-funk era around 1992–96, not the style’s invention or end. No complete prominence curve is assigned.

nodes.name: Gabber
nodes.description: A Dutch hardcore dance style that emerged around Rotterdam in the early 1990s, marked by fast tempos, forceful kick drums, and deliberately distorted production. Its history belongs to the wider European hardcore continuum.

phases.note: Rotterdam Records began releasing local hardcore in 1992, following earlier Dutch hardcore events.
Mid-1990s mass parties, Thunderdome compilations, chart hits and television exposure.
Sound and Vision says the scene had collapsed by the millennium; hardcore continued as a niche interest.
Revival of interest in gabber and hardcore in wider club culture.

nodes.phaseNote: Editorial shading, not measured popularity. Gabber emerged in Rotterdam around 1992 and peaked in the mid-1990s. It declined sharply by 2000 but continued through Thunderdome and the hardcore scene. Revival interest is visible from 2019. Boundaries are approximate.

nodes.name: Gagaku
nodes.description: Japanese court music and dance encompassing instrumental repertories and vocal forms, shaped through historical exchange with continental Asian traditions. UNESCO describes it as the oldest of Japan’s traditional performing arts.

phases.note: Broad sixth/seventh-century marker for the combination of continental music and native songs; not an exact origin.
Broad tenth-century marker for the developed court tradition; not a measured popularity peak.

nodes.phaseNote: Sources distinguish early continental transmission from the later developed court repertory. Circa 600 and circa 900 represent broad sixth/seventh- and tenth-century stages, respectively. The Imperial Household Agency dates incoming continental music earlier, from approximately the fifth century; that is a precursor rather than the completed form.

nodes.name: Gamelan
nodes.description: An umbrella term for Indonesian ensemble traditions, including distinct Javanese and Balinese repertories, instruments and tuning systems; it does not describe one uniform style.
nodes.phaseNote: No phases: this umbrella covers diverse, continuously practiced regional traditions; a single shared lifecycle or prominence curve is inappropriate.

nodes.name: Gangsta rap
nodes.description: A rap style whose narratives often draw on street life, violence, policing and survival. It developed across multiple cities and is not synonymous with all hip-hop from Black urban communities.

phases.note: Early-1990s national visibility documented by historical accounts and commercial success; this is not a measured genre-wide peak.

nodes.phaseNote: Late-1980s emergence and early-1990s national prominence are historical markers, not a universal lifecycle; regional scenes and later artists continued beyond the 1990s.

nodes.name: Garage house
nodes.description: A New York house lineage associated with the Paradise Garage and DJ Larry Levan, where house, disco, soul, gospel, and extended DJ mixing overlapped. The label describes a scene and a range of records rather than a single fixed sound.
nodes.phaseNote: The New York scene predates the 1987 closure of Paradise Garage; the sound and its later classification as a distinct genre have different histories. No complete prominence curve is assigned.

nodes.name: Garage rock
nodes.description: Raw, stripped-down rock associated retrospectively with 1960s amateur and regional bands, drawing on rock and roll, blues and R&B. The term “garage rock” gained currency later, particularly through 1970s criticism and the Nuggets compilation; subsequent revival scenes reused the label.
nodes.phaseNote: Mid-1960s regional bands formed a style later grouped under the retrospective garage-rock label, with subsequent revivals. No complete prominence curve is assigned.

nodes.name: Girl groups
nodes.description: A vocal-group style associated with the late 1950s and 1960s, often pairing close harmonies and expressive lead vocals with polished songwriting and studio production. Groups such as the Ronettes, the Shangri-Las and the Supremes helped define it.
nodes.phaseNote: The 1958 emergence and early-1960s market peak refer to the classic U.S. girl-group sound; the broader term also covers earlier and later groups. No complete prominence curve is assigned.

nodes.name: Glam rock
nodes.description: Early-1970s British rock foregrounding theatrical performance, visual artifice, pop songwriting and amplified rock sounds.
nodes.phaseNote: No phase labels retained: evidence supports a short British prominence period, but not a standardized genre-wide “golden age” boundary.

nodes.name: Gothic rock
nodes.description: Post-punk development featuring dark atmospheres, dramatic vocals and romantic or alienation themes; goth music scene overlaps with but is not identical to goth subculture.
nodes.phaseNote: Bauhaus’s 1979 recording is often treated as an origin marker, but scholarship challenges a single-track origin and the wider goth field continued to evolve. No complete prominence curve is assigned.

nodes.name: Gqom
nodes.description: A stark, percussive South African dance style that emerged in Durban in the early 2010s, using sparse, tense rhythms and heavy low end. Vocal and instrumental approaches developed alongside one another.
nodes.phaseNote: Sources distinguish local formation around 2008, Durban scene circulation in the early 2010s and international visibility from 2016. No complete prominence curve is assigned.

nodes.name: Grime
nodes.description: London electronic rap style that emerged in the early 2000s around pirate radio, MC crews and fast, synthetic production shaped by UK garage, jungle, dancehall and hip-hop. Wiley, Dizzee Rascal and local crews helped establish early forms; the scene expanded beyond its original underground networks.
nodes.phaseNote: Early-2000s east London scene formation and 2002 recordings are documented; the genre’s naming and first-track claims remain contested. No complete prominence curve is assigned.

nodes.name: Grunge
nodes.description: A Pacific Northwest scene and style whose bands drew on punk, metal, and other rock traditions. Sub Pop’s local releases and Nirvana’s 1991 “Nevermind” helped bring some Seattle-area music to international mainstream attention; grunge was never a single sound or the whole region’s music.
nodes.phaseNote: A Pacific Northwest scene preceded the 1991–92 mainstream breakthrough associated with Nevermind; the scene and its artists continued in varied directions. No complete prominence curve is assigned.

nodes.name: Hard bop
nodes.description: Bebop extended through blues, gospel, and rhythm-and-blues phrasing, with a strong groove and earthy ensemble sound.

phases.note: Early-1950s Blue Note sessions by Silver and Blakey; Clifford Brown’s “De-Dah” (1953).
Jazz Messengers, Brown–Roach quintet and Silver quintets; the term is current by the mid-1950s.
Modal, free and fusion styles take the spotlight; Blakey and Silver keep hard bop working.
Young Lions/neo-traditionalist return to hard bop around the Marsalis brothers and Blakey’s Messengers.

nodes.phaseNote: Editorial shading, not a measured ranking: hard bop takes shape in early-1950s Blue Note sessions and peaks in the mid-to-late 1950s (Carnegie Hall, Britannica, Guardian). The former 1965 end was removed because the idiom persisted (Blakey’s Messengers to 1990, Silver into the 1990s) and was revived by the 1980s Young Lions. Boundaries are approximate.

nodes.name: Hard rock
nodes.description: A loud, blues-influenced rock style built around amplified electric guitar, forceful rhythm sections and powerful vocals. Its mid- to late-1960s roots include Cream, the Jimi Hendrix Experience, Blue Cheer and Steppenwolf; hard rock continued through later arena, club and metal-adjacent scenes.

phases.note: Mid- to late-1960s roots in blues-based British and American rock; the label was not necessarily used consistently by the musicians at the time.
Early-1970s consolidation through influential heavy rock bands; this marks a historical prominence wave, not an end.

nodes.phaseNote: Provisional editorial staging of emergence, the defining prominence wave, and later niche status. Boundaries are approximate and not a measured ranking; the source record should be checked for each transition.

nodes.name: Hardstyle
nodes.description: A hard dance style that took shape in the Netherlands and nearby European scenes, combining hard electronic kick drums with influences from hard trance and hardcore.

phases.note: Project One and Headhunterz-era crossover; hardstyle reached major EDM stages in the 2010s.
Pandemic cancellations and later restructuring of flagship Q-dance events.

nodes.phaseNote: Editorial shading, not measured popularity. Hardstyle emerged around 2000 and peaked from the late 2000s through the 2010s crossover. From 2020, it continued as an established scene. Boundaries are low-confidence estimates.

nodes.name: Heavy metal
nodes.description: Amplified heaviness, distortion, emphatic riffs, and dramatic performance developed from late-1960s hard rock.
nodes.phaseNote: Late-1960s heavy-rock roots are broadly documented, but no single origin band or genre-wide peak is established. No complete prominence curve is assigned.

nodes.name: Hi-NRG

phases.note: Oxford scholarship dates the San Francisco gay disco sound’s emergence to 1978; Hi-NRG as a later label should not be read back as universal contemporary terminology.
The UK pop-production/chart era provides a later recognition marker, not a worldwide peak.

nodes.phaseNote: Markers distinguish San Francisco post-disco roots from later named UK chart visibility. Removed unsupported universal “golden age,” duplicative established stages and arbitrary 1995 niche label; queer club and pop legacies continued.
nodes.description: A high-tempo, synthesizer-led development of disco associated with North American queer club culture and later UK pop production. Its visibility varied by territory: specialist club and trade charts, crossover singles, and later dance styles document different parts of its history.

nodes.name: Highlife
nodes.description: A family of West African popular dance traditions most strongly associated with Ghana and Nigeria, combining local musical practices with imported and diasporic influences. Ghanaian styles include brass-band and guitar-band forms; a 1928 Kumasi Trio recording is one documentary milestone, not the invention of highlife. The music continued beyond the 1970s in changing local scenes.
nodes.phaseNote: Ghanaian highlife developed through multiple strands; a 1928 Kumasi Trio recording is an early documentation marker rather than an origin date. No complete prominence curve is assigned.

nodes.name: Hindustani classical
nodes.description: North Indian classical music built around raga and tala, transmitted through lineages and performance traditions. The date marks a broad modern period of public circulation, not the beginning of the tradition.
nodes.phaseNote: No single lifecycle phase: Hindustani music traditions predate 1700 and continued through court, colonial, public, recording and modern institutional settings. This entry’s date is only a loose historical transition marker.

nodes.name: Hip-hop
nodes.description: A musical and cultural movement that developed in New York’s Bronx during the 1970s, shaped by Black and Puerto Rican communities and Caribbean diasporic practices. DJing, MCing, dance, visual art, and later regional rap scenes are connected but distinct parts of its history.
nodes.phaseNote: The 1973 Bronx party is a commonly commemorated milestone, and the late-1980s/early-1990s U.S. Golden Age is a debated critical periodization rather than a global peak. No complete prominence curve is assigned.

nodes.name: Honky-tonk
nodes.description: Country music forged in the bars and dance halls of Texas and Oklahoma oil and boom towns, pairing steel guitar, fiddle and an electrified backbeat with blunt songs of drinking, cheating and heartbreak. Ernest Tubb, Hank Williams and Lefty Frizzell defined its postwar peak; George Jones and later neotraditionalists carried it on.

phases.note: Ernest Tubb's electrified 'Walking the Floor Over You' (1941) and Texas dance-hall bands shape the style.
Hank Williams' 'Lovesick Blues' (1949) and Lefty Frizzell's 1950 breakthrough open the classic era.
The Nashville Sound eclipses it on the charts, but Jones, Bakersfield and 1980s neotraditionalists keep it alive.

nodes.phaseNote: Editorial shading, not a measured ranking: emergence in early-1940s Texas dance halls, a late-1940s–1950s golden age, then a continuing established style. The former 1960 end and 'niche' phase were removed because honky-tonk remained an active idiom (Jones, George Strait's back-to-basics honky-tonk).

nodes.name: Horrorcore
nodes.description: A lyrical and theatrical branch of rap that uses horror imagery, macabre storytelling and shock aesthetics. Its artists range from Houston groups to Detroit’s Insane Clown Posse, with distinct approaches under the same broad label.
nodes.phaseNote: Horror-themed rap antecedents predate the mid-1990s genre label; the name and the artists grouped under it have contested histories. No complete prominence curve is assigned.

nodes.name: House
nodes.description: A post-disco electronic dance music tradition formed in Chicago club culture and developed through Black and queer DJs, producers and dancers. It became a global family of distinct local scenes and subgenres.

phases.note: The Warehouse’s opening and related queer Black and Latino Chicago club networks provide a scene anchor; house’s precise origins remain contested and developed over years.
Early Chicago house records such as “On & On” mark the transition from club practice to recorded production; first-record claims are contested.
“Jack Your Body” charted in the UK from January 1987 and later reached No. 1, a specific crossover milestone rather than global genre peak.

nodes.phaseNote: Milestones distinguish Chicago club culture, early records and one UK crossover event. Removed 1985 “golden age,” 1990 and 1996 generalized established markers because they lacked a stable global or regional measure. House continued as a wide family of local scenes and subgenres.

nodes.name: Hyphy
nodes.description: A Bay Area rap movement and party sound associated with energetic production, local slang, dance and car culture. Mac Dre, E-40 and Keak da Sneak are among its best-known figures.
nodes.phaseNote: The Bay Area movement was prominent in 2000s discourse, with documented national media visibility in the mid-2000s; these markers do not establish a genre-wide peak or endpoint. No complete prominence curve is assigned.

nodes.name: IDM / intelligent dance music
nodes.description: A broad label for experimental electronic music associated with Warp’s Artificial Intelligence releases and later scenes. The term became visible through an online discussion list in 1993; artists and listeners have criticized “intelligent” as a value-laden tag, and many prefer other descriptions.

nodes.name: Impressionism
nodes.description: A late-19th- and early-20th-century compositional style associated especially with Debussy and Ravel, using color, modal or whole-tone harmony and fluid forms. “Impressionism” is an imperfect retrospective label that Debussy resisted.

nodes.name: Indie rock
nodes.description: Rock identity that grew from independent production and distribution networks into a broad stylistic category; musical conventions vary widely by scene and decade.
nodes.phaseNote: No lifecycle phases retained: scholarly sources document scene and infrastructure shifts, not a single genre-wide peak or transition into niche status.

nodes.name: Industrial metal
nodes.description: A metal style that combines distorted guitar riffs with industrial electronics, samples and mechanical production. Ministry and Nine Inch Nails helped bring the sound to wider audiences.

nodes.name: Italo disco
nodes.description: An Italian-centered electronic dance style that developed through disco, independent production and international record circulation. Despite its name, it remained marginally recognized in Italy; later niche listening, DJ sets and reissues sustained it after its early-1980s peak.

nodes.name: J-pop
nodes.description: A broad and changing label for Japanese popular music. “J-pop” entered radio usage in the late 1980s and expanded during the 1990s, while Japanese popular music itself has a much longer history.

nodes.name: Jazz
nodes.description: African American music emerging in New Orleans around the turn of the twentieth century, built on improvisation, rhythmic interplay, and blues traditions. The umbrella for many distinct jazz styles.

phases.note: New Orleans beginnings at the turn of the 20th century.
The first jazz record (ODJB, February 1917) becomes a national hit; Jazz Age and swing era follow.
The swing era ends in the mid-1940s; jazz continues as a diversified art music.

nodes.phaseNote: Editorial shading, not a measured ranking: emergence around 1900 (Britannica), mass popularity from the first jazz record in 1917 through the swing era (Smithsonian, Britannica), and continuing but less dominant presence after the mid-1940s. The former 1915–2010 “golden age” was too long and was split at the end of the swing era.

nodes.name: Jazz fusion
nodes.description: Jazz improvisation meets rock amplification, electric instruments, and funk rhythms. An evolving family of approaches rather than a single formula.

phases.note: Late-1960s jazz musicians adopt rock rhythms and electric instruments.
Davis’s In a Silent Way and Bitches Brew (1969) open fusion’s peak; Mahavishnu, Weather Report, Headhunters in the early 1970s.
After a decade of 1970s popularity fusion continues beside smooth jazz; Grammy jazz-fusion category through the 1980s.

nodes.phaseNote: Editorial shading, not a measured ranking: emergence in the late 1960s, a peak from Davis’s 1969 albums through the 1970s (Britannica, Carnegie Hall), then continued activity. The former 1980 end and 1978 niche phase were removed because fusion kept a Grammy category and active practitioners into the 1980s and beyond.

nodes.name: Jazz rap
nodes.description: A hip-hop branch that places jazz sampling, instrumentation and improvisational ideas alongside rap. Groups such as A Tribe Called Quest, De La Soul and Gang Starr helped establish its distinctive sound.

nodes.name: Jùjú
nodes.description: A Yoruba popular music tradition from Nigeria, shaped by interlocking guitars, percussion and talking drums. Its ensembles expanded dramatically in the mid-twentieth century.

nodes.name: Jungle
nodes.description: A Black British club and sound-system formation that emerged from the UK rave continuum in the early 1990s, bringing chopped breakbeats into dialogue with Jamaican sound-system practices, reggae and dancehall bass, MCs and pirate radio. It developed into multiple branches and later drum-and-bass scenes.

nodes.name: K-pop
nodes.description: South Korean popular music and a changing industry category that blends local language and performance conventions with global pop, hip-hop, R&B and electronic production. First-generation groups appeared in the early 1990s; later generations and the Korean Wave expanded its international reach.

nodes.name: Tuvan throat singing (xöömei)
nodes.description: Tuvan vocal tradition in which one singer sustains a drone while articulating harmonic melodies above it, rooted in herders' imitation of animals, wind and water. The circa-1800 start is a placeholder for a far older oral practice; the first commercial Tuvan discs appeared in 1934.

phases.note: Placeholder for an already-established pastoral oral tradition; its origin cannot be dated.
First Tuvan music discs (Moscow, 1934); Soviet state ensembles later professionalize performance.
Smithsonian Folkways' Tuva CD (1990), Huun-Huur-Tu (1992) and 1993 US tours bring xöömei to world-music audiences.

nodes.phaseNote: Editorial shading, not a measured ranking. Circa 1800 is a low-confidence placeholder: Levin (via Huun-Huur-Tu) and the BBC describe xöömei as an old practice invented by nomadic herders, but no source dates its origin. 1934 marks the first Tuvan recordings (documentation, not invention); 1990 marks international recognition. No golden age is asserted.

nodes.name: Krautrock

phases.note: Approximate anchor for the late-1960s emergence described in the scholarship.
Early-1970s creative peak of the original scene (debuts and key albums by Faust, Can, Neu! and others).
Scholarship frames the movement as thriving from the late 1960s to the mid-1970s; it was a marginal force commercially and the original scene dispersed afterwards.
Rediscovery traced from the mid-1990s (Julian Cope's Krautrocksampler, 1995), followed by catalogue reissues and a 2000s wave of Krautrock-inspired bands.

nodes.phaseNote: Editorial shading: emergence c. 1968, the original scene’s early-1970s peak, a low-profile phase after the movement dispersed in the mid-1970s, and established canonical status after the mid-1990s rediscovery. Boundaries are approximate; this is not a measured popularity ranking.
nodes.description: An umbrella label, coined by the British music press in the early 1970s, for the experimental rock that emerged in West Germany in the late 1960s. Can, Amon Düül II, Faust, Neu! and early Kraftwerk took very different approaches to repetitive rhythm, improvisation, tape collage, and electronics.

nodes.name: Kwaito
nodes.description: A South African electronic dance and popular music form that emerged around the political transition of the early 1990s. Its sound and meaning developed through local youth culture and global musical flows; scholarship cautions against treating it as a simple, singular response to apartheid’s end.

nodes.name: Latin music
nodes.description: An umbrella category that gathered diverse Latin American and diasporic styles within the United States music industry and popular culture. It does not describe one sound or a shared origin; the category took shape in U.S. markets during the 1930s.

nodes.name: Latin jazz
nodes.description: A family of jazz styles shaped by Latin American and Caribbean rhythms, including Afro-Cuban and Brazilian elements. It developed through exchanges between jazz musicians and Latin bandleaders from the 1940s onward.

phases.note: Machito and his Afro-Cubans founded in New York in 1940 under Mario Bauzá; “Tanga” (early 1940s).
Cubop (Gillespie–Pozo “Manteca”, Kenton, 1947), Afro-Cuban Jazz Suite (1950) and the Palladium era to 1966.
From the 1970s a diversified field (Irakere, Fort Apache Band, new soloists).

nodes.phaseNote: Editorial shading, not a measured ranking: Britannica dates the fusion to Machito’s 1940 orchestra, describes vigorous growth from Cubop through the 1950s–60s, and a diversified, still-acclaimed field from the 1970s. The former 1955–2010 golden age was too long; boundaries are approximate.

nodes.name: Math rock
nodes.description: An experimental rock style associated with intricate, irregular meters, angular guitar figures and tightly coordinated ensemble playing. The label is a loose critical category; some associated musicians have resisted it.

nodes.name: Medieval music
nodes.description: A broad historical span of Western sacred and secular music, including chant, troubadour song, instrumental repertories and early polyphony. Dates mark a conventional era boundary, not the end of living repertories or practices.

nodes.name: Merengue
nodes.description: A Dominican music-and-dance tradition with regional and ensemble variations, including merengue típico and later orchestral forms. Its 19th-century origins are debated; it remains central to Dominican culture and has continued to evolve.

nodes.name: Metalcore
nodes.description: A hybrid style linking hardcore punk and heavy metal. Metallic hardcore scenes developed in the late 1980s and 1990s; the more codified, commercially visible metalcore category expanded in the 2000s and continues in multiple waves.

nodes.name: Minimal techno
nodes.description: A techno approach built around sparse materials, repetition, and small changes over time. Detroit figures including Robert Hood and Daniel Bell helped establish an influential early-1990s strand; later scenes developed distinct versions.
nodes.phaseNote: Early-1990s Detroit development and the 1994 Minimal Nation release are documented milestones, not a sole origin or a complete prominence history. No complete prominence curve is assigned.

nodes.name: Minimalism
nodes.description: A diverse tendency in postwar experimental music emphasizing repetition, sustained tones, modular patterns and gradual processes. La Monte Young’s sustained-tone works, Terry Riley’s In C (1964), and later music by Steve Reich and Philip Glass became central reference points; the label and boundaries remain debated.
nodes.phaseNote: Foundational work developed in the 1960s, while early-1980s institutional recognition is a distinct historical milestone rather than a measure of global listening. No complete prominence curve is assigned.

nodes.name: Modal jazz
nodes.description: A jazz approach that builds improvisation around modes and longer harmonic spaces rather than frequent chord changes. Miles Davis’s 1958 “Milestones” and 1959 Kind of Blue are key documented milestones, but modal practice continued as one strand within jazz.

nodes.name: Modern classical
nodes.description: A broad, shifting label for Western art music since the late 19th century, spanning modernism, contemporary composition and experimental work. It is not a single sound or universally agreed period; more specific movements and compositional practices are clearer categories.

nodes.name: Neo-soul
nodes.description: A 1990s-forward R&B movement that reworked soul performance and songwriting through hip-hop-era rhythms, production and artist-led album making.
nodes.phaseNote: D’Angelo’s 1995 Brown Sugar is an early commercial marker; the neo-soul label later encompassed a broader marketed category. No complete prominence curve is assigned.

nodes.name: New jack swing
nodes.description: A late-1980s R&B style that fused soul singing and melodic hooks with hip-hop rhythms, sampling and production. Producer Teddy Riley and groups including Guy and New Edition helped define its sound.

nodes.name: New wave
nodes.description: A historically shifting pop-rock field that emerged from mid-1970s punk and moved toward more accessible song forms, synthesizers, art-school ideas and dance rhythms. Its U.S. mainstream prominence crested in the early 1980s; the label remains in use for later music and retrospectives.

nodes.name: Noise rock
nodes.description: A noisy underground rock field that foregrounds distortion, feedback, dissonance and unconventional performance. It overlaps with punk, no wave, post-punk and experimental music; the boundaries between these labels were often loose.

nodes.name: Nu metal
nodes.description: A 1990s heavy style that combined metal riffs with hip-hop rhythms, alternative rock, turntable or electronic textures, and a wide range of vocal approaches. The scene was diverse and its boundaries remain debated.

nodes.name: Old-school rap
nodes.description: An early New York rap style built around party rhymes, DJ-led breaks, call-and-response and the block-party culture from which hip-hop emerged. The label is retrospective; the style continues to be performed.

nodes.name: Pansori
nodes.description: A Korean epic vocal art in which one singer narrates and sings a long story with a drummer. Its surviving repertory and performance practice carry regional histories and continue to evolve.

phases.note: Circa 1700 represents the late-seventeenth/early-eighteenth-century origin estimate; the earliest known written mention is dated 1754.
Broad nineteenth-century anchor for expansion among social classes and the master-singer tradition, not an exact boundary.

nodes.phaseNote: The National Institute of Korean History estimates an origin in the late seventeenth to early eighteenth century; UNESCO gives the seventeenth century. Circa 1700 is an approximate origin, not a first-documentation date. Nineteenth-century expansion and the 1964 safeguarding designation are documented; no measured popularity peak or continuous unchanging practice is implied.

nodes.name: Peking opera
nodes.description: A Chinese operatic tradition that took shape in Beijing from regional theatrical forms, combining stylized singing, speech, gesture, martial arts and percussion-led orchestras.

nodes.name: Pop
nodes.description: A broad, changing popular-music category shaped by memorable songwriting, recording technology, mass media and cross-pollination with many styles; it is not a single-origin genre.

nodes.name: Pop-punk
nodes.description: Punk-derived rock pairing brisk tempos and power-chord energy with concise melodies and pop songwriting; later waves differ from early punk-pop.
nodes.phaseNote: No complete prominence curve is assigned. The graph date marks late-1970s punk-pop precursors and early contemporary usage, not a fully stabilized modern subgenre label. AllMusic documents a significant mainstream-popularization wave for Green Day/Weezer in 1994; no single lifecycle applies to later waves.

nodes.name: Post-hardcore
nodes.description: Diverse outgrowth of hardcore punk retaining intensity while exploring broader dynamics, structures and textures through distinct regional scenes.

nodes.name: Post-punk
nodes.description: Punk's independence redirected into experimental structures, angular guitars, and influences from dub, funk, and electronic music.

nodes.name: Post-rock
nodes.description: Contested term for experimental rock using rock instrumentation while moving beyond conventional song forms, often toward texture, repetition or studio construction.

nodes.name: Progressive rock
nodes.description: Rock expanded through extended suites, shifting meters, concept albums, and borrowings from classical music and jazz, crystallising in late-1960s Britain with King Crimson, Yes and Genesis. It lost critical and industry favour in the punk era but continued through neo-prog and later revival waves.

phases.note: King Crimson's 1969 debut is widely treated as refining a nascent genre into its defining form.
Prog’s classic era is usually said to end in the late 1970s as punk diverted press, A&R and radio attention.
Renewed visibility around 2009–2010: a dedicated Prog magazine, festival prog stages and prog-influenced chart rock.

nodes.phaseNote: Editorial shading: emergence from late-1960s psychedelia, a classic peak from 1969 to the late 1970s, then continuing lower-profile activity with a modest later revival. The previous 1975 end date was removed because the genre did not stop. Not a measured popularity ranking.

nodes.name: Psychedelic rock
nodes.description: Rock reshaped in the mid-1960s by LSD-era counterculture, studio experimentation, droning and Indian-influenced timbres, and long improvisations, with San Francisco and London as key centres. Its original wave peaked around 1967 and fed into progressive rock, hard rock, and later neo-psychedelic revivals.

phases.note: The first self-described psychedelic album appeared in October 1966; within a year psychedelia dominated, culminating in 1967’s Summer of Love.
The original psychedelic era fizzled out by the end of the 1960s; its ideas continued in hard rock and prog and returned in neo-psychedelic waves from the early 1980s.

nodes.phaseNote: Editorial shading: a brief mid-1960s emergence, a 1966–1969 peak, then lower-profile continuation and periodic revivals. The previous 1970 end date was removed because the style continued. Not a measured popularity ranking.

nodes.name: Psytrance
nodes.description: A psychedelic electronic dance style that developed from Goa trance and later globalized through festival and club scenes.

nodes.name: Punk rock
nodes.description: Short, urgent songs and a do-it-yourself ethos challenged rock spectacle and helped establish independent musical networks.

nodes.name: Qawwali
nodes.description: A South Asian Sufi devotional song tradition performed in shrine and community settings. Its performance practices and meanings are tied to particular religious and social contexts.

nodes.name: Rhythm and blues
nodes.description: A shifting name for Black American popular music, first used for postwar blues-based dance and vocal music and later covering several distinct R&B traditions.

nodes.name: Reggae
nodes.description: Jamaican popular music that developed from ska and rocksteady, with a strong bass-and-drum foundation and many later branches including roots reggae, dub and dancehall.
nodes.phaseNote: No complete prominence curve is assigned. The first phase marks the emergence of reggae as a distinct Jamaican style around 1968. The second marks the documented roots-reggae golden age, approximately 1968–1983, identified by Smithsonian Folklife. These are different scopes (genre emergence and roots-reggae era); graph phase endpoints are necessarily approximate.

nodes.name: Reggaeton
nodes.description: A Spanish-language Caribbean urban dance style that developed through Puerto Rican and Panamanian scenes, blending reggae and dancehall rhythms with hip-hop and electronic production.

nodes.name: Renaissance music
nodes.description: Interwoven vocal polyphony, masses, motets, and madrigals in Renaissance Europe. Era boundaries are approximate; the repertoire is still performed.

nodes.name: Rock
nodes.description: A broad family of popular music that grew from mid-century rock and roll into many guitar-centered and electronic, vocal, and studio-based forms. It overlaps with, but is not identical to, the narrower early rock-and-roll category.

phases.note: The mid-1960s British bands are credited with turning rock & roll into a modern, experimental rock era.
Approximate marker for rock losing its position as the dominant popular genre; press reports on this shift were blocked during review.

nodes.phaseNote: Editorial staging of emergence from rock and roll, a long peak from the mid-1960s, and continuing but less dominant activity from the 2010s. Boundaries are approximate and not measured popularity data.

nodes.name: Rock and roll
nodes.description: A mid-20th-century popular style formed through African American rhythm and blues, country, gospel, and other regional traditions. It reached broad youth and national audiences in the United States in the mid-1950s, while its roots and early contributors predate that commercial breakthrough.

phases.note: Broad mid-century convergence; roots in African American blues, R&B, gospel and country traditions predate the label. The commercial term and music do not begin on one exact date.
Mid-1950s national youth-market breakthrough, following earlier regional Black music and recordings.

nodes.phaseNote: Approximate U.S. popular-music visibility: related Black and country traditions predate the mid-1950s, when rock and roll reached broad national and youth audiences. The phases mark that commercial breakthrough and subsequent diversification, not the invention of its roots or a global popularity curve.

nodes.name: Rocksteady
nodes.description: A short-lived Jamaican style that slowed ska’s pulse and foregrounded bass, vocal harmony and a relaxed groove; it bridged ska and reggae.

phases.note: Jamaica Information Service dates the short heyday from around summer 1966 to spring 1968. Label describes prominence, not a measured dataset.

nodes.phaseNote: Provisional editorial shading for a short, concentrated prominence window. The dates follow this graph’s estimated period; they are not measured popularity data, and the exact boundaries need source-level review.

nodes.name: Romantic music
nodes.description: Expanded orchestras, expressive harmony, virtuoso soloists, and musical storytelling. Dates describe a historical era whose repertoire remains active.

nodes.name: Russian folk
nodes.description: A broad label for diverse Russian vernacular song and instrumental traditions. This node is a starting point for regional and community-specific documentation, not a single uniform national style.

phases.note: Documentation anchor: song collections (Lvov–Prach, 1790) record an already old peasant oral tradition.
Andreyev's folk-instrument orchestra (1896) and Piatnitsky's choir (1911) bring folk to urban stages.
Pokrovsky's village-style revival gains international world-music attention.

nodes.phaseNote: Editorial shading, not a measured ranking. The circa-1800 start is a documentation anchor for a much older oral tradition, not its origin; later markers follow professionalization (1896–1930s state ensembles) and the 1970s authentic-performance revival. The former 'emerging' first phase was removed as unsupported.

nodes.name: Outlaw country

period.estimateNote: Landmark 1973 recordings and an Outlaw program in Nashville anchor the movement’s early years.

nodes.description: A 1970s country movement associated with artists seeking greater control over what they recorded and how they recorded it. The 1976 compilation Wanted! The Outlaws brought the movement to a national audience.

nodes.name: Salsa
nodes.description: A pan-Caribbean and New York-centered dance-music movement drawing especially on Cuban son and related Afro-Cuban forms, with distinct regional histories.

nodes.name: Samba
nodes.description: A Brazilian music and dance family whose forms vary by region and setting, including Rio de Janeiro’s urban popular and Carnival traditions.

nodes.name: Serialism
nodes.description: A compositional approach that organizes musical elements through ordered series; its most influential early form was twelve-tone technique. Schoenberg, Berg and Webern were central to its development.

nodes.name: Neoclassicism

period.estimateNote: The style became established in the 1920s, with earlier precedents.

nodes.description: A twentieth-century composition movement that adapted older Classical and Baroque forms and textures. Stravinsky’s Pulcinella and Prokofiev’s Classical Symphony illustrate different ways of reworking earlier musical models.

nodes.name: Shoegaze
nodes.description: Late-1980s/early-1990s British indie rock marked by layered guitar effects, dense noise, blended vocals and introspective songwriting.

nodes.name: Hardcore punk

period.estimateNote: Early hardcore scenes took shape in the late 1970s and early 1980s.

nodes.description: A branch of punk rock that developed in the late 1970s and early 1980s. Early scenes in Southern California and Washington, D.C., pushed punk toward faster tempos, louder playing and a more abrasive sound.

nodes.name: Ska
nodes.description: Jamaican dance music that developed in the late 1950s from local performance traditions and American rhythm and blues, with horns and an accented offbeat. Ska became a precursor to rocksteady and reggae, then circulated internationally through later revival scenes including British 2 Tone and third-wave ska.

phases.note: Late-1950s Jamaican emergence; style was popularized in the early 1960s by artists and studio groups including the Skatalites.
Approximate marker for the British 2 Tone revival and a transnational phase; not an end to Jamaican ska or a measured peak.

nodes.phaseNote: Provisional editorial staging of emergence, the defining prominence wave, and later niche status. Boundaries are approximate and not a measured ranking; the source record should be checked for each transition.

nodes.name: Roots reggae
nodes.description: A Jamaican reggae style closely tied to Rastafari. Its songs gave voice to Black history, spiritual belief and African identity in the years after independence.

nodes.name: Son cubano
nodes.description: Cuban song-and-dance tradition formed through Afro-Cuban and Spanish-language practices, later providing an important basis for son montuno and salsa.

nodes.name: Soukous
nodes.description: Congolese dance-music style developed from Congolese rumba, with interlocking electric guitars, vocals and an extended dance section often called sebene. The term soukous has been used differently across Africa and Europe, and should not be projected onto all earlier Congolese rumba.
nodes.phaseNote: The broad 1960s transition from Congolese rumba toward styles later called soukous has contested naming and boundaries. No complete prominence curve is assigned.

nodes.name: Soul

phases.note: Ray Charles’ 1955 recording is an early gospel-to-R&B milestone; Carnegie Hall dates the style’s emergence to the late 1950s.
Carnegie Hall describes soul as a distinctive popular style in the 1960s.
Carnegie Hall places its popularity peak in the mid-1970s; this dates a U.S. commercial peak, not an end to the genre.

nodes.phaseNote: Broad markers for U.S. recorded popular-music emergence, distinct 1960s identity, and mid-1970s popularity peak. The peak is source-described; labels are a simplified editorial timeline, not a global chart measurement.
nodes.description: A Black American popular-music family formed through gospel and rhythm-and-blues practices, with distinct label, regional, and studio traditions. Soul became a prominent crossover style in the 1960s; later artists continued to rework its vocal and musical approaches.

nodes.name: Chicago blues

period.estimateNote: This placement marks the emergence of the electric style around the end of World War II.

nodes.description: An urban blues style shaped in Chicago as musicians arriving from the American South brought their traditions into the city. Electric guitar and lead harmonica became characteristic sounds.

nodes.name: Southern rap
nodes.description: A regional umbrella for rap scenes across the U.S. South, including distinct sounds from Atlanta, Houston, New Orleans, Memphis and Miami. It spans party music, storytelling, gangsta rap and many other approaches.

phases.note: Regional rap scenes developed across multiple southern cities in the 1980s and early 1990s; there is no single Southern origin scene.
Late-1990s expansion of labels and national popular usage of Dirty South is documented; this label is not synonymous with all Southern rap.

nodes.phaseNote: Provisional editorial staging of emergence, a defining recognition wave, and continuing activity in the current graph snapshot. These broad markers are not measured popularity data; source-level review remains needed.

nodes.name: Spiritual jazz
nodes.description: A broad jazz current that joined improvisation with spiritual, devotional and transcendent themes, especially in the 1960s and 1970s. The label covers varied musical approaches, not a single formal sound.

nodes.name: Stoner rock
nodes.description: Heavy rock built around fuzzed guitar, low tunings, groove and extended riffs, drawing on hard rock, psychedelia and metal.

nodes.name: Surf rock
nodes.description: Instrumental rock associated with Southern California surf culture, featuring reverb-heavy electric guitar and rhythmic drive; the style later influenced wider rock music.
nodes.phaseNote: No complete prominence curve is assigned. The c.1959 start represents the earliest Southern California surf-instrumental scene; 1961 marks Dick Dale’s “Let’s Go Trippin’” and a broader surf-music craze. This phase describes a documented early-1960s wave only. Later revival and surf-influenced music continue.

nodes.name: Southern rock

period.estimateNote: The Allman Brothers Band formed in 1969, an early milestone for the style.

nodes.description: A rock style that emerged in the American South around the turn of the 1970s. The Allman Brothers Band’s blend of rock and roll, blues, country and jazz helped establish the genre.

nodes.name: Swing
nodes.description: A jazz style and dance-music idiom built around swinging rhythms, arranged sections, and improvisation, performed by large bands and smaller groups. It became the dominant U.S. popular-music form in the 1930s and 1940s, while later swing traditions continued in different settings.
nodes.phaseNote: No complete prominence curve is assigned. The swing era of roughly 1935–45 marks big-band swing’s concentrated US popularity; the broader swing style predates that period and continues in performance. The graph’s single sourced popularity phase should not be read as a style endpoint.

nodes.name: Synth-pop
nodes.description: Pop-oriented electronic music in which synthesizers and electronic production are prominent, alongside voices, guitars, drums, and other instruments. The style emerged across several scenes in the late 1970s and early 1980s; Kraftwerk and British new wave acts were influential, but neither alone defines it.
nodes.phaseNote: No complete prominence curve is assigned. The first marker covers late-1970s formation and precursor usage; the early-1980s marks a major British commercial wave. Synth-pop persisted beyond the 1985 peak and revived repeatedly; phases describe selected history, not terminal lifecycle.

nodes.name: Dance-pop
nodes.description: Dance-pop pairs pop hooks and compact song structures with rhythms made for the dance floor. Madonna brought the style from New York clubs to a mass audience in the early 1980s.

nodes.name: Hyperpop

period.estimateNote: The date marks the 2019 breakthrough of 100 gecs. The sound took shape earlier in the decade.

nodes.description: An experimental strain of pop that pushes digital production to extremes with distorted synths and pitch-shifted vocals. Early PC Music releases laid groundwork, and 100 gecs helped bring the sound to a wider audience in the late 2010s.

nodes.name: Synthwave
nodes.description: An internet-mediated electronic genre reimagining 1980s film scores, synth-pop, game music and electronic production through nostalgic, cinematic synth textures. It emerged in the mid-2000s and gained visibility in the early 2010s.

phases.note: Scholarship dates the genre’s existence to the mid-2000s.
A peer-reviewed study identifies early 2010s mainstream visibility and links a boost to the 2011 film Drive and Kavinsky’s “Nightcall”; this is a visibility marker, not a golden age.

nodes.phaseNote: Broad scene emergence and later mainstream visibility markers, not measured popularity rankings. Synthwave continued beyond the 2010s.

nodes.name: Tango
nodes.description: A music-and-dance tradition that developed around the Río de la Plata, especially Buenos Aires and Montevideo, with African, European and local histories that should not be reduced to a single origin story.

phases.note: Approximate emergence of tango in the Río de la Plata; scholarship emphasizes contested, intertwined origins.
International circulation documented by the Library of Congress’s 1914 US tango dance manual.

nodes.phaseNote: These phases mark approximate local emergence and later transnational circulation, not a measured popularity curve. Tango has changed through the 20th and 21st centuries.

nodes.name: Mambo
nodes.description: Cuban dance music built on syncopated riffs and driving percussion. Pérez Prado’s recordings in Mexico and the mambo bands at New York’s Palladium Ballroom brought it to a wider audience.

nodes.name: Latin trap

period.estimateNote: The timeline uses 2012 as a marker for the emerging Puerto Rican online scene. Earlier recordings already experimented with the sound.

nodes.description: Spanish-language rap that adapts the bass-heavy beats of Southern U.S. trap. An early-2010s scene in Puerto Rico grew through SoundCloud and local music sites before reaching a wider audience.

nodes.name: Tech house
nodes.description: A club style combining house grooves and arrangements with techno’s stripped-down timbres and repetition; borders with minimal techno and progressive house shift across scenes.

nodes.name: Progressive house
nodes.description: A house style that emerged in the early 1990s. Early British records layered dub-influenced bass and breakbeats over a steady house kick.

nodes.name: Techno
nodes.description: A family of electronic dance music first named and codified around Detroit in the mid-1980s, then developed through distinct scenes across the world. Repetitive machine rhythms and studio production are common reference points, while sound and social context vary widely.

nodes.name: Thrash metal
nodes.description: Fast, aggressive heavy-metal style developed through early-1980s underground scenes, especially in California, combining extreme speed, tightly articulated riffs and influences from punk and earlier metal. Metallica, Slayer, Megadeth and Anthrax are commonly grouped as the US Big Four, though this simplifies a wider scene.

phases.note: Early-1980s formation across several scenes and bands; not one definitive origin event.
Mid- to late-1980s critical and subcultural consolidation; this does not bound continuing production or performance.

nodes.phaseNote: Provisional editorial shading for a short, concentrated prominence window. The dates follow this graph’s estimated period; they are not measured popularity data, and the exact boundaries need source-level review.

nodes.name: Power metal
nodes.description: Power metal emphasizes fast playing, clear high-register singing and strong melodies. West German bands such as Helloween helped establish a sound that often turned to fantasy and mythology for its lyrics.

nodes.name: Progressive metal
nodes.description: A blend of heavy metal and progressive rock that took shape in the 1980s. Shifting meters are a hallmark, and Queensrÿche’s 1988 concept album Operation: Mindcrime was an early landmark.

nodes.name: Trance
nodes.description: A family of electronic dance styles with sustained rhythmic motion and extended, often melodic development. Early German scenes, especially Frankfurt around 1990–92, helped shape the genre alongside wider European club networks. Later substyles developed distinct sounds and audiences.

phases.note: Frankfurt projects including Dance 2 Trance and Jam & Spoon are early documented scene markers; the wider genre has multiple roots and no uncontested birth event.
Robert Miles’s Children reached number two in the UK, demonstrating crossover in that market only; it does not establish worldwide genre-wide popularity.

nodes.phaseNote: Medium confidence for both phase anchors. Frankfurt activity around 1990 marks early formation. The 1996 UK chart milestone marks crossover in one market. Later trance releases continued to chart.

nodes.name: Acid techno
nodes.description: A techno style built around the squelching tones of the Roland TB-303. London’s free-party scene helped establish the sound in the early 1990s.

nodes.name: Trap rap
nodes.description: A Southern US hip-hop style associated with stark programmed drums, heavy low end and narratives rooted in Atlanta trap culture; later usage broadened considerably.
nodes.phaseNote: No complete prominence curve is assigned. The 1995 start marks early lyrical use and Atlanta precursors, not a fully formed sonic genre. Trap became recognized as a distinct sound in the early 2000s; T.I.’s Trap Muzik (2003) marks an influential articulation, not sole invention. Later electronic trap and pop uses expanded the label.

nodes.name: Trip-hop
nodes.description: A press-coined label for downtempo, sample-based, jazz-, funk- and soul-inflected experimental breakbeat music associated with 1990s UK scenes. The Bristol Sound is related but not identical; Massive Attack, Portishead and Tricky have rejected the trip-hop label.
nodes.phaseNote: No complete prominence curve is assigned. The early-1990s start marks the emergence of the associated UK/Bristol downtempo scene. 1994 is a label/popularization milestone, while the Bristol Sound is neither identical to nor universally accepted as trip-hop. The scene persists through later releases; phases are not a measured popularity curve.

nodes.name: UK garage

phases.note: Mid-1990s development through clubs, imported US garage, pirate radio and rave networks; this marks scene formation, not a single origin event.
Turn-of-century UK chart and national club visibility; editorial prominence marker rather than a measured peak.
Later UK garage activity and revival; evidence supports continued scene presence, not a distinct synchronized revival phase.

nodes.phaseNote: Approximate UK chart and club visibility: scene growth in the mid-1990s, chart breakthrough around the turn of the millennium, and later revival waves are documented by charts and specialist histories. These intervals describe UK visibility, not the genre’s worldwide popularity or the persistence of its underground scenes.
nodes.description: A London-centered dance style that developed in the mid-1990s from circulating US garage records and UK club, pirate-radio, and rave practices. Speed garage and 2-step brought different rhythms and production choices; later branches include grime and dubstep, without making them interchangeable genres.

nodes.name: Liquid drum and bass
nodes.description: Also called liquid funk, this melodic strand of drum and bass emerged in the late 1990s, drawing on soul and funk and often featuring vocals.

nodes.name: Vaporwave
nodes.description: An internet-born music and visual culture using slowed, looped and transformed samples—often commercial, lounge and corporate soundtrack material—to engage with consumerism, nostalgia and digital circulation.

phases.note: Scholarship traces the genre to the early 2010s and cites Eccojams (2010) and Far Side Virtual (2011) as formative records.

nodes.phaseNote: Early-2010s emergence marker only. The form and community diversified and its definition remains contested; the prior “golden age,” “established,” and “niche” dates lacked support and were removed.

nodes.name: Ambient house
nodes.description: A late-1980s British club style that grew out of chill-out rooms, combining house music with ambient textures and sampled sounds.

nodes.name: Vocal jazz
nodes.description: Jazz singing that treats standards as material for interpretation, rhythmic phrasing and improvisation, rather than simply presenting a fixed popular-song performance. It spans big-band vocalists, small-group singers and later generations.
nodes.phaseNote: No complete prominence curve is assigned. Vocal jazz reaches back to jazz’s early recorded decades. A 1930s/40s phase marks the rise and visibility of major singers and jazz vocal interpretation; it is not the origin or endpoint of vocal jazz, which continues.

nodes.name: New Orleans jazz

period.estimateNote: The start marks the formative late-nineteenth-century period described by the National Park Service.

nodes.description: An early New Orleans style of jazz known for collective improvisation. Cornet, clarinet and trombone often improvised interlocking parts, drawing on the city’s brass-band and dance traditions.

nodes.name: Soul jazz
nodes.description: A jazz style that grew out of hard bop in the late 1950s. Blues phrasing and strong grooves give the music its character, and small groups often feature a Hammond organ.

nodes.name: West Coast rap
nodes.description: A regional family of styles associated with California and the wider western United States, including gangsta rap, G-funk and later Bay Area movements. Its sound and subject matter have never been uniform.

phases.note: NMAAHC traces West Coast hip-hop development to the late 1970s.
AllMusic describes N.W.A.’s Straight Outta Compton as a landmark that established a more identifiable West Coast style.

nodes.phaseNote: Regional scene formation and a widely cited late-1980s consolidation marker. Removed the unsupported exact 1994 “golden age” and 2018 status marker; regional traditions continue.

nodes.name: Emo rap
nodes.description: A branch of hip-hop that reached a wide audience through SoundCloud in the late 2010s. Its melodic delivery and lyrics about heartbreak and isolation often draw on emo and pop-punk.

nodes.name: Accordion
nodes.description: Bellows-driven free-reed instrument named in Cyrill Demian and his sons’ 1829 Vienna patent. The patented five-button chord instrument differs from later melody-and-accompaniment keyboard designs. Accordion-making and forms spread and diversified across regions, including in Colombian cumbia.

phases.note: Patent-year anchor for Demian’s named accordion, not the invention of free reeds or all modern accordion forms.
French craft-history source describes wider European popularization from around 1860; regional adoption marker, not global prevalence.

nodes.phaseNote: The exact 1829 patent is documented. Later phase marks European spread described by a French instrument-making institution; it is not a worldwide popularity curve.

nodes.name: Auto-Tune
nodes.description: Pitch-correction software released by Antares in 1997. Cher’s 1998 “Believe” made its conspicuous robotic effect widely known; later uses include trap, where the software became a creative instrument as well as a corrective tool.
nodes.phaseNote: The first marker is the documented commercial release; the second marks the highly visible stylistic use on “Believe.” Scholarly work documents later routine and creative use in 2010s trap. Removed unsupported 2000 “golden age” and 2010 establishment markers: no evidence here supports a general popularity curve.

nodes.name: Balalaika
nodes.description: Three-stringed Russian folk lute documented in 1688. Vasily Andreyev revived its popularity and standardized concert forms for orchestral ensembles in the late 19th century; its ancestry remains debated.
nodes.phaseNote: The 1688 marker is the earliest documented reference cited by Powerhouse, not the instrument’s invention. The 1886 marker denotes Andreyev’s public revival and later concert standardization. Removed the unsupported 1950 marker; Powerhouse describes Soviet-era prominence broadly (1917–1991), without evidence for a specific 1950 transition.

nodes.name: Bandoneon
nodes.description: A square-ended, button-operated free-reed instrument developed from German concertinas in the mid-nineteenth century and associated with instrument dealer Heinrich Band, whose name it bears. It became central to tango in the Río de la Plata after reaching Argentina around 1870; it is one regional branch of a wider concertina family.

phases.note: Mid-century development and naming are better supported than one exact invention year.
Approximate early-twentieth-century adoption in Río de la Plata tango, not a worldwide popularity threshold.

nodes.phaseNote: These mark development in Germany and later regional adoption in tango. Removed the unsupported exact 1855 birth claim; surviving sources distinguish instrument development, trade naming and arrival in Argentina.

nodes.name: Banjo
nodes.description: Gourd-bodied banjo predecessors were developed in the Americas by enslaved Africans and their descendants from West African instrument traditions. The instrument was documented by the 17th century, commercialized in the 19th century, and later became central to old-time and bluegrass music.

phases.note: Early 19th-century minstrel performance spread the banjo and drove commercialization; this marker names a historical expansion, while recognizing the racist blackface context.
Approximate mid-20th-century folk revival consolidated the banjo in Appalachian folk and bluegrass traditions.

nodes.phaseNote: These are qualitative historical markers, not a popularity ranking. The early date is decade-level because the sources checked support 17th-century documentation but do not substantiate a specific year. NPS supports early-19th-century minstrel-era spread/commercialization and a mid-20th-century folk revival.

nodes.name: Bansuri
nodes.description: Side-blown bamboo flute with long roots in South Asian music. Pannalal Ghosh adapted the bansuri for the North Indian classical concert stage in the 1930s–40s; it is now performed as a Hindustani classical solo instrument.
nodes.phaseNote: The 1940s marker describes Pannalal Ghosh’s adaptation for the classical stage, not invention of the flute. Smithsonian Folkways documents a Hindustani bansuri recital recorded in 1974 and released in 1989, showing established performance by then; the exact 1980 adoption threshold is editorial and low-confidence. Removed the unsupported 1960 “golden-age” marker.

nodes.name: Bassoon
nodes.description: Low double-reed woodwind that succeeded the curtal or dulcian. The jointed bassoon form developed in the second half of the 17th century; it became an important bass voice in Baroque continuo and orchestral writing.
nodes.phaseNote: Oxford’s Bate Collection places added keys around 1650 and identifies the curtal as predecessor; the V&A catalogue describes the four-jointed bassoon as a second-half-17th-century modification. The Met documents its Baroque continuo role. Removed unsupported “golden-age” and 1800 transition markers.

nodes.name: Bongos
nodes.description: Pair of small, open-bottomed hand drums developed in eastern Cuba from African-derived drum traditions. The Cuban-born bongos became a distinctive part of son; Smithsonian Folkways notes bongo players on recordings by 1918.
nodes.phaseNote: The circa-1880 origin is retained as a low-confidence late-19th-century estimate: Smithsonian confirms eastern Cuban development but gives no date, and the earliest evidence checked here is bongo performance on 1918 recordings. Removed 1940 “golden-age” and 1960 establishment markers because these sources do not show those instrument-wide transitions.

nodes.name: Cello
nodes.description: Bowed bass member of the violin family whose form developed through experimentation in 16th-century Italy. Early cellos varied in size and string count before later forms became standardized.
nodes.phaseNote: The Met identifies Andrea Amati’s mid-16th-century “King” cello and describes early experimentation in size and string count; its later 1610–20 Amati cello record shows those early forms continued to vary. Removed broad 1700 “golden-age” and 1800 establishment claims because the cited sources do not substantiate those popularity shifts.

nodes.name: Charango
nodes.description: Small fretted Andean lute combining Spanish-guitar features with Indigenous adaptations. The Met says the charango is known from the early 18th century; it is used across Andean musical traditions.
nodes.phaseNote: The early-18th-century origin is supported by the Met curator’s account, while Duke’s collection suggests Potosí/Bolivia and Indigenous makers but cites secondary materials. LOC documents worldwide diffusion of Andean sound through 1960s Nueva Canción; this is indirect evidence for charango visibility, not proof of an instrument-specific peak. Removed the unsupported 1980 marker.

nodes.name: Clarinet
nodes.description: Single-reed woodwind developed from the chalumeau around the beginning of the eighteenth century. Tradition attributes the clarinet to Johann Christoph Denner, but museum and historical sources treat the precise inventor and date cautiously. It later became established in classical, jazz and many other traditions.
nodes.phaseNote: The approximate early-eighteenth-century development marker is documented, while attribution to a single inventor remains disputed. No complete prominence curve is assigned.

nodes.name: Claves
nodes.description: Pair of hardwood sticks struck together. A Cuban music history citing ethnographer Fernando Ortiz places claves in Havana in the 16th–17th centuries; today the sticks articulate clave patterns central to Afro-Cuban music and salsa.
nodes.phaseNote: The early marker follows a secondary Cuban account attributing the Havana origin to Fernando Ortiz; it is a historical attribution, not direct documentary verification. Smithsonian sources document the claves’ present-day structural role in salsa. Removed unsupported 1900 and 1950 prominence transitions.

nodes.name: Conga
nodes.description: Tall, single-headed Afro-Cuban drum, also called tumbadora. The exact origin is uncertain: NPS places its creation among Afro-Cuban dock workers in Matanzas in the late 19th century; a University of Arizona thesis says its earliest mention is in the early 20th century and documents its entry into rumba in the 1930s.
nodes.phaseNote: The late-19th-century start follows NPS, while the specialist thesis distinguishes this proposed development period from the earliest mention (early 20th century) and adoption into rumba (1930s). Removed unsupported 1940 “golden age” and 1960 establishment markers; these sources do not establish a general popularity curve.

nodes.name: Dobro resonator guitar
nodes.description: Trade-name single-cone resonator guitar associated with the Dopyera brothers’ Dobro company, formed around 1928–29. The Smithsonian dates one surviving Dobro guitar to about 1933–37; resonators were designed to increase acoustic volume and later became influential in country and blues.
nodes.phaseNote: The 1928 marker reflects the company/name origin, not a surviving instrument dated that year; Smithsonian’s cataloged Dobro specimen is c.1933–37. Removed later “golden-age” and 1950 establishment markers because no source here supports an instrument-wide popularity curve.

nodes.name: Double bass
nodes.description: Largest and lowest-pitched bowed string instrument in the modern orchestra. Its form draws on both viol and violin-family traditions, and its precise lineage remains debated; it later became common in orchestral, jazz, blues, rockabilly, and bluegrass settings.
nodes.phaseNote: An organology reference places the earliest specimens recognizably leading to the modern double bass in the late 16th century, around the 1590s, while cautioning that they differed from modern basses. Vienna Symphonic Library notes acceptance into opera orchestras around 1700. Removed unsupported 1930s “golden age” and 1950 marker.

nodes.name: Drum kit
nodes.description: A coordinated set of drums, cymbals, pedals, and auxiliary percussion arranged so one player can perform multiple percussion parts. Bass-drum pedals enabled the late-19th-century trap set; the modern drum kit coalesced with early jazz in New Orleans.
nodes.phaseNote: Smithsonian Folkways traces trap sets to late-19th-century pedals and dates Ludwig & Ludwig’s pedal improvement to 1909; its drum-set history links early kit proliferation to New Orleans jazz in the early 20th century. These are development/use milestones, not a popularity ranking. Removed unsupported 1930 golden-age and 1950 establishment phases.

nodes.name: Electric bass
nodes.description: Electrically amplified fretted bass guitar. Paul Tutmarc’s Seattle Audiovox Model 736 is documented by museum records as a 1935–36 early fretted electric bass; Leo Fender’s Precision Bass, marketed in 1951, brought the practical design to a much wider market.

phases.note: Museum dates the Audiovox Model 736 c.1935, while its object essay calls it a 1936 model.
Fender’s first marketed Precision Bass marks a commercial breakthrough, not immediate universal adoption.

nodes.phaseNote: Distinguishes the less widely adopted Audiovox instrument from Fender’s successful 1951 commercial model. Removed unsupported 1960 golden-age and 1980 transition phases.

nodes.name: Electric guitar
nodes.description: A guitar whose pickups convert string vibration into an electrical signal for amplification. The Frying Pan was designed in 1931 and marketed by 1932; later solid-body models such as the Gibson Les Paul and Fender Stratocaster broadened the instrument’s role in popular music.
nodes.phaseNote: The 1931 design date and 1932 marketing date are distinct; 1932 is retained as the commercial launch marker. Smithsonian sources document influential solid-body models in the 1950s, but do not establish a measurable electric-guitar “golden age” or a 1960 establishment threshold. Removed those unsupported phases.

nodes.name: Electric piano
nodes.description: Electromechanical keyboard instruments with struck strings, reeds, or tines captured by pickups. The Neo-Bechstein electroacoustic grand appeared in 1931; Wurlitzer launched a struck-reed model in 1954, and Fender Rhodes introduced its tine-based full-size piano in 1965. Rhodes became popular in 1970s rock, R&B, and jazz.
nodes.phaseNote: The graph’s 1954 origin omitted the 1931 Neo-Bechstein, an earlier electroacoustic piano. Museum/manufacturer sources distinguish this string-based instrument from Wurlitzer’s 1954 struck-reed piano and the 1965 Rhodes. Smithsonian describes Rhodes popularity in 1970s rock, R&B, and jazz; “golden age” is a qualitative description, not a measured market peak. Removed the unsupported 1975 phase.

nodes.name: French horn
nodes.description: Brass instrument whose familiar hoop-shaped hunting-horn form emerged in 17th-century France. Horns appeared in Lully compositions by 1664, entered instrumental ensembles during the 18th century, and gained chromatic range with the widespread adoption of valves in the mid-19th century.
nodes.phaseNote: Yale’s instrument-history essay supports the French hoop form and 1664 compositional use, followed by regular ensemble and solo use in the 18th century. Yale dates widespread valve-horn adoption to the mid-19th century, a technological change rather than evidence for a popularity peak. Removed the unsupported 1800 phase.

nodes.name: Güiro
nodes.description: Scraped idiophone, commonly made from a ridged gourd and important in Caribbean music. Taíno associations are documented in Smithsonian educational material, while origins are described variously; the often-repeated 1788 date is not a secure first mention of the instrument itself.
nodes.phaseNote: One cautious documentary marker only: the 1788 reference is disputed as an instrument attestation. Removed broad “golden age” and later phases unsupported by evidence.

nodes.name: Guitar
nodes.description: Fretted plucked instrument with a written history reaching back to Renaissance Europe. Course counts changed over time: four-course guitars preceded the five-course Spanish guitar, while six single strings spread from the late 18th and early 19th centuries; Antonio de Torres standardized key modern classical-guitar features from the 1850s.
nodes.phaseNote: Broad historical markers only: Renaissance written record and 19th-century concert-guitar standardization are documented. Removed unsupported “golden age” and generic 1950 phase; prominence labels are editorial, not quantitative.

nodes.name: Hammond organ
nodes.description: Electromechanical tonewheel organ patented by Laurens Hammond in 1934 and first sold in 1935. The B-3, introduced in 1954, became especially prominent in gospel, jazz, soul and rock; Jimmy Smith’s 1950s recordings helped establish the organ in jazz.

phases.note: Patent and manufacture date; the first Smithsonian-documented organ was purchased by a church in 1935.
Jazz-specific adoption marker associated with Jimmy Smith’s Blue Note breakthrough, not a universal instrument-wide prominence threshold.

nodes.phaseNote: Separates invention/manufacture from later use in jazz. The 1956 marker is a genre-specific adoption milestone, not the beginning of Hammond use in gospel or other music.

nodes.name: Harmonica
nodes.description: Pocket-sized free-reed mouth organ whose commercial development began in 1820s Germany. Hohner began manufacturing in 1857; the harmonica later became prominent in blues and other American popular traditions.
nodes.phaseNote: Smithsonian Magazine places the “golden age” between the World Wars and documents postwar blues and later folk/rock/soul use. These are editorial cultural markers, not measured popularity estimates.

nodes.name: Harmonium
