nodes.name: Raï
nodes.description: A popular song tradition from western Algeria, shaped by rural poetic singing and the urban culture of Oran. Cheikhas and later young singers developed its frank lyrics and, over time, incorporated electric instruments and new production styles.

phases.note: UNESCO traces the song tradition to Algerian rural elders and notes urban change at the turn of the twentieth century; bpb describes instrumentation changes in Oran from the 1920s.
bpb dates an internationally popularized modern form to the late 1970s in Oran.

nodes.phaseNote: Approximate local-to-international shifts, not a popularity curve. Deleted the unsupported generic 1980 and 2000 markers.

nodes.name: Gnawa

period.estimateNote: UNESCO connects the communities practicing Gnawa with the slave trade dating back at least to the sixteenth century. This is a broad historical placement, not evidence that the musical tradition began in 1500; a single origin remains unknown.

nodes.description: Moroccan musical and ritual tradition practiced by Gnawa communities, combining African-derived practices with Arab-Muslim and Amazigh contexts. Lila ceremonies and public performances use singing, guembri and metal castanets. Community history is connected to the trans-Saharan slave trade, but scholarship cautions that a single origin date cannot be established.
nodes.phaseNote: The tradition’s connection to the trans-Saharan slave trade is historical context, not a defensible single origin year for the music. No complete prominence curve is assigned.

nodes.name: Algerian chaâbi
nodes.description: An urban popular tradition associated with the Casbah of Algiers, shaped by Andalusian musical forms, sung poetry and musicians including El Anka. It is distinct from Moroccan styles also called chaâbi.

phases.note: Research dates the founding generation of Algerian chaâbi to the 1920s and identifies El Anka as a central innovator.

nodes.phaseNote: The early twentieth-century founding period is documented; removed unsupported 1950 “golden age” and 1960 continuation labels. The tradition continues.

nodes.name: Mbalax
nodes.description: Senegalese urban dance music combining local vocal and sabar-drum traditions with electric bands and influences from across Africa and the Atlantic. Dakar groups and singers including Youssou N’Dour helped develop its modern sound.

phases.note: The source set supports a late-20th-century emergence but does not establish one exact year; 1970s is a broad scene marker.
Oxford’s musicology reference credits N’Dour and peers with developing the sound, and his international career helped make it known beyond Senegal.

nodes.phaseNote: Broad emergence and expansion markers only. Removed the unsupported 1980s “golden age” and generic 1990s established marker; mbalax remains an active Senegalese popular tradition.

nodes.name: Makossa
nodes.description: A Cameroonian dance-music style associated with Douala, whose modern sound developed around prominent bass, guitars and horns. Manu Dibango’s 1972 recording “Soul Makossa” carried one jazz- and soul-inflected interpretation to international audiences.

phases.note: Historical reference places Makossa’s beginnings in 1950s Douala, with roots in Duala dance and varied musical influences.
Soul Makossa brought one Makossa-inflected recording to international audiences; it is not equivalent to the genre’s complete history or a measured golden age.

nodes.phaseNote: Confidence: medium. The 1970s marker reflects its international visibility, including Manu Dibango, while later phases represent continued local and diasporic practice. Editorial shading, not a measured ranking.

nodes.name: Taarab
nodes.description: A Swahili coastal music tradition associated with Zanzibar and East Africa, shaped by exchanges among African, Arab and Indian Ocean cultures. Orchestras and singers including Siti binti Saad brought its songs into recordings, clubs and community celebrations.

phases.note: Academic sources trace taarab to late nineteenth-century Zanzibar court culture and cross-cultural musical exchange.
Siti binti Saad’s Swahili taarab recordings and performances popularized the form beyond elite court settings in the 1920s.

nodes.phaseNote: Late-nineteenth-century formation and 1920s popularization markers. Removed unsupported 1930 “golden age,” 1960 and 2000 generalized phases; taarab remains diverse across the Swahili coast.

nodes.name: Morna

period.estimateNote: A contextual anchor, not a settled origin: some accounts trace early forms to lundu in eighteenth-century Cabo Verde, while UNESCO describes the living practice without assigning a start date.

nodes.description: Traditional Cabo Verdean music-and-dance practice combining voice, instrumental music, poetry and dance. It may be sung or performed instrumentally, with guitar, violin, ten-string guitar and cavaquinho among its instruments, and is linked to community life in Cabo Verde.

nodes.name: Afro house
nodes.description: House music shaped in South Africa through layered percussion and local vocal and rhythmic traditions. Producers such as Black Coffee and Culoe De Song helped carry the sound to dance floors abroad.

nodes.name: Cheikha Rimitti
nodes.description: Algerian singer and songwriter whose career began in the 1940s and whose recordings and performances linked early raï traditions to later generations.

nodes.name: Khaled (Cheb Khaled)
nodes.description: Oran-born Algerian raï singer who began performing in his teens and recording in the 1970s. His later international hits, including “Didi” (1992), brought raï to a broad global audience.

nodes.name: Cheb Mami
nodes.description: Algerian raï singer who began gaining notice in the early 1980s, made his first public festival appearance in 1985, and later helped bring raï to wider international audiences.

nodes.name: Cheb Hasni
nodes.description: Algerian raï singer known for sentimental raï. His recording career began in 1986, and his duet “El Baraka” with Cheba Zahouania helped establish his early profile.

nodes.name: Cheba Zahouania
nodes.description: Algerian raï singer who began by performing in women’s meddaha ensembles at family and religious gatherings. Her early recordings date to 1981; the 1986 song “Khali ya Khali” brought broader recognition.

nodes.name: Maâlem Mahmoud Guinia
nodes.description: Moroccan Gnawa maalem, singer and guembri player from a family of Gnawa musicians. A 1992 Montreal performance and recording brought his work to a wider international audience; it was a documented milestone, not the start of his musical life.

nodes.name: Maâlem Hamid El Kasri
nodes.description: Moroccan Gnawa maâlem, singer and guembri player, born in Ksar El Kebir in 1961 and trained from childhood by master musicians Alouane and Abdelouahed Stitou. He is known for blending northern and southern Gnawa styles. The graph’s 2004 start marks a documented high-profile festival collaboration with jazz pianist Joe Zawinul, not the start of his musical career.

nodes.name: Hassan Hakmoun
nodes.description: Moroccan Gnawa musician and guembri player who began studying tagnawit in childhood under local masters. He later introduced Gnawa music to international audiences through collaborations and performances.

nodes.name: El Hadj M'Hamed El Anka
nodes.description: Algerian singer, mandole player and teacher who established chaâbi as a major form of urban popular music. His reputation spread through recordings from 1927, and he later trained generations of musicians.

nodes.name: Dahmane El Harrachi
nodes.description: Algerian chaâbi singer-songwriter and performer of banjo and mandole, born Abderrahmane Amrani. He performed in Algiers before emigrating to France in 1949, where he continued performing for Algerian communities. His first record is commonly dated to 1956; “Ya Rayah,” written and recorded later in the 1960s, became internationally known through Rachid Taha’s 1990s version. Died in 1980.

nodes.name: Abdelkader Chaou
nodes.description: Algerian chaâbi singer and mandole player whose first records appeared in 1970; his 1973 hit “Djah Rebi Ya Djirani” established his public success.

nodes.name: Youssou N’Dour
nodes.description: Senegalese singer and songwriter who joined Dakar’s Star Band as a teenager, then formed Étoile de Dakar in the late 1970s. His work helped popularize mbalax and later reached international audiences.

nodes.name: Omar Pène
nodes.description: Senegalese singer and composer who began performing professionally with the band Cad in 1975 and became a central voice of Super Diamono and mbalax.

nodes.name: Thione Seck
nodes.description: Senegalese singer and songwriter who joined the Dakar Star Band as a teenager and became a prominent Orchestra Baobab vocalist in the 1970s. He later led Raam Daan and recorded mbalax as a solo artist.

nodes.name: Manu Dibango
nodes.description: Cameroonian saxophonist, composer and bandleader who became a professional musician in 1957. His career spanned jazz, makossa and African popular music, with “Soul Makossa” bringing international attention in 1972.

nodes.name: Eboa Lotin
nodes.description: Cameroonian singer-songwriter whose first recorded single, “Mulema Mwam, Elimba Dikalo,” appeared in 1962. He became one of the country’s notable popular singers and composers.

nodes.name: Petit-Pays
nodes.description: Cameroonian singer and songwriter whose first documented release “Ça fait mal” appeared in 1987. Known for blending makossa with contemporary popular styles.

nodes.name: Siti binti Saad
nodes.description: Zanzibari taarab singer who became the first East African artist to make commercial gramophone recordings. Her 1928 HMV session in Bombay helped spread Swahili-language taarab across East Africa.

nodes.name: Bi Kidude
nodes.description: Zanzibari taarab and ngoma singer whose age and early chronology are uncertain. She performed traditional styles for decades, experienced a long lull in her singing career, and returned to wider attention in the 1980s.

nodes.name: Culture Musical Club
nodes.description: Zanzibari taarab orchestra officially founded in 1958. Originally connected to a youth organization during the independence movement, it evolved into a leading ensemble while sustaining and adapting taarab traditions.

nodes.name: Oran
nodes.description: A city in western Algeria associated with the urban development of raï.

nodes.name: Algiers
nodes.description: The Algerian capital and home of the Casbah chaâbi tradition.

nodes.name: Morocco
nodes.description: North African country where Gnawa musical and ritual practices are widely rooted.

nodes.name: Essaouira
nodes.description: Moroccan coastal city that hosts the Gnaoua World Music Festival.

nodes.name: Dakar
nodes.description: Senegalese capital and an important center of mbalax.

nodes.name: Douala
nodes.description: Cameroonian city associated with the development of makossa.

nodes.name: Zanzibar
nodes.description: East African archipelago associated with the development of taarab.

nodes.name: Mumbai
nodes.description: Indian city formerly known as Bombay, where Siti binti Saad recorded in 1928.

nodes.name: Algerian mandole
nodes.description: Large-bodied, long-necked plucked instrument central to Algerian chaâbi. Singer El Hadj M’hamed El Anka later recalled drawing its design in 1935 and giving it to luthier Jean Bélido; this is a reported design date, while some secondary accounts give different build dates.
nodes.phaseNote: A 2022 Algerian press history quotes El Anka’s recollection of a 1935 design. Removed exact 1932 claim and unsupported “golden age”/1960 phases.

nodes.name: Didi
nodes.description: Khaled’s 1992 raï single, which reached audiences beyond Algeria.

nodes.name: Soul Makossa
nodes.description: Manu Dibango’s 1972 recording blends makossa with jazz and soul.

nodes.name: Siti binti Saad records taarab in Bombay
nodes.description: Siti binti Saad and her musicians recorded in Bombay in 1928, helping Swahili-language taarab circulate on commercial records beyond Zanzibar.

nodes.name: Gnaoua World Music Festival begins in Essaouira
nodes.description: The first Essaouira festival created a recurring public stage for Gnawa musicians and exchanges with artists from other traditions.

nodes.name: Gnawa is inscribed on UNESCO’s heritage list
nodes.description: UNESCO inscribed Morocco’s Gnawa practices on its Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity, recognizing music, ritual and community transmission.

nodes.name: Raï is inscribed on UNESCO’s heritage list
nodes.description: UNESCO inscribed raï, the popular folk song of Algeria, on its Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.

nodes.name: Carl Cox
nodes.description: British DJ and producer who began DJing as a teenager and became a defining figure in the late-1980s acid house and rave scene. His 1988 Sunrise set helped establish his three-turntable style.

nodes.name: Laurent Garnier
nodes.description: French DJ and producer who began DJing in earnest at Manchester’s Haçienda in 1987, becoming a key figure in French house and techno.

nodes.name: David Guetta
nodes.description: French DJ and producer who started playing Paris clubs as a teenager in the mid-1980s. He later became a prominent figure in French house, then reached global pop audiences through dance-pop collaborations.

nodes.name: Calvin Harris
nodes.description: Scottish DJ, producer and songwriter whose early homemade tracks circulated on MySpace before his 2007 debut album. His later pop collaborations made him one of the most commercially successful dance artists of the 2010s.

nodes.name: Tiësto
nodes.description: Dutch DJ and producer whose club residencies in the Netherlands began in 1985. He became a leading figure in trance before later moving into broader electronic dance styles.

nodes.name: Skrillex
nodes.description: American musician who first came to prominence as Sonny Moore, vocalist for From First to Last from 2004. He began releasing electronic music as Skrillex in 2010, becoming a leading figure in dubstep and electronic dance music.

nodes.name: Diplo
nodes.description: American DJ and producer whose Philly club night Hollertronix launched his profile around the turn of the millennium. His 2004 album Florida and later collaborations helped carry dance and electronic sounds into mainstream pop.

nodes.name: Martin Garrix
nodes.description: Dutch DJ and producer who released his first single in 2012 and gained international recognition with “Animals” in 2013.

nodes.name: Bob Sinclar
nodes.description: French DJ and producer Christophe Le Friant, who began DJing in the late 1980s under earlier identities before adopting the Bob Sinclar name in the late 1990s. His later productions became associated with French house.

nodes.name: Kaytranada
nodes.description: Haitian-Canadian producer and DJ who began releasing music online in 2010 as Kaytradamus, before adopting the Kaytranada name and gaining broader attention through a viral Janet Jackson remix.

nodes.name: Peggy Gou
nodes.description: South Korean DJ and producer who moved to Berlin in 2014 and developed her club career there; her first widely documented EP releases followed in 2016. Her breakout single “It Makes You Forget (Itgehane)” arrived in 2018.

nodes.name: Nina Kraviz
nodes.description: Russian DJ, producer and singer who first issued a record in 2007, then developed a solo electronic career from 2008–09 after leaving the band MySpaceRocket.

nodes.name: Charlotte de Witte
nodes.description: Belgian DJ and producer who began DJing in 2010 as Raving George, then released her first EP under her own name in 2015. She became a leading international techno artist.

nodes.name: Ben Klock
nodes.description: German techno DJ and producer who began playing Berlin clubs in the mid-1990s, released records from 1998, and later became a resident DJ at Berghain.

nodes.name: Black Coffee
nodes.description: South African DJ and producer who began DJing in 1994, later forming the trio Shana while studying music. He became a major figure in South African house and an international ambassador for the scene.

nodes.name: Paul Oakenfold
nodes.description: English DJ and producer who began playing soul records in a Covent Garden wine bar in the late 1970s. His 1987 Ibiza experience helped shape the Balearic and acid house scenes; production work began in 1988.

nodes.name: Sasha
nodes.description: Welsh DJ and producer who entered the Manchester club scene in the late 1980s, then built a major following through residencies at Shelly’s and Renaissance in the early 1990s.

nodes.name: John Digweed
nodes.description: English DJ and producer who began DJing as a teenager in the early 1980s and promoted local events in Hastings. His national breakthrough came later through Renaissance and the 1994 mix album.

nodes.name: Eric Prydz
nodes.description: Swedish DJ and producer whose releases began in the early 2000s; “Call on Me” (2004) was his major international breakthrough. He also releases club music as Pryda and Cirez D.

nodes.name: Four Tet
nodes.description: English electronic musician Kieran Hebden, who began releasing solo work as Four Tet in 1998 while also active in the post-rock band Fridge. His debut album Dialogue followed in 1999.

nodes.name: Fred again..
nodes.description: English producer, songwriter and DJ whose early credited work included Brian Eno and Karl Hyde projects in 2014. He began releasing solo music as Fred again.. in 2019 and rose to wider prominence with the Actual Life albums.

nodes.name: Moby
nodes.description: American musician, producer and DJ whose musical activity dates to the late 1970s. He later played in post-punk bands, worked as a New York club DJ, and began releasing electronic singles in the early 1990s.

nodes.name: DJ Premier
nodes.description: American DJ and producer who debuted as one half of Gang Starr in 1987, later becoming one of hip-hop’s most influential producers.

nodes.name: Pete Rock
nodes.description: American hip-hop producer, DJ and rapper. Early exposure came through DJ work on Marley Marl’s New York radio show; his first documented co-production credits were on Heavy D & the Boyz Big Tyme (1989), followed by his partnership with C.L. Smooth in the early 1990s. Known for layered jazz and soul sampling and remix work.

nodes.name: J Dilla
nodes.description: Detroit producer, rapper and member of Slum Village whose early collective work dates to the early 1990s; his first major production credits appeared by the mid-1990s. His solo career ran alongside his group work until his death in 2006.

nodes.name: Madlib
nodes.description: American producer, DJ and MC who first received commercial production credits in the early 1990s with Lootpack and Tha Alkaholiks, before building a broad catalog of solo and collaborative projects.

nodes.name: Marley Marl
nodes.description: American DJ and producer who helped shape Queensbridge hip-hop through early-1980s radio and studio work. His 1984 production “Roxanne’s Revenge” brought a major breakthrough, followed by leadership of the Juice Crew.

nodes.name: Justice
nodes.description: French electronic duo Gaspard Augé and Xavier de Rosnay, who began making music together and appeared on a compilation in 2003. Their 2007 single “D.A.N.C.E.” became an international breakthrough.

nodes.name: Disclosure
nodes.description: English electronic duo Guy and Howard Lawrence, who released their first single and uploaded early work in 2010. Their 2012 single “Latch” brought wider attention, followed by the 2013 debut album Settle.

nodes.name: Jamie xx
nodes.description: English musician, DJ and producer who joined The xx in the mid-2000s and co-produced the band’s 2009 debut. The Jamie xx solo identity appeared in 2009, with solo releases following in 2011.

nodes.name: Ukulele
nodes.description: Four-string plucked instrument developed in Hawaiʻi in the late nineteenth century by adapting Madeiran instruments such as the braguinha/machete and rajão. Portuguese immigrant makers—including Manuel Nunes, Augusto Dias and José do Espírito Santo—shaped its early forms. It became an important Hawaiian instrument before later vaudeville and U.S. pop waves.

phases.note: Approximate early-1880s instrument-development marker; 1879 Portuguese immigrant arrival is not itself an invention date.
Met documents three local makers producing instruments by 1888; this is Hawaiian adoption, not worldwide prominence.

nodes.phaseNote: The Met and MIM distinguish 1879 immigrant arrival from instrument development in the early 1880s; 1888 documents local production. Later U.S. mainland popularity is a separate wave, not the origin.

nodes.name: Euphonium
nodes.description: Low-register valved brass instrument, usually in B-flat, with a more conical bore than the baritone horn. Ferdinand Sommer’s 1843 Sommerophone/Euphonion is a commonly cited point in its development, though earlier related designs and competing invention attributions make a single origin year uncertain. It is used principally in military, brass and concert bands, with occasional orchestral use.
nodes.phaseNote: Circa 1843 is a conventional development marker, but related designs and an alternative 1838 attribution complicate a single invention date. No complete prominence curve is assigned.

nodes.name: Timpani
nodes.description: Tunable kettledrums with military and ceremonial antecedents. European screw-tensioned forms developed in the 16th century and entered orchestral use in the 17th; modern pedal instruments provide pitched percussion and rhythmic emphasis.

phases.note: Approximate 16th-century development of screw-tensioned European kettledrums, not the origin of kettledrums worldwide.
Approximate orchestral-adoption anchor given by Museums Victoria; not an absolute first-use claim or global popularity threshold.

nodes.phaseNote: The timeline follows European tunable timpani: circa 1500 marks screw-tension development and circa 1675 orchestral adoption. Older kettledrum traditions predate both. Dates are approximate; no golden age is inferred.

nodes.name: Triangle
nodes.description: Suspended metal rod bent into an open triangle and struck with a metal beater. European depictions are documented by the late Middle Ages; it entered Western opera around 1710 and symphony orchestras by the mid-18th century.

phases.note: Approximate documentary horizon based on late-medieval depictions, not invention; the sources do not support a circa-1000 origin.
Approximate symphonic adoption by the mid-18th century; triangle parts in Western opera are documented by 1710.

nodes.phaseNote: The circa-1000 boundary remains provisional and low confidence: Blades discusses a medieval manuscript, but the relevant PDF text is incompletely extracted and its exact dating has not been verified. It must not be read as a proven invention date. Later medieval illustrations and modern use are better supported.

nodes.name: Piccolo
nodes.description: Small transverse flute, normally pitched an octave above the concert flute, used in orchestras and military or concert bands. Early keyed forms developed during the 18th century; its high register adds brilliance and color.

phases.note: Broad early-18th-century development anchor for keyed transverse piccolos, not an exact invention date; early instrument names can also denote recorders.
Mid-18th-century regular orchestral use is better supported than the former circa-1800 boundary; opera and military-band uses overlap. Approximate adoption, not universal establishment.

nodes.phaseNote: Circa 1700 represents broadly dated early keyed forms with low confidence in the numerical boundary. Circa 1800 represents symphonic adoption, not invention or universal establishment. No measured popularity peak is claimed.

nodes.name: Bass clarinet
nodes.description: Low-register single-reed member of the clarinet family, with surviving experimental forms from the 18th century. Nineteenth-century developments supported its orchestral role, including dark colors and exposed solos in Romantic and later repertoire.

phases.note: Approximate anchor for the Mayrhofer instrument dated 1760–1770; earlier prototypes and classifications remain uncertain. Not an exact invention year.
Early 19th-century orchestral solo role emerged by 1834–36, including Mercadante’s Emma d’Antiochia and Meyerbeer’s Les Huguenots; this is repertoire adoption, not broad universal establishment.

nodes.phaseNote: Separate 18th-century experimental instruments from mid-19th-century orchestral establishment. Circa 1765 represents a surviving instrument’s estimated date, not a first invention claim. Circa 1850 reflects orchestral adoption, not worldwide popularity or a golden age.

nodes.name: Cor anglais
nodes.description: Double-reed member of the oboe family, also called English horn, pitched in F a fifth below the oboe. Its early forms developed through several shapes in the 18th century; a documented orchestral part appears in Jommelli’s Ezio around 1749. The modern instrument is known for its mellow lower-register color.

phases.note: Approximate development of curved, bulb-bell forms; related tenor oboes and bulb bells existed earlier. Not a precise invention date.
Approximate wider-use marker from the Met’s mid-1800s account; orchestral parts existed by the mid-18th century.

nodes.phaseNote: Replace the unsupported circa-1800 origin with circa-1720 early-form development. Separate that from wider use around the mid-19th century. Both are approximate historical markers; neither denotes a measured popularity peak.

nodes.name: Roland JUNO-106
nodes.description: Six-voice programmable analog synthesizer introduced in 1984, with digitally controlled oscillators, patch memory, MIDI and built-in chorus. Roland identifies its model period as 1984–85; later production history is not the same as the instrument’s continued musical use.

phases.note: Documented product availability from 1984; a single phase represents continuing use, not immediate widespread adoption.

nodes.phaseNote: 1984 is a well-supported release year. A single editorial phase avoids inventing a peak. Manufacturer pages disagree about production duration; no production end is used as an end to musical use.

nodes.name: Dune
nodes.description: German electronic dance project led by Oliver Froning, initially formed with producers Jens Oettrich and Bernd Burhoff. Its 1995 debut single “Hardcore Vibes” became a European chart hit; the project’s sound spans techno, rave and happy hardcore.

nodes.name: Berry Gordy establishes Tamla Records
nodes.description: Berry Gordy began his independent record company in Detroit on 12 January 1959, initially as Tamla Records. The Motown name followed later in 1959; Motown Record Corporation was formally incorporated in 1960. The founding laid the groundwork for the label’s influential artist, songwriting, production and studio system. A major Black-owned independent record company grew into a defining force in American soul and pop music.

nodes.name: Menlo Park
nodes.description: New Jersey community whose Edison laboratory was the site of the 1877 tinfoil phonograph invention.

nodes.name: Pittsburgh
nodes.description: Pennsylvania city and early broadcasting center; KDKA’s November 1920 election-results broadcast originated at a Westinghouse site in East Pittsburgh.

nodes.name: Junior Murvin

period.estimateNote: Approximate mid-1960s to 2013 career span, following the biographical chronology of early Junior Soul recordings and later performances. This estimates musical activity, not his disputed birth year.

nodes.description: Jamaican reggae singer best known for the 1976 roots-reggae recording “Police and Thieves,” produced by Lee “Scratch” Perry at Black Ark Studio.

nodes.name: Jamie Principle
nodes.description: Chicago house vocalist, songwriter and producer. His early recording of “Your Love” and later collaboration with Frankie Knuckles became part of the formative Chicago house repertoire.

nodes.name: Steve Roach

period.estimateNote: The official biography places the start of his music-making in the late 1970s. 1978 represents that approximate period, rather than treating his first solo album in 1982 as his career beginning.

nodes.description: Electronic and ambient pioneer whose synthesizer music ranges from the suspended harmonies of Structures From Silence to sequencer-driven and tribal-ambient soundworlds.

nodes.name: DJ Scud

period.estimateNote: Approximate mid-1990s placement from XLR8R's account of the early Ambush and breakcore scene. Neither his first DJ performance nor a definitive retirement date is established; the open end is provisional.

nodes.description: Breakcore DJ and producer behind the Ambush label; his work with Nomex, including “Total Destruction,” helped establish the style’s mixture of hyperkinetic breaks, noise and Jamaican elements.

nodes.name: Toro y Moi

period.estimateNote: Approximate late-2000s project start from the biographical chronology and the 2009 recordings discussed by Consequence and the Guardian. Earlier private music-making is not assigned an exact boundary.

nodes.description: Singer, songwriter and producer Chaz Bundick, whose early Toro y Moi recordings helped define chillwave through hazy synth textures, intimate vocals and groove-oriented pop.

nodes.name: The Chopstars

period.estimateNote: Approximate collective period from the reported 2007 formation and the continuing remix practice documented by NPR. This is not the start of the members' individual careers.

nodes.description: DJ collective extending DJ Screw’s chopped-and-screwed tradition through projects including Purple Moonlight and reworkings of Frank Ocean, Solange and Beyoncé.

nodes.name: Rites of Spring
nodes.description: Washington, DC punk group whose vulnerable lyrics, melodic intensity and explosive performances helped catalyze Revolution Summer; their sound gave rise to the terms emocore and emo.

nodes.name: Ebo Taylor

period.estimateNote: Approximate span from his early highlife-band work before studying in London in the early 1960s through the 2025 Jazz Is Dead album described in the Guardian obituary. The start is rounded to the mid-1950s; the end reflects late recorded work, not an automatic death-date boundary.

nodes.description: Ghanaian guitarist, arranger, composer and bandleader who developed highlife alongside jazz, funk and Afrobeat influences, recording with his own bands and collaborating with Pat Thomas.

nodes.name: Pat Thomas

period.estimateNote: Approximate mid-1960s career start: the biographical account describes the 2015 album as marking 50 years of his musical career, alongside Music In Africa's account of his highlife work.

nodes.description: Ghanaian vocalist and songwriter known for his work with Ebo Taylor’s highlife bands, including the Blue Monks, and for recordings spanning highlife, Afrobeat and Afro-pop.

nodes.name: Don Caballero

period.estimateNote: Broad career envelope from the reported 1991 formation through the announced 2026 reunion. Includes substantial breaks, notably 2000-2003 and 2009-2026; the continuous bar does not assert uninterrupted activity.

nodes.description: Rock group associated with the formative math-rock scene; Pitchfork identifies Don Caballero alongside Polvo and Ruins as bands that spearheaded the sound.

nodes.name: Hella

period.estimateNote: Approximate band period from the reported 2001 formation through the 2011 recording era. These are broad activity boundaries, not exact first-performance or formal dissolution dates.

nodes.description: Sacramento band formed around guitarist Spencer Seim and drummer Zach Hill, whose intensely choreographed, technically intricate music combines noise-rock force with adventurous rhythmic interplay.

nodes.name: Arsenio Rodríguez

period.estimateNote: Rounded career placement from the biographical 1929-1970 activity span, supported by the recorded-work history discussed by Timba. The boundary around 1930 is an estimate, not a birth date or an exact debut.

nodes.description: Cuban tres player, composer and bandleader whose son recordings transformed ensemble arranging through piano, conga, multiple horns and innovative melodic bass patterns.

nodes.name: Pharoah Sanders

period.estimateNote: Approximate career envelope around the West Coast activity in 1959, New York move in 1961 and late work including Promises in 2021, described by NPR's 2022 obituary. Neither boundary asserts an exact first or final performance.

nodes.description: Tenor and soprano saxophonist whose spirit-driven improvisation, work with John Coltrane and Impulse! recordings such as Karma, Thembi and Black Unity helped shape a lasting jazz tradition.

nodes.name: Terry Francis

period.estimateNote: Broad 1990s placement for the releases and established DJ practice preceding fabric's opening in 1999. The resident biography supports earlier activity, not an exact 1990 debut.

nodes.description: DJ and producer associated with London’s formative tech-house scene, releases on Wiggle and related labels, and a long-standing residency at fabric.

nodes.name: James Ferraro

period.estimateNote: Approximate early-2000s start from the biographical chronology of the Skaters and early solo work. Far Side Virtual in 2011 is a later milestone, not the beginning of his career.

nodes.description: Experimental electronic musician whose 2011 album Far Side Virtual helped establish vaporwave’s utopian-virtual strand through pristine digital sounds drawn from computer and consumer culture.

nodes.name: Glastonbury Festival
nodes.description: Music and performing-arts festival at Worthy Farm in Pilton, England, first held in 1970. Its early editions brought together pop, folk and blues performers.

nodes.name: Montreux Jazz Festival
nodes.description: Swiss festival founded by Claude Nobs in 1967 on Lake Geneva. Its programme extends beyond its jazz roots to soul, blues, rock and other styles.

nodes.name: Newport Jazz Festival
nodes.description: Jazz festival inaugurated in Newport, Rhode Island, in July 1954. Its first edition featured Billie Holiday, Dizzy Gillespie and Ella Fitzgerald.

nodes.name: Roskilde Festival
nodes.description: Danish music and cultural festival first held in 1971 under the name Sound Festival. Its stage archive documents performances including Bob Marley in 1978.

nodes.name: Rock in Rio
nodes.description: Brazilian music festival created by Roberto Medina in Rio de Janeiro in 1985. Later editions also took the festival to Portugal and Spain.

nodes.name: WOMADelaide
nodes.description: Music, arts and dance festival in Adelaide, Australia, first presented in 1992. Its inaugural programme included Nusrat Fateh Ali Khan and Youssou N’Dour.

nodes.name: Fuji Rock Festival
nodes.description: Japanese music festival first held at Fuji Tenjinyama in 1997, with a programme spanning rock and electronic music. It moved to Naeba Ski Resort in 1999.

nodes.name: Gnaoua and World Music Festival
nodes.description: Festival created in Essaouira, Morocco, in 1998. It brings Gnaoua masters together with musicians from other traditions through concerts and collaborations.

nodes.name: Cape Town International Jazz Festival
nodes.description: South African jazz festival launched in Cape Town in 2000, initially in partnership with the North Sea Jazz organisers. Its history documents both South African and international performers.

nodes.name: Festival de Música del Pacífico Petronio Álvarez
nodes.description: Festival of Pacific Colombian music held in Cali since 1997. Colombia’s public broadcasting archive preserves recordings of its early editions, including marimba ensembles.

nodes.name: Pilton
nodes.description: Village in Somerset, England, where Worthy Farm hosts Glastonbury Festival.

nodes.name: Montreux
nodes.description: Swiss lakeside town associated with the Montreux Jazz Festival.

nodes.name: Newport, Rhode Island
nodes.description: US city where the inaugural Newport Jazz Festival took place at the Newport Casino in 1954.

nodes.name: Roskilde
nodes.description: Danish city on Zealand, west of Copenhagen, that hosts Roskilde Festival.

nodes.name: Adelaide
nodes.description: South Australian city whose Botanic Park hosts WOMADelaide.

nodes.name: Naeba
nodes.description: Japanese ski-resort area in Niigata where Fuji Rock moved in 1999.

nodes.name: Cape Town
nodes.description: South African city that hosted the first Cape Town jazz festival at the Good Hope Centre in 2000.

nodes.name: Woodstock Music & Art Fair
nodes.description: The August 1969 gathering in Bethel, New York became a defining image of the rock counterculture. Performances by Jimi Hendrix, the Who and others made the original festival an enduring reference point for large outdoor music gatherings; this entry covers the 1969 event.

nodes.name: Monterey International Pop Festival
nodes.description: The June 1967 California festival helped establish rock festivals as major artistic gatherings and provided a breakthrough platform for Janis Joplin. Its programme brought Ravi Shankar together with rock and soul performers including Jimi Hendrix and Otis Redding. This entry concerns the original 1967 festival.

nodes.name: Newport Folk Festival
nodes.description: Founded in Rhode Island in 1959, Newport became a meeting place for the American folk revival and civil-rights-era protest music. Bob Dylan’s electric performance in 1965 made the festival a focal point in debates about the relationship between folk and rock.

nodes.name: Bayreuth Festival
nodes.description: Richard Wagner’s festival opened in Bayreuth in 1876 with a theatre designed around his music dramas. Its purpose-built auditorium, darkened audience area and recessed orchestra made the presentation of opera itself part of the festival’s artistic project.

nodes.name: Bayreuth
nodes.description: German city where Wagner’s festival theatre opened in 1876.

nodes.name: Salzburg Festival
nodes.description: Founded in 1920, Salzburg developed an international festival model combining opera, concerts and spoken theatre. Mozart’s repertoire and modern works share its programme, linking the city’s musical heritage with changing approaches to performance.

nodes.name: Donaueschinger Musiktage
nodes.description: Founded in 1921 as a forum for advanced chamber music, Donaueschingen became a durable platform for contemporary composition and experimental sound. Collaboration with the broadcaster SWF, later SWR, expanded its orchestral and vocal programming after 1950.

nodes.name: Donaueschingen
nodes.description: German city associated with the contemporary-music festival founded in 1921.

nodes.name: Isle of Wight Festival
nodes.description: The original 1968–1970 festivals helped define the scale of the British outdoor rock gathering. The 1970 edition featured Jimi Hendrix, the Who and Joan Baez; after a long interruption, the festival returned in 2002.

nodes.name: Isle of Wight
nodes.description: English island that hosted the original 1968–1970 festivals and the later revival.

nodes.name: Reading Festival
nodes.description: The festival traces its lineage to the National Jazz Festival launched in 1961, before its later home in Reading. Its rock history includes Nirvana’s 1992 headline set, recognised by the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame as a landmark festival performance.

nodes.name: Reading
nodes.description: English town associated with the later Reading Festival; the 1961 precursor did not begin here.

nodes.name: Sónar
nodes.description: Launched in Barcelona in 1994 around electronic and experimental music, Sónar joined performance to multimedia art and technological experimentation. Its Sónar+D programme and international editions extended that meeting point between music, creativity and digital culture.

nodes.name: Barcelona
nodes.description: Spanish city where Sónar began in 1994.

nodes.name: Tomorrowland
nodes.description: Founded in Boom in 2005, Tomorrowland grew from a Belgian electronic-music gathering into an international festival brand. Its themed stage environments, online films and broadcasts became a prominent example of the spectacle surrounding global dance-music festivals.

nodes.name: Boom
nodes.description: Belgian town where the first Tomorrowland took place in 2005.

nodes.name: Movement / Detroit Electronic Music Festival
nodes.description: Beginning as the Detroit Electronic Music Festival in 2000, this festival celebrated Detroit’s role in the development of techno. Carl Craig helped organise its first edition; Derrick May took over production in 2003, when the Movement name was introduced. Later producers and names belong to this evolving festival history.

nodes.name: WOMAD
nodes.description: The first World of Music, Arts and Dance festival in Somerset in 1982 placed musicians from many countries alongside British rock acts. Co-founder Peter Gabriel described its aim as giving artists outside the Western mainstream headline status; the format later travelled internationally.

nodes.name: Shepton Mallet
nodes.description: Somerset town associated with the Bath and West Showground, site of the first WOMAD in 1982.

nodes.name: Reggae Sunsplash
nodes.description: First staged in Montego Bay in 1978, Reggae Sunsplash provided an international concert platform for Jamaican reggae. Its preserved performance archive documents the festival’s role in presenting reggae and dancehall to audiences beyond the island.

nodes.name: Montego Bay
nodes.description: Jamaican city where Reggae Sunsplash was first staged in 1978.

nodes.name: FESPAM — Pan-African Music Festival
nodes.description: First held in Brazzaville in 1996, FESPAM combines performances with research and professional exchange around African music. Preservation, cultural circulation and Pan-African cooperation are stated institutional aims, not independently measured outcomes.

nodes.name: Festival au Désert
nodes.description: Founded in northern Mali in 2001, the Festival au Désert connected Tuareg gathering traditions with visiting international musicians. Its collaborations made it a meeting point for Saharan and global music; insecurity later displaced the festival into exile and touring projects.

nodes.name: Northern Mali
nodes.description: Malian region associated with the Festival au Désert’s original Saharan gatherings and later sites near Timbuktu.

nodes.name: Sauti za Busara
nodes.description: Founded in Zanzibar in 2004, Sauti za Busara gives African and diaspora musicians a platform spanning traditional and contemporary styles. Its programme connects Zanzibar’s taarab heritage with wider African live-music circuits and includes singer Bi Kidude among its past artists.

nodes.name: Festival Nacional de Folklore de Cosquín
nodes.description: Founded in 1961, Cosquín became a gathering place for Argentina’s regional folk traditions. The official chronology records Mercedes Sosa’s 1965 debut, introduced by Jorge Cafrune, as one of its defining moments in the history of Argentine song.

nodes.name: Cosquín
nodes.description: Argentine town where the national folklore festival began in 1961.

nodes.name: Viña del Mar International Song Festival
nodes.description: The Chilean song festival began in 1960 and developed folk and international song competitions. Chile’s National Library documents how Cecilia’s 1965 victory and the exchange with Spain’s Benidorm festival helped take Chilean Nueva Ola to Europe.

nodes.name: Viña del Mar
nodes.description: Chilean coastal city where the song festival was launched in 1960.

nodes.name: Rock al Parque
nodes.description: Founded in Bogotá in 1995, Rock al Parque gave Colombian bands a major public stage alongside international guests. Its development as a broadly accessible outdoor festival helped establish a municipal model for supporting live music and subsequent Al Parque festivals.

nodes.name: Bogotá
nodes.description: Colombian capital where Rock al Parque began in 1995.

nodes.name: Sawai Gandharva Bhimsen Mahotsav
nodes.description: Bhimsen Joshi established a festival in Pune in 1953 in memory of his teacher Sawai Gandharva, according to a collectors’ journal and a government-commissioned festival study. The long-running gathering is associated with Hindustani classical performance; retrospective details beyond its origin need further critical review.

nodes.name: Pune
nodes.description: Indian city where Bhimsen Joshi established the Sawai Gandharva memorial festival in 1953.

nodes.name: Java Jazz Festival
nodes.description: First held in Jakarta in 2005, Java Jazz established a large Indonesian meeting place for local and international jazz musicians. Its early editions brought many performances together in one programme, expanding the festival circuit for jazz in Southeast Asia.

nodes.name: Jakarta
nodes.description: Indonesian city that hosted the first Java Jazz Festival at the Jakarta Convention Center in 2005.

nodes.name: Coachella Valley Music and Arts Festival
nodes.description: First held on 9–10 October 1999 at the Empire Polo Club in Indio, California, Coachella brought rock, electronic and alternative acts into one programme. The inaugural line-up and early financial difficulties are documented by the Recording Academy and the festival’s programme archive.

nodes.name: Indio
nodes.description: Californian city associated with the Coachella Valley Music and Arts Festival.

nodes.name: Lollapalooza
nodes.description: Created by Perry Farrell in 1991 as a touring farewell for Jane’s Addiction, Lollapalooza brought alternative rock and other scenes into a shared travelling programme. It later settled in Chicago in 2005 and developed international editions, changing from a tour into a festival network.

nodes.name: Sanremo Music Festival
nodes.description: First broadcast by RAI from Sanremo’s casino in 1951, the Italian song contest became a recurring national stage for postwar popular song. Its history links musical careers, broadcasting and the changing sound of Italian mass culture.

nodes.name: Sanremo
nodes.description: Italian city whose casino hosted the first Sanremo song festival in 1951.

nodes.name: New Orleans Jazz & Heritage Festival
nodes.description: Founded in 1970, Jazz Fest made Louisiana’s music, food, crafts and local performance traditions part of one festival model. The meeting of Mahalia Jackson, Duke Ellington and a brass-band parade at its first edition symbolised its connection between jazz and community heritage; its 2006 return also became a post-Katrina homecoming.

nodes.name: Wacken Open Air
nodes.description: First held in 1990 in the German village of Wacken, this gathering grew into an internationally recognised heavy-metal festival. Its history illustrates how a specialist metal audience built a durable festival destination outside a major city.

nodes.name: Wacken
nodes.description: German village that has hosted the Wacken Open Air metal festival since its first edition in 1990.

nodes.name: Baalbeck International Festival
nodes.description: Created in 1956 among Baalbeck’s ancient temples, the festival joined international performance with a platform for Lebanese artists. Its Lebanese Nights helped bring Fairuz, the Rahbani brothers and other local creators to wider audiences; the history includes a long civil-war interruption and a 1997 return.

nodes.name: Baalbeck
nodes.description: Lebanese city whose ancient temple complex is associated with the international festival created in 1956.

nodes.name: Pythian Games
nodes.description: Ancient religious festival of Apollo at Delphi whose musical contests preceded the addition of athletic events. Its Panhellenic reorganisation is conventionally placed in the early sixth century BCE, around 586–582 BCE; this is not the date of the first musical gathering. It is an important ancient precedent, not an established first music festival worldwide.

period.estimateNote: The start is a conventional reorganisation/numbering anchor around 586–582 BCE, not the first musical rites. The upper display anchor is 424 CE: scholarship discusses games at Delphi then and says the Pythian games were probably ongoing. This is not a proven final edition; it supersedes the museum’s traditional 393/394 cessation account.

nodes.name: Three Choirs Festival
nodes.description: Cathedral music meetings linking Gloucester, Worcester and Hereford, conventionally counted from about 1715 and known under the present name from 1838. The festival became a platform for choral repertoire and new works, with interruptions during wars and the pandemic. Its long-surviving classical tradition should not be confused with the first music festival in history.

period.estimateNote: 1715 is the conventional date from which the meetings are counted, not a securely proven first edition. The present festival name appeared in 1838; wartime and pandemic interruptions prevent a claim of uninterrupted annual operation.

nodes.name: Delphi
nodes.description: Ancient Greek sanctuary of Apollo associated with the Pythian musical and athletic contests.

nodes.name: Gloucester
nodes.description: English cathedral city whose choir participates in the Three Choirs Festival.

nodes.name: Worcester
nodes.description: English cathedral city whose choir participates in the Three Choirs Festival.

nodes.name: Hereford
nodes.description: English cathedral city whose choir participates in the Three Choirs Festival.

nodes.name: Pythian musical contests become part of a Panhellenic festival

period.estimateNote: The 586–582 BCE range covers the conventional reform/numbering chronology; 582 BCE is a reference point, not a precisely established founding date. Earlier musical contests predate it, and no world-first is established.

nodes.description: The reorganisation of Apollo’s festival at Delphi around 586–582 BCE expanded an older musical competition into a four-yearly Panhellenic gathering with musical and athletic contests. It documents an ancient institution for public musical competition, not the first music festival anywhere.

nodes.name: Three cathedral choirs establish recurring Music Meetings

period.estimateNote: 1715 is the conventional counting date, not a securely documented first edition; the event represents an early-eighteenth-century institutional development.

nodes.description: The cathedral choirs of Gloucester, Worcester and Hereford developed Music Meetings conventionally counted from about 1715. Their recurring collaboration underlies a long-lived British choral festival and later platform for new works. The exact first meeting is uncertain, and the present festival name dates from 1838.

nodes.name: The complete Ring cycle premieres at the first Bayreuth Festival
nodes.description: The first Bayreuth Festival presented Wagner’s complete Ring des Nibelungen cycle in August 1876 in a purpose-built theatre. Earlier performances of individual operas were not premieres of the complete cycle; the festival tied the musical drama to a distinctive auditorium and staging model.

nodes.name: Donaueschingen establishes a forum for contemporary chamber music
nodes.description: The first Donaueschingen chamber-music festival in 1921 gave new compositions a dedicated public forum. Its emerging-composer focus and later broadcasting partnership helped sustain a recurring institution for contemporary music, rather than a single stylistic school.

nodes.name: RAI broadcasts the first Sanremo song contest
nodes.description: The first Sanremo song contest was broadcast by RAI from the city’s casino in January 1951. The recurring national broadcast became an important meeting point between popular song, performers’ careers and Italian mass media.

nodes.name: Ellington’s Newport performance renews his orchestra’s prominence
nodes.description: Duke Ellington’s orchestra performed at Newport on 7 July 1956, with Paul Gonsalves’ extended solo on Diminuendo and Crescendo in Blue becoming the concert’s celebrated turning point. The performance and subsequent recording helped renew attention to Ellington’s orchestra; they did not create jazz or big-band music.

nodes.name: Dylan’s electric Newport set brings folk and rock into debate
nodes.description: Bob Dylan performed with an electric band at Newport Folk in July 1965, including Like a Rolling Stone. The set became a focal point in debates about the folk revival and rock; accounts differ about the audience’s reaction, and the performance was not the invention of electric folk music.

nodes.name: Mercedes Sosa’s Cosquín appearance expands her public recognition
nodes.description: Jorge Cafrune introduced Mercedes Sosa at Cosquín in January 1965. The appearance became a major step in her national recognition and connected a defining voice of Latin American song with the festival’s folk audience; it was not her first musical activity.

nodes.name: Viña’s song-contest exchange carries Chilean Nueva Ola abroad
nodes.description: Cecilia’s winning performance at Viña del Mar in 1965 was linked to an exchange with Spain’s Benidorm festival. Chile’s National Library identifies this route as helping bring Chilean Nueva Ola to Europe and strengthen its place in Chilean musical life.

nodes.name: Fairuz performs at Baalbeck as Lebanese Nights develops
nodes.description: Fairuz gave an outdoor concert at Baalbeck’s temple complex in 1957. The festival’s Lebanese Nights provided a platform for Fairuz, the Rahbani brothers and other Lebanese creators alongside international programming, helping establish a distinct national performance presence.

nodes.name: Reggae Sunsplash creates a large Jamaican concert platform
nodes.description: The first Reggae Sunsplash took place in Montego Bay in June 1978. Its concert platform and subsequent international reach became part of reggae’s circulation beyond Jamaica; the festival was not the origin of reggae or dancehall.

nodes.name: The first WOMAD brings international musicians to a shared festival stage
nodes.description: The first WOMAD took place at the Bath and West Showground in Somerset in July 1982. Its programme put musicians from many countries alongside British rock acts, giving a festival format to a project of cross-cultural musical exchange that later travelled internationally.

nodes.name: Rock in Rio brings a large international rock bill to Rio
nodes.description: Rock in Rio’s first edition in January 1985 brought Brazilian and international acts together on a large concert site in Rio de Janeiro. Queen’s documented headline appearances illustrate the event’s place in the expansion of international rock touring in Brazil; this was not Brazil’s first musical festival.

nodes.name: Rock al Parque establishes a public stage for Bogotá’s rock bands
nodes.description: The inaugural Rock al Parque in May 1995 brought Colombian bands and international guests into Bogotá’s public venues. The festival became a municipal platform for live music; its wider policy influence is a historical interpretation, and the first edition was not free at every venue.

nodes.name: Detroit Electronic Music Festival celebrates the city’s techno legacy
nodes.description: The first Detroit Electronic Music Festival took place at Hart Plaza in 2000 with Carl Craig involved in its organisation. It brought Detroit’s electronic-music legacy into a large public festival; later Movement and Fuse-In names involved different producers, and techno itself was already established.

nodes.name: Daft Punk’s Coachella pyramid reframes electronic live production
nodes.description: Daft Punk’s 2006 Coachella set combined an illuminated pyramid with tightly synchronised music and multimedia. The Rock and Roll Hall of Fame identifies it as a turning point in electronic dance performance production; that assessment concerns presentation and influence, not the invention of electronic live music.

nodes.name: Glastonbury Fair introduces its first Pyramid Stage
nodes.description: The free Glastonbury Fair of 1971 introduced the festival’s first Pyramid Stage and a programme including David Bowie. Its combination of music, performing arts and countercultural gathering became part of the festival’s developing identity; this was a second edition, not its 1970 founding.

nodes.name: Petronio Álvarez gives Pacific Colombian music a festival platform
nodes.description: The Petronio Álvarez festival began in Cali in 1997 according to Colombian broadcasting archives and university histories. It created a public platform for Pacific Colombian musical traditions, including marimba ensembles. The checked Spanish Wikipedia article instead gives 1996, so the dating discrepancy remains explicit.

nodes.name: New Orleans Jazz Fest joins music with Louisiana community heritage
nodes.description: The first New Orleans Jazz & Heritage Festival in 1970 placed music alongside local crafts, food and community performance. Mahalia Jackson and Duke Ellington appeared at the inaugural gathering; the model presented local cultural traditions as central to the festival rather than as background to visiting headliners.

nodes.name: Lollapalooza puts alternative acts into a touring festival programme
nodes.description: The first Lollapalooza tour in 1991 brought acts including Nine Inch Nails into a shared travelling programme conceived by Perry Farrell around Jane’s Addiction’s farewell. Archive material and popular-music scholarship place it within the growth of the alternative-rock festival circuit; it was not yet the later Chicago event.

nodes.name: Sónar combines electronic music with multimedia arts
nodes.description: The first Sónar in Barcelona in 1994 joined electronic and experimental music with multimedia arts. An academic case study documents this combination as central to the festival’s format; the later Sónar+D congress should not be backdated to the first edition.

nodes.name: Sergei Prokofiev
nodes.description: Composer and pianist whose works include the Classical Symphony, Romeo and Juliet and Alexander Nevsky.

nodes.name: Paul Hindemith
nodes.description: Composer, violist and conductor whose works include Kammermusik and the symphony Mathis der Maler.

nodes.name: Little Walter

period.estimateNote: The start approximates his move to Chicago in the late 1940s, after earlier performances in New Orleans.

nodes.description: Blues harmonica player who joined Muddy Waters’s band in Chicago and recorded the instrumental hit “Juke.”

nodes.name: Howlin’ Wolf

period.estimateNote: The year of his first guitar provides a documented anchor for early performing activity that began in his teens.

nodes.description: Blues singer and guitarist who performed in the Mississippi Delta before recording for Chess and moving to Chicago.

nodes.name: Joe “King” Oliver

period.estimateNote: The date places his early brass-band career in turn-of-the-century New Orleans.

nodes.description: New Orleans jazz cornetist and bandleader who mentored Louis Armstrong and formed the Creole Jazz Band in Chicago.

nodes.name: Willie Nelson

period.estimateNote: The date approximates the start of his documented recording career in the mid-1950s.

nodes.description: Country singer, songwriter and guitarist who helped establish outlaw country and recorded Shotgun Willie.

nodes.name: Waylon Jennings
nodes.description: Country singer and guitarist who won greater creative control in Nashville and made Honky Tonk Heroes in 1973.

nodes.name: Jessi Colter
nodes.description: Country singer-songwriter whose solo hits include “I’m Not Lisa” and who appeared on Wanted! The Outlaws.

nodes.name: The Allman Brothers Band
nodes.description: Band formed in 1969 that helped define Southern rock through its blend of blues, country, jazz and rock and roll.

nodes.name: Lynyrd Skynyrd
nodes.description: Jacksonville band that adopted the name Lynyrd Skynyrd in 1969 and released its debut album in 1973.

nodes.name: The Marshall Tucker Band
nodes.description: Band formed in Spartanburg, South Carolina, in 1972, whose early songs include “Can’t You See.”

nodes.name: Bad Brains
nodes.description: Washington, D.C. band that paired very fast hardcore songs with dub-influenced reggae on its self-titled debut.

nodes.name: Black Flag
nodes.description: Southern California band that became an influential early act in American hardcore.

nodes.name: Dead Kennedys
nodes.description: San Francisco punk band founded in 1978 by musicians including East Bay Ray and Jello Biafra.

nodes.name: Helloween
nodes.description: Hamburg band whose Keeper of the Seven Keys albums helped set the template for European power metal.

nodes.name: Blind Guardian
nodes.description: Krefeld band that grew out of speed metal and became known for layered vocals and fantasy-themed songs.

nodes.name: Gamma Ray
nodes.description: German power metal band formed by guitarist and singer Kai Hansen after he left Helloween.

nodes.name: Janet Jackson
nodes.description: American singer whose 1986 album Control, made with Jimmy Jam and Terry Lewis, helped shape dance-pop.

nodes.name: Lil Peep
nodes.description: Rapper and singer who built songs around emo and pop-punk samples and programmed drums.

nodes.name: Juice WRLD
nodes.description: Chicago-area rapper whose melodic delivery and introspective lyrics reached a broad audience with Lucid Dreams.

nodes.name: XXXTentacion
nodes.description: Florida rapper who built a SoundCloud audience and broke through with Look at Me!.

nodes.name: Burning Spear
nodes.description: Jamaican singer Winston Rodney made the teachings of Marcus Garvey a recurring theme in his roots reggae recordings.

nodes.name: Culture
nodes.description: Jamaican vocal trio led by Joseph Hill, whose 1977 album Two Sevens Clash became a roots reggae landmark.

nodes.name: Pérez Prado
nodes.description: Cuban pianist, arranger and bandleader whose Mexican recordings, including Mambo No. 5, helped turn mambo into an international dance craze.

nodes.name: Culoe De Song
nodes.description: South African DJ and producer whose tracks for Black Coffee’s circle and the Innervisions label helped carry Afro house abroad.

nodes.name: Black Motion
nodes.description: South African house act known for bringing live percussion into its DJ performances and recordings.

nodes.name: Leftfield
nodes.description: British electronic music act formed by Neil Barnes and Paul Daley. Its 1990 single Not Forgotten helped establish progressive house.

nodes.name: The KLF
nodes.description: Electronic music duo of Bill Drummond and Jimmy Cauty. Their 1990 album Chill Out helped define ambient house.

nodes.name: Mixmaster Morris
nodes.description: British DJ and producer Morris Gould, who recorded as The Irresistible Force and became a figure in the chill-out scene.

nodes.name: Chris Liberator
nodes.description: London techno DJ and producer who helped found Stay Up Forever with the Liberator DJs.

nodes.name: D.A.V.E. The Drummer
nodes.description: British producer and DJ Henry Cullen, who worked with the Liberator DJs and founded Hydraulix.

nodes.name: The Geezer
nodes.description: London acid techno producer Guy McAffer, who released records on Stay Up Forever and founded the RAW label.

nodes.name: Fabio
nodes.description: London DJ who started in pirate radio and later championed liquid funk through radio, DJ sets and the Creative Source label.

nodes.name: Calibre
nodes.description: Belfast producer and DJ Dominick Martin, whose early drum and bass releases appeared on Fabio’s Creative Source label.

nodes.name: High Contrast
nodes.description: Drum and bass producer and DJ Lincoln Barrett, who made his recording debut on Hospital Records in 2001.

nodes.name: 100 gecs
nodes.description: Duo of Laura Les and Dylan Brady whose 2019 album 1000 gecs helped bring hyperpop to a wider audience.

nodes.name: Charli XCX
nodes.description: English singer and songwriter who began releasing music online and performing at London warehouse parties. She went on to work with PC Music founder A. G. Cook.

nodes.name: A. G. Cook
nodes.description: London-born producer who founded PC Music in 2013 and became a longtime collaborator of Charli XCX.

nodes.name: Anuel AA
nodes.description: Puerto Rican rapper whose early trap recordings and collaborations include “Esclava Remix” and “La Ocasión.”

nodes.name: Bryant Myers

period.estimateNote: The timeline uses the 2015 release of “Esclava” to anchor Myers’s early SoundCloud activity.

nodes.description: Puerto Rican rapper whose song “Esclava” spread through SoundCloud and went viral in Puerto Rico.

nodes.name: Jimmy Smith
nodes.description: Organist whose Blue Note sessions helped make the Hammond organ a mainstay of small-group jazz.

nodes.name: Lou Donaldson
nodes.description: Alto saxophonist whose blues-inflected playing helped shape hard bop and soul jazz.

nodes.name: Queensrÿche
nodes.description: American metal band whose concept album Operation: Mindcrime became an early progressive metal landmark.

nodes.name: Fates Warning
nodes.description: Progressive metal band that released its debut album Night on Bröcken in 1984 and helped shape the genre.

nodes.name: Dream Theater
nodes.description: Progressive metal band whose album Images and Words brought its intricate arrangements to a wider audience.

edges.note: Ranks Cassius’s “1999” among the great French touch tracks and describes its characteristic sound. Direct track/genre evidence.

AllMusic classifies the song as rocksteady/reggae; RBMA describes the 1968 “54-46” as Toots’s post-release hit during reggae’s emergence. Graph title “That’s My Number” is a variant of commonly listed “Was My Number”; verify entity/title normalization.
LOC calls it a soulful ode and an anthem of the Civil Rights Movement; supports both soul association and anthem stature.

The former identifies the album as foundational spiritual jazz; GRAMMY describes its role in accelerating spiritual-jazz exploration. Strong album/genre link; anthem is a reasonable canonical framing.
AllMusic lists Rap and Southern Rap/Dirty South styles for this release. Genre association is direct; anthem status is culturally plausible but this source alone does not establish it.
Describes the composition as bebop-style and recounts Gillespie calling it an “anthem to bebop.”
A defining and widely successful pop-punk anthem; Louder identifies Blink-182 as punk-pop and this track as their indelible anthem, while AllMusic classifies the song as pop punk.
Places Khan among qawwali’s most famous performers and specifically describes opening a 1985 WOMAD performance with “Allah Hoo,” in devotional qawwali context.

Pitchfork calls it an anthem of determination; the scholarly article examines its protest/Black Lives Matter role. Anthem status is strong. These sources do not directly classify the song as “conscious hip-hop”; keep genre confidence moderate or add a direct classification source.
Official artist site calls it widely regarded as the definitive punk anthem.
Identifies Burial’s *Untrue* as dubstep and singles “Archangel” out as an instant classic.
Places Daft Punk’s “Around the World” among French house/French touch exemplars.

SWR1 says Kraftwerk were previously called a Krautrock group, while “Autobahn” opened a new electronic-music chapter. This is a transitional work; the edge can stand as historical context, but “Krautrock anthem” overstates the track’s genre identity.
Sony confirms “Automatic” as her debut hit. Broad J-pop placement is defensible, but the sources checked do not directly call the track J-pop and its R&B/dance-pop character merits a note.
Describes it as a perfect pop-punk anthem and contextualizes its punk audience.
Identifies the Ronettes as a classic girl group and treats “Be My Baby” as their defining/signature recording.

KEXP identifies the single and calls Bauhaus a goth-rock pioneer; the scholarly article’s abstract specifically locates the song as gothic rock’s launching point/sine qua non. Academic full text was access-blocked, so KEXP is the opened full-text support.
Names “Birdland” as a Weather Report landmark and describes the group as fusion trailblazers.

AllMusic describes the album as solidifying jazz-rock fusion; LOC documents it as a new musical direction. Direct association is with the album; edge title/target should make clear it refers to the title track as well as album.

AllMusic identifies Pearl Jam as grunge frontrunners; Louder places “Black” on the breakthrough grunge-era *Ten* and calls it an enduring fan favorite. This supports context and stature, though the track’s anthem status is less explicit.
Track-focused history presents “Blind” as a foundational/birth moment for nu metal.
AllMusic describes the song as quickly becoming a punk-rock anthem.
AllMusic lists Big Beat/Funky Breaks styles; Mixmag ranks the track among the best big-beat tracks and identifies the Chemical Brothers as pioneers.

Official track tags include doom metal; the track-specific write-up links it to the doom scene; Louder credits Saint Vitus with helping birth doom. Sources establish genre importance, but explicit “anthem” language is less authoritative.

Song history describes it as a classic metal riff, a globally performed Priest staple and a major crowd-participation number; article explicitly places the video in heavy metal. Strong genre and anthem evidence.
Insomniac identifies *New Forms* as a drum & bass record and “Brown Paper Bag” as a representative hit; DJ Mag calls it a drum & bass classic and recounts its legacy.

AllMusic directly classifies the song as West Coast Rap/G-Funk/Gangsta Rap. This verifies genre; the opened source does not by itself establish “anthem” status, so medium is safer absent a track-focused cultural-history source.

Insomniac calls it a seminal, resonant early house recording and canonical Chicago-house history, but does not specifically label it deep house. RA page loaded without article text in the accessible view. Deep-house association is plausible but should remain moderate until a source explicitly links this recording to deep house.

AllMusic’s page could not be opened (403); its search metadata described the track as iconic to the synth-pop era but was not treated as checked evidence. Track and artist association are clear, but this batch did not establish the genre claim from accessible full text; retain medium at most and replace/augment the note with an accessible source.

PBS calls it Compay Segundo’s signature song and a classic son, explaining its son rhythm; EL PAÍS calls it Buena Vista Social Club’s great anthem and near-national emblem. Direct support for genre and iconic status.

João Gilberto’s July 1958 recording is described by Brazil’s Senate news agency as the formal birth of bossa nova; the claim reflects one common historical framing, with earlier precursors acknowledged.
A melodic dream-trance crossover that reached number two on the UK singles chart in 1996.
The foundation explicitly lists “Cross Road Blues” among enduring anthems of country blues; Duke identifies the recording as Robert Johnson Delta blues.

The official release verifies Khan’s recording under “Dam Mast Qalandar”; the opened sources establish the track identity, but not a track-specific qawwali classification or anthem claim. The composition has multiple performers/versions, so avoid attributing the song’s broader anthem status solely to Khan’s rendition.

The Guardian and AllMusic song/artist pages were not accessible in this check; the official label page confirms the album context but not the specific alternative-rock label. Pixies’ broader association is well established, but track-level genre and anthem claims need an accessible direct source.
Track-focused Kerrang article calls “Du Hast” Rammstein’s best-known tune and describes it as industrial metal. Direct genre and signature-song support.

Big Hit explicitly describes “Dynamite” as disco-pop; Korea.net identifies BTS as a K-pop group and the song as their first English-language single. Its K-pop context is valid, but the track’s immediate style is disco-pop; anthem evidence is primarily popularity/crossover, not genre-defining status.
Mozarteum verifies the work/date (1787), authorship, and that it is one of Mozart’s best-known pieces; Morgan describes it as exemplifying the Classical era. Strong.

Glass’s official page quotes Eno recalling Glass as “described as a minimalist,” while the scholarly excerpt says Glass rejected applying “minimalism” to much of his later stage work, including *Einstein*. It remains commonly situated in minimalism, but the composer disputed the label; confidence should be moderate with this caveat.

These opened sources establish the track/album and group but did not directly classify this track as jazz rap or document anthem status. The group's jazz-rap context does not alone prove this track’s subgenre. Keep medium pending a direct song-level source.

Official archive verifies the single and its chart success; AllMusic was access-blocked, so no opened source here directly classifies it as synth-pop. The genre fit is plausible, but the note should cite an accessible track-specific source and temper the anthem claim until then.
The work is widely popular within gagaku; this edge describes its canonical standing in the tradition, not a specific Reigakusha recording.

GRAMMY calls it a widely used protest anthem and says it cemented Public Enemy as a voice of hip-hop. Scholarly excerpt describes it as a political hip-hop anthem. Anthem and hip-hop claims are strong; the narrow “conscious hip-hop” genre label is not directly stated in the sources opened.
The 1998 E-Werk Remix established the track as a trance anthem. The original appeared on 45 RPM in 1994.

JazzDisco documents the 1961 Coleman double-quartet album and its two-part “Free Jazz” composition; AllMusic search metadata identifies the album style as Free Jazz, but its page was access-blocked. This is historically foundational to the genre, though relation points to the composition/title track rather than the album node.

Metal Archives identifies the Mayhem release with Black Metal Records; Apple confirms the track and release. These verify the artist/track scene context, but the opened sources do not establish “anthem” stature; confidence should remain medium until a specific history of the song’s genre role is cited.

Korea Herald describes “Gangnam Style” as the first K-pop song to achieve worldwide success and documents its global breakthrough; the Guardian interview complicates the label, noting Psy was Korean/pop but not mainstream K-pop at the time. It is a K-pop/global crossover landmark, but genre boundaries and “anthem” phrasing deserve that nuance.
Rock Hall explicitly describes “Gimme Shelter” as an anthem of youthful rebellion; AllMusic and ABKCO verify the Rolling Stones recording and *Let It Bleed* context.
A representative concert tango from Piazzolla’s nuevo tango repertoire.
An early Ellington orchestra standard. Its standing in the band’s repertoire supports the swing association.
Basie’s 1937 Decca recording was his orchestra’s signature theme and a landmark of Kansas City big-band swing.

The UCLA archive and Smithsonian support the Puente recording and iconic composition. The CSUEB analysis classifies the 1962 arrangement as cha-cha-chá, a Cuban dance form; “Latin jazz” is a broad career/context tag for Puente, not the most precise description of this recording. NPR and Smithsonian establish lasting fame, but the original Puente version is less clearly a Latin-jazz “anthem” than the later Santana Latin-rock version is a crossover standard. Keep cautiously at low-medium for the full edge, or refine target/version and anthem rationale.

Exact Air track and its *Moon Safari* context are supported. ABC describes it as a queer anthem; AllMusic frames it as the song that brought Air/French dance music to wider UK/US attention. Downtempo is a reasonable broad classification, though the anthem label has a specific cultural context rather than universal genre-canon evidence.

Official Charts verifies Skepta’s exact single. Contemporary Guardian coverage identifies it as grime and a defining 2015 track, describing its crowd response and anti-police refrain. Strong scene-anthem case; keep high.

Ahn Sook-sun is documented presenting the complete pansori work `Simcheongga`, a well-known tale. That validates artist/work/genre association, but the cited item describes a performance event, not a uniquely identified released track/master. A work’s canonical standing does not by itself establish this particular recording as a pansori anthem. Keep cautious pending exact recording evidence.
Already an audience favorite, the piece featured in Goodman’s landmark 1938 Carnegie Hall swing concert.

Official material verifies the track on *Nevermind*; HistoryLink documents its role as an anthem and grunge-scene breakthrough, while AllMusic identifies its grunge style and watershed status. Exact version, endpoint and canonical claim all hold.

Sources verify Deep Purple’s recording and hard-rock context; the Rock Hall essay emphasizes the riff’s embedded place in popular culture. Strong canonical claim and reasonable broad anthem label, but evidence is more direct for cultural recognition than for “anthem” wording.
Official catalog verifies the exact track and ensemble on *Kind of Blue*. AllMusic describes its modal approach as a blueprint for modal jazz. Genre-canonical status is clear; retain high.

Blue Note calls the tune indelible in the jazz canon and discusses its hard-bop groove; label catalog verifies the exact Silver release. Strong genre/canon evidence supports high, even if “anthem” is a shorthand.

Official label and chart records establish the Portishead recording; *Dummy* is firmly situated in trip-hop, with the track central to the album’s identity. The genre association is reliable, but checked material more clearly supports classic/representative track status than an explicit trip-hop anthem claim. Medium is appropriate.
Sources verify the Bee Gees recording and *Saturday Night Fever* context, document major cultural impact, and credit the film/song with helping bring disco into the mainstream. High is justified.

Disco developed from Black dance-music traditions including soul and funk, among other influences. A directed influence better communicates this multi-source history than strict derivation.
Funk’s breakbeats, production, and musical vocabulary influenced hip-hop; direction is funk → hip-hop, not hip-hop derived from funk alone.

Italo disco grew from Italian disco and Eurodisco contexts, but scholarship warns against conflating 1970s Italian disco with the fully electronic post-disco style of the 1980s. Keep the lineage and preserve that historical distinction.

Sources describe Hi-NRG as a faster electronic variation that developed from late disco. Keep the narrower genre as derived from disco while recognizing its later distinct club culture and production idiom.

Electro crystallized from early hip-hop culture, funk, and synthesizer/drum-machine technology; “Planet Rock” is a key example. Calling electro derived from hip-hop alone omits its hybrid formation; a fusion edge or a note naming the other inputs is more faithful.
Disco edits, disco DJ practice, soul, and drum machines all fed Chicago house. The descent is real but the current wording should avoid presenting disco as its sole origin.
